entries.snippet: Step-by-step keyboard manual for recording and editing audio in Audacity.
entries.text: accessible audio manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible media accessible audio recording and editing manual record, review, edit, save, and export audio in audacity. basic how-tos advanced how-tos command list basic how-tos create and save a new project what you will learn: complete create and save a new project independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: ctrl+n creates a project. ctrl+s saves it. open audacity and press ctrl+n. press ctrl+s before recording. choose a folder you can find again. enter a descriptive project name and confirm save. what should happen: the project name in the audacity window title. if that does not happen: use alt+f and choose save project. do not export yet; a project file and an audio file serve different purposes. practice: repeat create and save a new project with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. record and stop what you will learn: complete record and stop independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: r starts recording. space stops recording or playback. connect the microphone and reduce background noise. press r once and speak a short practice sentence. press space to stop. press ctrl+s to save the project. what should happen: recording feedback and a changing time position. if that does not happen: stop before trying again. check the selected input device and whether another application controls the microphone. practice: repeat record and stop with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. play and navigate what you will learn: complete play and navigate independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: space plays or stops. p pauses or resumes. home moves to the track start. end moves to the track end. press home. press space and listen from the beginning. press p to pause at a point you want to inspect. press p again to continue or space to stop. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: confirm that an audio track exists and the audacity window is active. practice: repeat play and navigate with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. advanced how-tos select and delete unwanted audio what you will learn: complete select and delete unwanted audio independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: shift+right arrow or shift+left arrow extends a selection in small steps. delete removes the confirmed selection. ctrl+z undoes. press ctrl+s to protect the project. move playback near the unwanted sound and stop. hold shift while using an arrow key to extend the selection. use audacity’s selection toolbar or screen-reader feedback to verify start and end times. press delete, then listen across the edit. press ctrl+z immediately if the wrong audio was removed. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: undo and create a smaller selection. never delete an unverified range. practice: repeat select and delete unwanted audio with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. record a second track what you will learn: complete record a second track independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard command: shift+r starts recording on a new track in current audacity versions. save the project and move to the intended start time. press shift+r. record the second part and press space to stop. use track navigation and solo or mute controls to review tracks separately. save again. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: undo the new recording and confirm audacity’s recording preference and active track. practice: repeat record a second track with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. export an mp3 or wav file what you will learn: complete export an mp3 or wav file independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: use alt+f to open file, then choose export audio. press ctrl+s to save the editable project. open file and choose export audio. choose mp3 for a smaller listening copy or wav for higher-quality uncompressed audio. select the destination and enter a new filename. review format settings and activate export. open the exported file and verify its duration and sound. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: keep the project open. check the destination, filename, format, and any error dialog. practice: repeat export an mp3 or wav file with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. apply an effect safely what you will learn: complete apply an effect safely independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: select audio, open the effect menu with alt+c in many audacity versions, and choose an effect by name. save a backup project. select only the audio that should change. open the effect menu and choose the effect. preview it when available. apply it, listen again, and use ctrl+z if the result is worse. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: cancel the dialog rather than accepting settings you do not understand. practice: repeat apply an effect safely with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. quick command list r: record shift+r: record a new track space: play or stop p: pause or resume home / end: start / end ctrl+s: save project ctrl+z: undo delete: remove selected audio return to manuals

entries.title: Accessible Job Search Screen Reader Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible Job Search Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: accessible job search screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual accessible job search screen reader manual keyboard-first employment skills independent self-study guide for finding and applying for work all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches an independent, accessible workflow for finding jobs, evaluating postings, preparing resumes, completing online applications, requesting application-process accommodations when needed, and interviewing with common digital tools. platforms: the main desktop examples use windows with jaws, nvda, or narrator, but the workflow also applies to voiceover and talkback. dedicated sections cover linkedin and indeed, while company career sites are treated as variable third-party systems. legal scope: the accommodation section provides general u.s. employment-access information and practical communication guidance, not individualized legal advice. how to use this manual build your resume and reusable application information before starting a live application. open every job posting in a separate tab or save the link so you can return to it while applying. read the entire job description before investing time in the application. keep a private application tracker with employer, role, date, link, status, contact, and next action. use headings, landmarks, form controls, and browser find rather than only tab through long pages. when an application is inaccessible, document the barrier and use the employer accommodation/contact route rather than repeatedly fighting the same control. never pay an employer or recruiter to apply, receive equipment, cash a check, buy gift cards, or release a job offer. before interviews, test the meeting platform, microphone, camera if used, screen reader, headphones, and any requested accommodation. table of contents part 1 - build a job-search workspace part 2 - prepare an accessible resume part 3 - resume file formats and uploads part 4 - read a job posting efficiently part 5 - evaluate qualifications and essential functions part 6 - search on linkedin with a screen reader part 7 - apply on linkedin part 8 - search and apply on indeed part 9 - company career sites and ats systems part 10 - online application forms part 11 - dropdowns, date pickers, autocomplete, and custom controls part 12 - resume parsing and re-entering work history part 13 - cover letters and application questions part 14 - assessments and timed tests part 15 - requesting an application accommodation part 16 - disability disclosure and interview boundaries part 17 - job-search scams part 18 - email and recruiter communication part 19 - interview scheduling part 20 - zoom, teams, and video interviews part 21 - interview preparation with a screen reader part 22 - after the interview part 23 - application tracking and follow-up part 24 - mobile job search part 25 - troubleshooting inaccessible applications part 26 - independent practice course part 27 - quick reference checklists part 28 - official resources part 1 - build a job-search workspace create a folder named job search with subfolders for resume, cover letters, applications, and interview notes. keep one master resume and create role-specific copies from it. keep a plain-text file with frequently requested information: employment dates, supervisor names, addresses, phone numbers, education dates, certifications, and references. keep a private application tracker. do not store social security numbers, passwords, full banking details, or identity documents in the tracker. use a professional email address that you check regularly. 1.1 create an application tracker what you will learn: track jobs so you know what you applied to and what comes next. before you begin: open excel, google sheets, or another accessible spreadsheet. exactly how to do it create columns for employer, job title, job id, location, date found, date applied, source/link, contact, status, follow-up date, and notes. enter one practice job. save the tracker in your job search folder. after every application, update the status immediately. what should happen: you can answer “what have i applied to?” without searching your email. if that does not happen: if a spreadsheet is cumbersome, use a simple word table or structured text list instead. practice: track three practice postings. part 2 - prepare an accessible resume use real word headings for major sections such as summary, skills, experience, and education. use simple one-column reading order. prefer standard fonts and ordinary text over text boxes, floating shapes, icons, charts, or infographic skill bars. use actual bullet lists for achievements. write employer, job title, dates, and accomplishments as text that reads logically linearly. do not use color alone to communicate meaning. use meaningful link text for linkedin/portfolio links. run word accessibility checker before exporting. 2.1 check resume reading order what you will learn: make sure the resume reads correctly from top to bottom. before you begin: open the resume in word. exactly how to do it press ctrl+home. use ctrl+down arrow or your screen reader reading commands to move through the document. listen for each section in the intended order. use the screen reader heading list to verify section headings. use tab to identify hyperlinks and confirm their text is meaningful. run review > check accessibility and fix relevant issues. what should happen: the resume makes sense without visual position cues. if that does not happen: if information is announced out of order, remove text boxes/columns and rebuild that area in normal paragraphs or a simple table. practice: read your resume from top to bottom without using sighted layout cues. part 3 - resume file formats and uploads task how docx usually best when the employer explicitly requests word or when an ats parses word documents well. pdf useful when you want layout preserved; export from an accessible source and verify the pdf has real selectable/tagged text. plain text useful as a fallback for copy/paste fields; not usually the primary polished resume. image/scanned pdf avoid. it may be unreadable and difficult for ats/screen readers. 3.1 upload a resume reliably what you will learn: use a file-upload control without losing your place. before you begin: keep the resume in a known folder with a clear filename. exactly how to do it focus the upload resume or choose file button. press enter or space. in the file chooser, press ctrl+l if needed to type the folder path, or use the normal file explorer navigation. find the resume filename. press enter. return to the application and listen for the uploaded filename or success message. if the site parsed your resume into fields, review every parsed field before submission. what should happen: the correct filename is attached and the application recognizes it. if that does not happen: if the filename is not announced, inspect nearby status text or re-focus the upload control. do not assume the upload worked. practice: upload a disposable resume copy to a safe form or practice environment. part 4 - read a job posting efficiently 4.1 build a posting summary what you will learn: extract the facts you need before applying. before you begin: open the job posting. exactly how to do it use h or your screen reader heading-navigation command to find the job title and major sections. use browser find (ctrl+f) for terms such as salary, location, remote, qualifications, required, preferred, schedule, travel, clearance, license, benefits, and accommodation. read the entire responsibilities and qualifications sections. write down the job id/requisition number. copy the posting link into your tracker. note the closing date if one is listed. what should happen: you can summarize the job without rereading the entire page. if that does not happen: if headings are poor, use browser find and landmarks/form controls ins

entries.title: Adobe Acrobat and Accessible PDF Screen Reader Manual
entries.course: Adobe Acrobat and Accessible PDF Screen Reader
entries.snippet: Adobe Acrobat and Accessible PDF Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: adobe acrobat and accessible pdf screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual adobe acrobat and accessible pdf screen reader manual reading, navigating, creating, and checking pdfs independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual adobe acrobat reader accessibility features purpose: this manual teaches how to read, navigate, complete, save, print, and evaluate pdfs with a screen reader, and how to recognize when a pdf needs ocr or accessibility remediation. reader versus acrobat pro: adobe acrobat reader is primarily for reading, forms, comments, and everyday pdf use. acrobat pro adds authoring and remediation tools such as accessibility checking, automatic tagging, reading order, and advanced tag repair. reference platform: main procedures focus on current acrobat/acrobat reader on windows. separate sections cover macos/voiceover and braille. how to use this manual a screen reader can only read what the pdf exposes as text and structure. a tagged pdf is usually easier to navigate than an untagged pdf. an image-only scanned pdf may contain no readable text until ocr is performed. use ctrl+f for text search, ctrl+0/1/2/3/4/5 for common view/reflow commands as supported, and ctrl+shift+5 for current-document reading settings. do not confuse adobe read out loud with your screen reader; read out loud is adobe text-to-speech, not a substitute for accessible tagging. for long untagged pdfs, reader may take time to analyze reading order. when a pdf reads badly, test whether the problem is the document before changing global screen-reader settings. table of contents part 1 - what a pdf is part 2 - acrobat reader vs acrobat pro part 3 - open a pdf and learn the window part 4 - page navigation part 5 - text reading and selection part 6 - search part 7 - links and bookmarks part 8 - forms part 9 - comments and annotations part 10 - saving, printing, and exporting part 11 - tagged vs untagged pdfs part 12 - scanned/image-only pdfs and ocr part 13 - reading order and document structure part 14 - reflow and reading settings part 15 - accessibility setup assistant part 16 - read out loud part 17 - creating and checking accessible pdfs in acrobat pro part 18 - fixing reading order in acrobat pro part 19 - tables, lists, headings, language, and alt text part 20 - narrator part 21 - nvda part 22 - jaws part 23 - voiceover part 24 - braille displays part 25 - pdf security and signatures part 26 - troubleshooting part 27 - independent practice course part 28 - quick reference part 29 - official adobe resources part 1 - what a pdf is pdf means portable document format. a pdf can preserve page appearance, but visual appearance does not guarantee accessibility. text pdf: contains selectable/extractable text. tagged pdf: contains a logical structure tree identifying headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, figures, links, and reading order. untagged pdf: may contain real text but little or no structural information. scanned/image-only pdf: may be only pictures of pages until ocr adds a text layer. form pdf: can contain interactive text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, buttons, and signatures. part 2 - acrobat reader vs acrobat pro product typical accessibility role acrobat reader read pdfs, use forms, comments, accessibility preferences, read out loud, save/print common pdfs. acrobat pro includes reader functions plus accessibility checking, tagging/remediation, reading order, ocr and advanced document repair. rule of thumb: if you only need to consume a pdf, reader may be enough. if you must repair or certify pdf accessibility, acrobat pro is normally required. part 3 - open a pdf and learn the window 3.1 open a local pdf what you will learn: open a known file in acrobat/reader. before you begin: know the pdf location. exactly how to do it press ctrl+o. navigate the windows open dialog to the pdf. press enter. wait for the document to load. press tab and shift+tab slowly to identify toolbar and document controls. use your screen reader reading command in the document area. what should happen: the pdf opens and accessible content is exposed to the screen reader. if that does not happen: if the screen reader announces only image, blank, or very little content, the pdf may be scanned or poorly structured. practice: open one known accessible pdf. browser pdfs: pdfs may open in chrome or edge instead of acrobat. download/open the file in acrobat when you need adobe-specific accessibility preferences or pro remediation tools. part 4 - page navigation task command next page page down or ctrl+page down depending view/context previous page page up or ctrl+page up depending view/context first page home/ctrl+home depending focus last page end/ctrl+end depending focus go to page use page-number field or navigation control; ctrl+shift+n is commonly used in acrobat for go to page 4.1 go to a specific page what you will learn: reach a page without reading every page before it. before you begin: open a multi-page pdf. exactly how to do it move to the page-number control in the toolbar, or invoke the go to page command available in your acrobat version. type the page number. press enter. use the screen reader to verify the page heading/text. what should happen: the requested page becomes active. if that does not happen: if the printed page number differs from the pdf page index, use bookmarks/headings/search for better orientation. practice: jump to three different pages. part 5 - text reading and selection 5.1 read pdf text with your screen reader what you will learn: read text using the screen reader rather than acrobat tts. before you begin: the pdf exposes selectable text. exactly how to do it move focus into the document pane. use your screen reader say all/read commands. use line, word, heading, link, and table commands when the pdf is tagged. stop speech with the screen reader stop-speech command when needed. what should happen: the screen reader follows the pdf text and document structure. if that does not happen: if reading order jumps unpredictably, the pdf may be untagged or incorrectly tagged. practice: read one page continuously, then navigate by structure. 5.2 select and copy text what you will learn: copy a short accessible passage. before you begin: use a pdf that allows copying. exactly how to do it move the screen reader/caret to the desired text. select with shift plus navigation keys or the screen reader selection mechanism. press ctrl+c. paste into a harmless text editor with ctrl+v to confirm. what should happen: the selected text copies in a sensible order. if that does not happen: if copied text is scrambled or unavailable, the pdf may use inaccessible encoding, permissions, or image-only pages. practice: copy one sentence. part 6 - search 6.1 find text what you will learn: locate a word in a long pdf. before you begin: pdf contains searchable text. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f. type a word or phrase. press enter. use the find next/previous controls or enter/shift+enter as available. press escape when finished. what should happen: acrobat moves to matching text. if that does not happen: if a visible word cannot be found, the page may be image-only or text extraction may be broken. practice: search for three terms. part 7 - links and bookmarks 7.1 use pdf bookmarks what you will learn: navigate a structured long document. before you begin: the pdf contains bookmarks. exactly how to do it open the bookmarks side panel with the acrobat navigation-pane controls. use arrow keys through bookmarks. press enter on the desired bookmark. return to the document pane and read from the new location. what should happen: the pdf jumps to the bookmarked section. if that does not happen: if no bookmarks exist, use headings/search/page navigation. practice: navigate to three bookmarks. 7.2 activate a link what you will learn: open a link deliberately. before you begin: focus a link in the pdf. e

entries.title: AI Fundamentals and Responsible Use Manual
entries.snippet: Comprehensive keyboard-first AI fundamentals and responsible-use manual for blind and low-vision learners.
entries.text: ai fundamentals and responsible use manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible artificial intelligence foundations ai fundamentals and responsible use manual independent self-study guide for responsible, accessible ai use. all manuals table of contents website practice procedures ai lessons purpose: this manual explains artificial intelligence from the beginning and teaches how to use ai tools responsibly. it assumes no prior technical knowledge. who this is for: students, employees, job seekers, independent learners, screen-reader and braille users, and anyone who wants to understand ai before relying on it. core principle: ai can be useful without being authoritative. treat ai output as assistance that may require verification, not as automatic truth. responsible-use foundation: the guide reflects current responsible-ai principles from nist and unesco, including risk management, transparency, fairness, privacy, human oversight, and awareness of generative-ai-specific risks. how to use this manual read parts 1 through 8 before using ai for important work; they establish the concepts needed to judge ai output. practice with low-risk tasks first, such as brainstorming, rewriting your own text, or generating study questions. do not paste confidential, private, regulated, or employer/client data into an ai system unless the relevant policy and service terms permit it. verify important factual claims using trustworthy independent sources. keep the human decision-maker responsible for important decisions. use ai to support accessibility and independence, but check outputs that describe images, documents, people, or environments. when an ai tool cannot provide sources, treat precise factual claims with extra caution. keep records of significant ai use when school, workplace, legal, or organizational policy requires disclosure. table of contents part 1 - what artificial intelligence is part 2 - ai, machine learning, deep learning, and generative ai part 3 - how generative ai produces an answer part 4 - large language models and tokens part 5 - training data, context, and knowledge limits part 6 - what ai is good at part 7 - what ai is not good at part 8 - hallucinations and confident errors part 9 - prompting fundamentals part 10 - better prompt structure part 11 - follow-up questions and iteration part 12 - sources, search, and grounding part 13 - verification and fact-checking part 14 - privacy and sensitive information part 15 - security and prompt injection part 16 - bias, fairness, and representation part 17 - copyright, attribution, and ownership part 18 - education and academic integrity part 19 - workplace and professional use part 20 - high-stakes decisions part 21 - accessibility and assistive technology part 22 - images, audio, video, and deepfakes part 23 - ai agents and automated actions part 24 - responsible human oversight part 25 - a practical responsible-use framework part 26 - troubleshooting poor ai results part 27 - practice course part 28 - quick reference checklists part 29 - official resources part 1 - what artificial intelligence is artificial intelligence is a broad term for computer systems designed to perform tasks that people associate with intelligent behavior, such as recognizing patterns, understanding language, generating content, making predictions, recommending actions, or controlling devices. ai is not one single technology. an ai system may be narrow and specialized, such as spam detection or speech recognition. an ai system may generate new content, such as text, images, audio, video, or code. an ai system may recommend or rank options without generating visible content. ai output is produced by a system, not by an independent human expert reviewing your situation. important distinction: a system can produce a fluent answer without having human experience, personal awareness, or guaranteed understanding of the real-world situation. part 2 - ai, machine learning, deep learning, and generative ai topic what to remember artificial intelligence (ai) the broad field of systems that perform tasks associated with intelligent behavior. machine learning (ml) a way of building systems that learn patterns from data rather than relying only on hand-written rules. deep learning machine learning using multi-layer neural networks; widely used in speech, vision, and modern generative systems. generative ai ai that creates new content such as text, images, audio, video, or code. large language model (llm) a generative model trained to work with language and related symbolic information. relationship: generative ai is part of ai. many current generative systems use deep-learning methods, but not every ai system is generative. part 3 - how generative ai produces an answer a generative model receives your input, combines it with the conversation/context and system instructions, and predicts a useful continuation. for language models, this involves predicting sequences of tokens. the answer is generated at request time; it is not normally retrieved as one complete prewritten paragraph. generation is influenced by the prompt, prior conversation, system instructions, model design, and available tools/data. a fluent answer can contain invented details because plausible language is not the same as verified truth. different prompts can lead to different answers to the same underlying question. mental model: think of generative ai as a powerful pattern-and-language engine with reasoning capabilities that still needs verification, not as an infallible encyclopedia. part 4 - large language models and tokens large language models process text in smaller units called tokens. a token can be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or another unit. long conversations consume context space. the model may pay less attention to older details when a conversation becomes very long. exact token counts depend on the model and tokenizer. giving clear, relevant context is usually more useful than giving large amounts of unrelated text. practical lesson: if an ai starts forgetting instructions in a long conversation, restate the key requirements or begin a clean conversation with a concise summary. part 5 - training data, context, and knowledge limits models learn statistical patterns during training. at use time, a model may also receive current context, uploaded files, retrieved information, or web/search results if the product supports those tools. training data is not the same thing as a live database. a model may not know that a fact has changed unless it has current retrieval/search access. a model may mix accurate information with outdated or incorrect information. an answer about current laws, prices, schedules, public figures, software versions, or news should be verified with current sources. uploaded documents and connected data can improve relevance but increase privacy responsibility. current information rule: for time-sensitive questions, ask the ai to verify with current sources when the product can browse or search. part 6 - what ai is good at brainstorming ideas and alternatives. explaining a concept at different reading levels. summarizing text you provide. rewriting your own material for clarity, tone, or structure. generating practice questions or study aids. creating outlines, checklists, templates, and first drafts. classifying or organizing information with human review. translating or simplifying material, with verification for important use. helping with code, formulas, and troubleshooting when results are tested. accessibility support such as describing visual structure or converting information into a more usable format. best use pattern: ai is often strongest when the user can evaluate the result or verify it independently. part 7 - what ai is not good at guaranteeing that a factual statement is true. knowing unstated facts about a person, event, image, or organization. replacing professional judgment in hi

entries.snippet: Android TalkBack Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: android talkback manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual android talkback manual touch gestures, navigation, typing, and apps independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual google android accessibility help - talkback purpose: this manual teaches android with talkback from the beginning. it explains physical orientation, touch exploration, navigation, typing, system gestures, web browsing, talkback settings, braille input/output, external keyboards, security, troubleshooting, and independent practice. device differences: android phones and tablets vary by manufacturer. pixel, samsung galaxy, motorola, oneplus, and other devices may place buttons differently or rename settings. the talkback concepts and core gestures are consistent, but exact menus can differ. current reference: the guide is aligned with current android accessibility help, including android 16-era talkback features and talkback 16.2 keyboard/braille changes. how to use this manual work through the first gesture sections slowly. talkback changes how ordinary touch works. touching an item normally speaks it; activating it usually requires a double-tap. one-finger swipes generally move talkback focus. two-finger gestures generally scroll or perform system navigation when gesture navigation is in use. use the built-in talkback tutorial and practice area whenever a gesture feels unreliable. on devices that support multi-finger gestures, a three-finger tap opens the talkback menu. reading controls change what an up/down swipe navigates: characters, words, headings, controls, and more. braille support is built into talkback. brailleback is not required for current supported braille displays. when typing with the talkback braille keyboard, normal talkback gestures are temporarily replaced by braille-keyboard gestures. never change several talkback settings at once while learning. change one setting, test it, and keep or reverse it. table of contents part 1 - what talkback is part 2 - physical orientation and android device types part 3 - turn talkback on and off part 4 - talkback tutorial and practice part 5 - explore by touch part 6 - core one-finger navigation part 7 - activate, long-press, and scroll part 8 - home, back, overview, notifications, and quick settings part 9 - talkback menu and reading controls part 10 - home screen and app drawer part 11 - notifications part 12 - quick settings part 13 - text entry with gboard part 14 - text editing and selection part 15 - voice typing and google assistant part 16 - chrome and web navigation part 17 - messages and email part 18 - phone and video calls part 19 - talkback settings and speech part 20 - hide screen and privacy features part 21 - talkback braille keyboard part 22 - refreshable braille displays part 23 - external keyboard and enhanced keymap part 24 - files, sharing, and downloads part 25 - device security and privacy part 26 - manufacturer differences part 27 - troubleshooting part 28 - independent practice course part 29 - quick reference gestures part 30 - official google resources part 1 - what talkback is talkback is android's built-in screen reader. it speaks or displays in braille what is focused, describes controls and alerts, and changes the touch interface so a blind or low-vision user can navigate independently. focus: the item talkback is currently describing. explore by touch: drag one finger around the screen and talkback speaks what is under the finger. swipe navigation: move focus in a predictable sequence without needing to know where items are visually. activation: after focusing an item, double-tap anywhere with one finger to activate it. reading controls: change the navigation unit used by up/down swipes. talkback menu: quick access to settings, voice commands, screen search, hide/show screen, and context actions. braille: talkback supports both an onscreen braille keyboard and connected refreshable braille displays. part 2 - physical orientation and android device types important: there is no single physical android layout. always identify your exact device model before memorizing button locations. most modern phones have a flat touchscreen on the front, one or more cameras near the top, and physical side buttons. common side buttons include power/side key and volume up/down. their side and vertical order vary by manufacturer. usb-c is the standard charging/data connector on most current android phones and tablets and is usually on the bottom edge. some tablets place usb-c on a side edge depending on orientation. some devices use on-screen gesture navigation; others use a three-button navigation bar with back, home, and overview/recents. foldable phones may have multiple displays and hinge-dependent layouts. 2.1 identify your device before learning gestures what you will learn: create a reliable physical map of your own phone/tablet. before you begin: have the device powered on and safely held. exactly how to do it find the screen: the large smooth glass surface on the front. find the power/side key and press it briefly once to hear whether the screen locks/wakes. find volume up and volume down by pressing each once and listening for the volume change. locate the charging port by touch without inserting a cable blindly at an angle. ask settings > about phone/tablet for the exact manufacturer and model name if you do not know it. write down the exact model and button layout in your own notes. what should happen: you have a model-specific physical map instead of relying on generic assumptions. if that does not happen: if you cannot identify a control safely, use the manufacturer's official hardware guide for that exact model. practice: locate each physical control three times with the screen off. part 3 - turn talkback on and off 3.1 turn talkback on in settings what you will learn: enable talkback using the standard android settings path. before you begin: the device is already set up and you can access settings. exactly how to do it open settings. open accessibility. open talkback. turn use talkback on. confirm the permission/confirmation prompt. listen to talkback begin speaking. what should happen: talkback starts and touch behavior changes. if that does not happen: menu names vary by manufacturer. use settings search for talkback if necessary. practice: turn talkback on and enter the tutorial. 3.2 configure the talkback shortcut what you will learn: make it possible to toggle talkback without navigating settings. before you begin: talkback is on. exactly how to do it open settings > accessibility > talkback. open talkback shortcut. turn the shortcut on. follow the device-specific instructions for the offered shortcut method. test the shortcut once to turn talkback off, then use it again to turn talkback on. what should happen: you can toggle talkback using the configured accessibility shortcut. if that does not happen: the shortcut varies by device and android version. do not assume one universal button combination. practice: toggle talkback off and back on without opening settings. 3.3 use google assistant to toggle talkback what you will learn: use voice control when assistant is already configured. before you begin: google assistant/gemini voice activation is available on the device. exactly how to do it say hey google. say turn on talkback or turn off talkback. wait for the change to complete. what should happen: talkback changes state by voice command. if that does not happen: if assistant is not configured, use settings or the accessibility shortcut instead. practice: use voice to turn talkback on once. android 16 keyboard option: google documents an android 16 external-keyboard shortcut for talkback using the action key + alt + t. the action key depends on the keyboard, such as windows key on a windows keyboard or command on a mac keyboard. part 4 - talkback tutorial and practice 4.1 open tutorial and help what you will l

entries.text: bard mobile manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual bard mobile manual iphone and ipad with voiceover; android with talkback independent self-study guide for nls patrons all manuals table of contents start of manual national library service: bard and bard mobile purpose: this manual teaches bard mobile from the beginning. it covers finding, downloading, managing, and reading nls audio and braille titles, with separate voiceover and talkback instructions where the platforms differ. current reference: the manual uses the current nls bard mobile ios guide and the current android 2.1.1 guide. nls app screens and available features can change, so the built-in bard mobile user guide remains the final authority for a particular app version. who can use bard mobile: bard mobile is for eligible nls patrons with an established bard account. new bard users must create/change their initial password through the bard website before signing into bard mobile. how to use this manual learn the four main bard mobile areas first: bookshelf, get books, settings, and now reading. download a title before expecting it to appear in bookshelf or play offline. opening a downloaded title moves you to now reading. audio and braille titles have different now reading controls. voiceover users can use a two-finger double tap as a fast play/stop command once bard mobile is the active media app. talkback users can also use a two-finger double tap for play/stop when bard mobile is the most recently playing audio app. use the navigation screen or jump by controls for chapters, sections, pages, bookmarks, and other navigation points when the title provides them. deleting a downloaded title removes the local copy; you can normally download it again from bard later. downloads require an internet connection. once a title is fully downloaded, reading normally works offline. braille books require a refreshable braille display for practical reading in bard mobile. table of contents part 1 - what bard and bard mobile are part 2 - get a bard account and first password part 3 - install and sign in part 4 - learn the four main tabs part 5 - bookshelf part 6 - get books part 7 - search for a title part 8 - wish list, recently added, popular, magazines, and previous downloads part 9 - download a title part 10 - open and read a downloaded title part 11 - now reading for audio part 12 - play, stop, rewind, and fast forward part 13 - jump by chapter, section, page, or bookmark part 14 - navigation screen part 15 - sleep timer part 16 - bookmarks part 17 - speed, tone, and reading position part 18 - recently read part 19 - delete and re-download titles part 20 - audio settings and background playback part 21 - cellular downloads and storage part 22 - reading braille titles part 23 - refreshable braille displays part 24 - braille reflow and autoscroll part 25 - iphone/ipad with voiceover part 26 - android with talkback part 27 - bluetooth, airplay, and external audio part 28 - siri and device media controls part 29 - offline reading and travel part 30 - privacy and account safety part 31 - troubleshooting part 32 - independent practice course part 33 - quick reference part 34 - official nls resources part 1 - what bard and bard mobile are bard stands for braille and audio reading download. it is the national library service for the blind and print disabled (nls) download service. bard mobile is the mobile app for downloading and reading bard audio and braille material on supported phones and tablets. audio books and magazines: narrated digital talking books. braille books and magazines: electronic braille titles intended for a refreshable braille display. bookshelf: titles already downloaded to the device. get books: search and browse bard for material to download. settings: playback, braille/display, account, and accessibility-related settings. now reading: controls for the currently opened audio or braille title. part 2 - get a bard account and first password 2.1 complete the first-time bard password step what you will learn: understand why a new account may not work in bard mobile immediately. before you begin: you must already be an eligible nls patron or have submitted the bard application. exactly how to do it open the email from your nls network library containing bard login information. activate the password-creation or temporary-login link. use a web browser to create the permanent password according to the rules on the page. confirm the password and submit. complete the bard reading pledge when required. write/store the bard login information securely in an accessible password manager if you use one. only after this web step, open bard mobile and sign in. what should happen: the bard website accepts the permanent password and your account is ready for bard mobile. if that does not happen: if the temporary password or setup link has expired, contact your network library instead of repeatedly guessing passwords. practice: explain the difference between an nls library account and a bard login. part 3 - install and sign in 3.1 install bard mobile on iphone/ipad what you will learn: install the official nls app from apple's app store. before you begin: use your own apple id/device. exactly how to do it open the app store. use search and type bard mobile. find the app published for the national library service / library of congress. activate get/download. after installation, open bard mobile. enter the bard username/email and permanent password. activate sign in. what should happen: the app opens to its main interface and presents the bard mobile tabs. if that does not happen: if sign-in fails, verify that you completed the first-time password step on the bard website and that the credentials are typed exactly. practice: install/open the app and identify the first screen. 3.2 install bard mobile on android what you will learn: install the official bard mobile app from google play. before you begin: use your own android device and google account. exactly how to do it open google play store. search for bard mobile. choose the official nls/library of congress application. activate install. open the app after installation. enter the bard account credentials. activate sign in. what should happen: bard mobile opens under your bard account. if that does not happen: if android warns about an old incompatible app or the wrong publisher, do not install it; return to the official play store result. practice: open the app and identify bookshelf. part 4 - learn the four main tabs tab purpose bookshelf downloaded audio books/magazines, braille books/magazines, help/user guide, and local organization. get books search, wish list, recently added, most popular, browse magazines, previous downloads, and search music where available. settings audio settings, braille and display settings, user/account settings, and accessibility/device settings depending on platform. now reading player/reader for the currently opened title. iphone/ipad orientation: the four-tab bar is at the bottom of the screen from left to right: bookshelf, get books, settings, now reading. android orientation: the current android guide places the tab bar near the top, below the action bar. device navigation controls at the bottom belong to android, not bard mobile. 4.1 move through the main tabs what you will learn: know where you are before choosing a command. before you begin: bard mobile is signed in. exactly how to do it move screen-reader focus to the tab bar. focus bookshelf and listen for selected/not selected state. move to get books and activate it. move to settings and activate it. move to now reading. if no book is open, expect it to be unavailable or to report that no book is selected. return to bookshelf. what should happen: you can identify every major app area. if that does not happen: if your tab position differs from this manual, read the built-in user guide because app layout can

entries.text: brailleblaster manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible technology manual brailleblaster accessible manual a keyboard-first guide for blind and low-vision learners using jaws. all manuals ten brailleblaster lessons my progress purpose and setup this manual supports independent practice with brailleblaster on windows. use the exact software version, device model, account permissions, and workplace policy available to you. commands and labels can change after updates. start jaws before opening the application or connecting a braille device. use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focus, and insert+1 for keyboard help. practice with fictional, public, instructor-provided, or redacted information only. never submit passwords, recovery codes, government identifiers, protected books, or private workplace data. save a backup before changing, deleting, converting, or remediating a file. basic and advanced how-tos open a source and save an editable project keyboard commands: ctrl+o opens a file. ctrl+s saves. ctrl+shift+s opens save as. open brailleblaster and press ctrl+o. select a practice docx, html, txt, or supported source file. confirm the print and braille views contain the expected text. press ctrl+shift+s and save an editable bbz project. close and reopen the bbz to confirm it works. if that does not happen: keep the source unchanged and record the import error, file type, and brailleblaster version. navigate and apply document structure keyboard commands: ctrl+home moves to the beginning, ctrl+end to the end, and ctrl+g opens go to page. work in the print view. move to a real section heading in the source. select only the heading text. use the styles menu to apply the correct heading style. review the corresponding braille view and repeat for lists and indented material. save the bbz project. if that does not happen: undo the style and confirm the selection does not include adjacent body text. insert and verify a page break keyboard command: ctrl+enter inserts a page break after the cursor when text follows it. save the project. place the cursor immediately before the text that should begin the new braille page. press ctrl+enter. check the braille view and page numbers on both sides of the break. undo if the break divides a heading from its following text. if that does not happen: confirm text exists after the cursor and use edit, page break. enter six-key braille keyboard command: alt+x toggles six key mode. f, d, s represent dots 1, 2, 3; j, k, l represent dots 4, 5, 6. save and place the cursor in print view. press alt+x and confirm six key mode. chord fds and jkl combinations to enter a short braille sample. compare print view and braille view. press alt+x again to leave six key mode. if that does not happen: some keyboards cannot register the required simultaneous keys; use a compatible keyboard or the menu. correct one translation and export brf keyboard command: ctrl+t opens correct braille translation for selected print text. proofread the source and braille views before making a correction. select only the incorrectly translated word or character in print view. press ctrl+t, enter the intended braille in the braille field, and confirm. recheck surrounding text and save the bbz. use the file menu to save or export a separate brf. open the brf on a braille display and verify headings, page numbers, breaks, and final lines. if that does not happen: keep the bbz and source copies; do not overwrite the editable project with the exported file. ten-lesson learning path lesson 1: interface, open, and save a bbz project — create a project log describing the interface and saved bbz file. lesson 2: navigate source and braille views — submit a navigation reference for the project views. lesson 3: apply headings and structure — structure a short workplace policy with two heading levels. lesson 4: create lists and indented material — format one bulleted and one numbered list. lesson 5: format simple tables — format a simple three-column workplace schedule. lesson 6: page numbers, running heads, and breaks — prepare a two-page practice document with verified numbering. lesson 7: styles, emphasis, and special text — correct inconsistent styles in an instructor-provided sample. lesson 8: math, graphics, and transcriber notes — create a decision log for three special-content examples. lesson 9: proofread, validate, and export brf — submit the final bbz or brf plus a proofreading checklist. lesson 10: final workplace transcription project — produce a complete braille-ready workplace procedure. accessible working routine confirm the window, document, device, or webpage title. identify keyboard focus before typing or activating a control. navigate by real structure—headings, lists, fields, tables, or menus—when available. review the result with jaws or a braille display from beginning to end. verify the destination and filename before saving, uploading, sharing, or deleting. save the requested practice file locally with the exact filename given in the lesson. assignment uploads are currently paused. important: these course controls complement, and do not replace, browser, operating-system, screen-reader, braille-display, or other assistive-technology settings. official references use these primary sources when a label or command differs from the lesson: aph brailleblaster brailleblaster documentation start brailleblaster lesson 1 return to manuals basic and advanced step-by-step procedures these procedures make the manual usable on its own. the separate lessons provide assignments and progress tracking when you want a course experience. basic 1: interface, open, and save a bbz project basic 2: navigate source and braille views basic 3: apply headings and structure basic 4: create lists and indented material basic 5: format simple tables advanced 6: page numbers, running heads, and breaks advanced 7: styles, emphasis, and special text advanced 8: math, graphics, and transcriber notes advanced 9: proofread, validate, and export brf advanced 10: final workplace transcription project basic procedure original practice document. save a separate working copy before changing structure or formatting. exactly how to do it open brailleblaster and identify the text, braille, and style areas. use file, open to open an instructor-provided accessible source. navigate by heading or line with jaws. use save as and preserve the original source. save the working project as brailleblaster-lesson-1.bbz. close and reopen the bbz project. jaws and keyboard tip: use insert+t to confirm the window title, insert+tab to identify focus, and insert+1 for keyboard help. commands can vary by software version entries.text: braillenote touch plus manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual braillenote touch plus manual braille-first android productivity independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches the braillenote touch plus from the beginning. it assumes no prior experience and provides physical orientation, exact braille-keyboard commands, expected speech/braille feedback, troubleshooting, practice, and independence checks. current reference: humanware's current support page lists braillenote touch plus user guide version 6. the command model in this guide follows humanware's current keysoft documentation and current support materials. important product note: the braillenote touch plus is an android-based braille notetaker with humanware's keysoft accessibility layer. it can also work as a braille display for a computer or mobile device through braille terminal. how to use this manual first learn the physical controls and keysoft navigation pattern before using email, web, or third-party apps. main menu: home button or space with dots 1-2-3-4-5-6. next item: next thumb key or space. previous item: previous thumb key or backspace. activate selected item: enter (dot 8) or a cursor-routing key. back/exit current screen: back button or space with e. contextual help: space with h. context menu: space with m or press and hold recent apps. braille panning: left and right thumb keys. use first-letter navigation in lists and menus whenever keysoft supports it. do not change android accessibility settings casually; keysoft is the accessibility layer that makes the touch plus usable. before connecting the touch plus as an external braille display, first pair/connect it, then configure the host screen reader, then test braille output, input, and routing. table of contents part 1 - what the braillenote touch plus is part 2 - physical orientation part 3 - power, charging, locking, and unlocking part 4 - braille keyboard and thumb keys part 5 - main menu and general navigation part 6 - contextual help and context menu part 7 - speech, braille, and visual display part 8 - notification shade and android settings part 9 - keyword word processor part 10 - keyfiles file manager part 11 - keymail and email part 12 - google chrome and web navigation part 13 - easyreader plus part 14 - keylist, keyplan, and keycalc part 15 - sd cards, usb drives, and external storage part 16 - wi-fi and bluetooth part 17 - braille terminal part 18 - connect to iphone/ipad part 19 - connect to windows with jaws/nvda/narrator part 20 - connect to mac and android part 21 - running apps and multitasking part 22 - google play and third-party apps part 23 - updates and system information part 24 - security, privacy, and backups part 25 - troubleshooting part 26 - independent practice course part 27 - quick reference part 28 - official humanware resources part 1 - what the braillenote touch plus is the braillenote touch plus combines a touchscreen android tablet, keysoft applications, speech, a 32-cell refreshable braille display, and a removable physical braille-keyboard cover. keysoft main menu: the primary accessible home screen. keyword: word processing. keymail: email. keylist: contacts. keyplan: calendar/planner. keyfiles: file manager. easyreader plus: accessible book-reading app. google chrome: web browser. braille terminal: turns the touch plus into an external braille display for another device. all applications: access to installed android and google play apps. part 2 - physical orientation 2.1 top face place the device flat with the touchscreen and braille display facing up and the seven front-edge buttons closest to you. the touchscreen occupies the upper portion of the top face. directly below the touchscreen is the 32-cell refreshable braille display. above each braille cell is a cursor-routing key. pressing a routing key moves the cursor or activates an item depending on context. internal stereo speakers are positioned to the left and right of the braille cells. an internal microphone is located to the right of the braille display, below the right speaker. the removable braille keyboard cover sits over the touchscreen when attached and provides perkins-style braille input. 2.2 front edge - seven buttons, left to right position control 1 previous thumb key 2 left thumb key 3 triangle back button 4 round home button 5 square recent apps button 6 right thumb key 7 next thumb key front-edge functions: previous/next move through items; left/right pan braille. back returns to the previous screen. home returns to keysoft main menu. recent apps shows running apps; press and hold it for the context menu. 2.3 left edge - top to bottom location control near top corner usb-c port for charging and computer connection below usb-c green led indicator below led oval power button below power volume up button below volume up volume down button 2.4 right edge - top to bottom location control near top corner microphone / line-in jack below microphone jack headphone / audio-out jack below headphone jack action button for recording, camera snapshots, and play/stop in supported contexts 2.5 rear edge - left to right location port near left corner full-size usb port for flash drives and other supported usb storage/devices next sdhc card slot next high-resolution video output port for external display/tv rightmost braille-keyboard-cover connector safety: do not force usb, sd, or keyboard-cover connectors. eject removable storage through keysoft before physically removing it. part 3 - power, charging, locking, and unlocking 3.1 charge the touch plus what you will learn: connect power safely. before you begin: use the supplied usb-c charging cable and suitable adapter. exactly how to do it locate the usb-c port at the upper-left edge. insert the reversible usb-c plug. connect the other end to the power adapter. plug the adapter into ac power. allow the battery to charge. what should happen: the led and/or spoken/braille status indicate charging. if that does not happen: if it does not charge, try the supplied cable/adapter and another outlet. charging from a computer can be slower. practice: locate the port and connect/disconnect the cable. 3.2 power on what you will learn: start keysoft. before you begin: the battery has charge. exactly how to do it press and hold the oval power button on the left edge. feel for the startup vibration. wait for 'starting keysoft' or equivalent braille/speech feedback. allow the main menu to finish loading. what should happen: the touch plus starts and keysoft becomes available. if that does not happen: if startup stalls, connect ac power and retry before attempting a reset. practice: power on from fully off and wait for main menu. 3.3 return to main menu and unlock what you will learn: recover from an unfamiliar screen. before you begin: the touch plus is on. exactly how to do it press the round home button to return to main menu. if the lock screen is active, press space with u. alternatively navigate to the unlock control with thumb keys and activate it. what should happen: the keysoft main menu is available. if that does not happen: if the device asks for a pin/password, enter the configured lock credential. practice: practice home and unlock commands. part 4 - braille keyboard and thumb keys task command / control enter dot 8 backspace dot 7 next item space or next thumb previous item backspace or previous thumb pan braille left left thumb pan braille right right thumb activate item enter or routing key back space+e or triangle back button main menu space+dots 1-2-3-4-5-6 or home command notation: 'space with h' means hold space and press the braille letter h. 'enter with dot 4' means hold enter (dot 8) while pressing dot 4. 4.1 navigate a menu what you will learn: use the universal keysoft pattern. before you begin: open main menu. exactly how to do it press space or next thumb. li

entries.text: brailliant bi x manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual brailliant bi x manual braille display commands and independent operation independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches the humanware brailliant bi x series from the beginning. it covers the bi 20x and bi 40x, including physical orientation, keysoft lite, reading and editing, online libraries, terminal mode, connections to computers and mobile devices, troubleshooting, practice, and quick-reference commands. current reference: humanware's current support pages list user guide version 2.6 and firmware version 2.6.0 build 5120 for the bi 20x and bi 40x. model difference: the bi 20x has 20 braille cells and no six-key command cluster. the bi 40x has 40 braille cells plus six configurable command keys, three on each side of the display. how to use this manual place the device flat with the braille cells closest to you. use previous and next thumb keys to move through menus. use left and right thumb keys to pan braille. press enter (dot 8) or any routing key to activate the selected item. press space+e to go back. press home or space+dots 1-2-3-4-5-6 to return to main menu. press space+h for help and space+m for the context menu. use first-letter navigation in keysoft lite lists and menus. terminal mode is different from keysoft lite: once connected to a host screen reader, host-screen-reader commands take precedence. connection rule: pair/connect first, configure the host screen reader second, then test output, input, and routing. before removing usb/sd storage, use enter+e to eject it safely. table of contents part 1 - what the brailliant bi x is part 2 - physical orientation part 3 - charging, power, and battery part 4 - core keysoft lite navigation part 5 - help, context menu, and status part 6 - braille profiles and speech part 7 - keypad text editor part 8 - keybrf braille editor part 9 - victor reader / book reader part 10 - keyfiles and external storage part 11 - calculator, quick notes, and utilities part 12 - wi-fi part 13 - online libraries: nls bard, bookshare, nfb-newsline, daisy online part 14 - wikipedia, wiktionary, and wordnet part 15 - terminal mode part 16 - iphone and ipad with voiceover part 17 - windows with jaws part 18 - windows with nvda and narrator part 19 - mac with voiceover part 20 - android with talkback part 21 - bluetooth and multiple host devices part 22 - terminal clipboard part 23 - user settings and one-handed mode part 24 - software updates part 25 - security and privacy part 26 - troubleshooting part 27 - independent practice course part 28 - quick reference part 29 - official humanware resources part 1 - what the brailliant bi x is the brailliant bi x series is a family of smart refreshable braille displays. the devices work independently with keysoft lite applications and can also become external braille displays for computers, phones, and tablets. bi 20x: 20 braille cells, perkins-style input keyboard, four thumb keys plus home, onboard wi-fi, bluetooth/usb host connections, rear sd-card slot. bi 40x: 40 braille cells, perkins-style input keyboard, four thumb keys plus home, six command keys, onboard wi-fi, bluetooth/usb host connections. keysoft lite: humanware's onboard menu/app environment. terminal mode: host-device braille display mode. keypad: text editor. keybrf: braille-file editor. victor reader: reading app for text and audio books. keyfiles: file manager. online services: nls bard, bookshare, nfb-newsline and daisy online accounts where eligible. part 2 - physical orientation 2.1 top face - both models place the brailliant flat with the braille cells closest to you. the front section of the top face contains the 20 or 40 braille cells. immediately above each cell is a routing key. in text editing, a routing key moves the cursor to that cell. in menus, a routing key activates the selected item. two space bars are positioned for the thumbs. farther away from you is the perkins-style braille keyboard. under the left hand: dots 1, 2, 3 and backspace (dot 7). dot 1 is under the left index finger; backspace is under the left little finger. under the right hand: dots 4, 5, 6 and enter (dot 8). dot 4 is under the right index finger; enter is under the right little finger. 2.2 bi 40x command keys only the bi 40x has six command keys around the braille display. left side of the display, from back to front: c1, c2, c3. right side of the display, from back to front: c4, c5, c6. current default functions include c1 previous item, c2 pan left, c3 next item, c4 switch language profile, c5 pan right, and c6 start auto-scroll. these command keys can be reassigned in user settings. 2.3 front edge - both models position control far left previous thumb key left-center left thumb key center round home button right-center right thumb key far right next thumb key use: previous/next move through menu items. left/right pan braille. home returns to main menu and exits terminal mode. 2.4 left edge - front to back location control / port front usb-a port behind usb-a power button behind power green status led back usb-c port for charging and usb host connection 2.5 right edge - front to back volume buttons. 3.5 mm audio jack. on the bi 40x, the right edge/top area also includes speaker hardware; audio features depend on current firmware/function. 2.6 bi 20x rear edge the bi 20x has an sd-card slot on the rear edge near the left side. the bi 40x does not use this bi 20x rear sd-card layout. part 3 - charging, power, and battery 3.1 charge the brailliant what you will learn: connect power without forcing the connector. before you begin: use the included usb-c cable and a suitable usb power adapter. exactly how to do it locate the usb-c port at the back end of the left edge. insert the usb-c plug gently. connect the other end to the power adapter. plug the adapter into ac power. allow the battery to charge. what should happen: the status led/braille status indicates charging. if that does not happen: if the device does not charge, try the included cable/adapter and a different outlet. practice: locate usb-c and connect/disconnect it correctly. 3.2 power on and check battery what you will learn: start the device and verify charge. before you begin: battery has some charge. exactly how to do it press and hold the power button for about two seconds. wait for keysoft lite to start. press enter+p. read/listen to the battery level. what should happen: main menu appears and the battery percentage/status is reported. if that does not happen: if nothing happens, connect power and retry. practice: power on and report battery level. firmware update warning: humanware states that units still on firmware 1.x must first install version 2.0 manually before updating to later firmware. part 4 - core keysoft lite navigation task command / control activate selected item enter or routing key back / escape space+e previous item previous thumb; bi40x c1; or space+dot 1 next item next thumb; bi40x c3; or space+dot 4 pan left / right left / right thumb; bi40x c2 / c5 top of list/text space+dots 1-2-3 bottom of list/text space+dots 4-5-6 main menu home or space+dots 1-2-3-4-5-6 4.1 navigate main menu what you will learn: move around without memorizing app order. before you begin: device is on. exactly how to do it press home. press next thumb repeatedly. read each app/item. press previous thumb to move backward. type the first letter of an app to jump among matching items. press enter or routing key on the desired app. what should happen: the selected app opens. if that does not happen: if letters enter text, you are in an edit field rather than a menu; press space+e and return home. practice: open options, return home, then open victor reader. part 5 - help, context menu, and status task command / control help space+h context menu space+m options space+o system information space+i battery ente

entries.text: chatgpt manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible chatgpt course chatgpt manual practical, responsible ai skills for work, learning, and independent problem-solving. basics prompting verification privacy screen readers lessons what generative ai does generative ai predicts and creates text or other content from patterns in training data and the information supplied in a conversation. it can help brainstorm, organize, explain, summarize, and draft. it does not understand a situation the way a person does, and it can produce confident but incorrect or invented information. use ai as an assistant, not as the final decision-maker. a person remains responsible for checking accuracy, appropriateness, accessibility, and compliance with workplace rules. a reliable prompt pattern task: state exactly what you want. context: explain the audience and purpose using nonprivate information. constraints: give length, tone, reading level, deadline, or other limits. format: request headings, bullets, a numbered procedure, or a simple table. checks: ask the tool to identify uncertainty and provide sources when appropriate. continue the conversation with specific follow-ups. for example: “shorten this to 150 words,” “explain the second step,” or “which statements need verification?” verify before using the result open original sources instead of trusting an ai summary or citation. confirm names, dates, quotations, calculations, contact details, laws, policies, and software instructions. prefer current primary sources from the organization responsible for the information. compare important claims with a second reliable source. test instructions safely before giving them to another person. rewrite the final result in your own voice and keep a record of corrections. privacy and workplace rules do not enter client records, medical or disability details, passwords, financial account information, private addresses, confidential workplace material, copyrighted documents you are not permitted to share, or information that identifies another person. use fictional or public information in these lessons. follow the employer’s approved-tool, retention, disclosure, and human-review requirements. a personal free account is not automatically approved for organizational data. never allow ai to make an employment, benefit, medical, legal, financial, safety, or accommodation decision for a person. accessible output ask for descriptive headings, short paragraphs, meaningful link text, numbered steps, and simple tables. ask for image descriptions when an image matters, but verify the description with a trusted person when accuracy is important. avoid layouts that communicate meaning only through color, position, or visual formatting. jaws, narrator, and nvda ai interfaces change often. use tab and shift+tab to move among controls, enter or space to activate a control, and the screen reader’s heading, landmark, link, button, edit-field, and browse-mode commands to review the page. use browser find to locate words such as “sources,” “copy,” or part of your prompt. jaws: h moves by heading, b by button, e by edit field, insert+f7 opens links, and insert+f5 opens form fields. nvda: h moves by heading, b by button, e by edit field, nvda+f7 opens the elements list, and nvda+space switches browse and focus modes. narrator: use caps lock or insert with arrow keys for scan mode navigation; press caps lock+space to toggle scan mode when needed. after sending a prompt, allow time for the
