entries.snippet: Accessible keyboard-first Choosing a Free Office Suite manual for blind and low-vision learners.
entries.text: choosing a free office suite manual - accessible learning center skip to main content free office software foundations choosing a free office suite manual no-cost office skills, accessible workflows, and microsoft-compatible file exchange. cost accessibility file formats screen readers compatibility lessons no-cost course rule this course must not require a purchase, subscription, paid trial, payment card, or new paid service. libreoffice is free and open source. google docs editors and microsoft 365 for the web have free account-based options, but internet access, account rules, storage limits, and available features can differ. use an employer-approved program and account for workplace information. a free personal account is not automatically approved for client or organizational data. accessibility comes before feature count before choosing a program, test the actual work tasks with the learner’s preferred screen reader, braille display, magnification, browser zoom, color settings, and keyboard. confirm that focus is announced, controls have useful names, editing feedback is understandable, and essential tasks do not require a mouse. use descriptive headings, real lists, clear table headers, meaningful links, alternative text, sufficient contrast, and logical reading order. do not communicate meaning only through color or visual position. run the program’s accessibility checker when available, but also perform a keyboard and screen-reader review. keep an original editable file before exporting pdf or converting formats. native and exchange formats libreoffice native formats odt for writer, ods for calc, and odp for impress preserve libreoffice editing features. microsoft exchange formats docx, xlsx, and pptx are often required by employers or instructors using microsoft 365. other formats csv carries plain spreadsheet data without formulas or formatting. pdf is useful for fixed-layout review but may be harder to edit and must be checked for accessibility. save the native version first. then save or download a separate exchange copy and review it in the receiving program whenever possible. jaws, narrator, and nvda interfaces vary by program and update. use tab and shift+tab for controls, arrow keys within menus and lists, enter or space to activate, alt or f10 for menus when supported, ctrl+s to save, ctrl+o to open, and ctrl+z to undo. listen for the current control name and state instead of memorizing screen position. jaws: use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focused-control information, and insert+1 for keyboard help. nvda: use nvda+t for the title, nvda+tab for focus, and nvda+1 for input help. narrator: use caps lock+t for the title and caps lock+1 for input learning. toggle scan mode only when the application or webpage requires it. browser-based editors may have their own screen-reader-support setting and keyboard shortcuts. read the current official help before changing screen-reader modes. compatibility review keep an untouched native copy. create a separate docx, xlsx, pptx, csv, or pdf copy. read every heading, cell range, slide title, link, table, image description, formula result, note, and page or slide count. check fonts, spacing, page breaks, charts, animations, formulas, comments, and accessibility metadata. correct the native file and export again rather than repeatedly converting the same exchange copy. never promise perfect compatibility without testing the actual document in the receiving software. privacy, accounts, and sharing use fictional or public information in these lessons. do not upload client records, medical or disability information, passwords, financial data, or confidential workplace material. for cloud tools, confirm the active account and sharing permission before entering content. for local tools, back up files to an approved location. official references libreoffice suite overview microsoft 365 for the web google docs editors help basic and advanced step-by-step procedures these procedures make the manual usable on its own. the separate lessons provide assignments and progress tracking when you want a course experience. basic 1: compare desktop and web office suites basic 2: check accessibility before choosing a program basic 3: understand office file formats and compatibility basic 4: create and exchange a word-processing file basic 5: create and exchange a spreadsheet file advanced 6: create and exchange a presentation file advanced 7: compare libreoffice and browser-based tools advanced 8: protect privacy and manage cloud storage advanced 9: build a free accessible work setup advanced 10: final free office suite recommendation basic procedure 1. compare desktop and web office suites what you will learn: compare libreoffice, google workspace, and microsoft 365 for the web using cost, internet, account, privacy, and file-format criteria. before you begin: use a nonprivate practice file and confirm which office program and file format you are testing. do not replace your only original copy. exactly how to do it read the choosing a free office suite manual sections on accessibility, screen readers, file formats, and compatibility. open your selected free office suite and confirm the window title or browser tab, active file, and current account when applicable. navigate the main controls using only the keyboard. record the labels announced by jaws, narrator, or nvda. compare libreoffice, google workspace, and microsoft 365 for the web using cost, internet, account, privacy, and file-format criteria. save frequently in the program’s preferred editable format. if working in a browser, confirm that changes are saved before closing. review the work from the beginning using keyboard and screen-reader navigation. correct unclear structure, labels, or data. create a separate microsoft-compatible or requested exchange copy. do not overwrite the editable original. open or re-import the exchange copy when possible and compare content, formatting, formulas, notes, links, and accessibility. write a short compatibility report naming anything that changed and how it was corrected. save the submission using the filename free-office-lesson-1.txt . screen-reader help: use tab and shift+tab for controls and listen to the current accessible name. jaws users can use insert+tab, nvda users nvda+tab, and narrator users scan mode commands when appropriate. application and web-editor commands may differ after updates. what should happen: you can complete the procedure and verify the result using the keyboard, your screen reader, or your braille display. if that does not happen: press escape to leave an unexpected menu or dialog, confirm the active window and keyboard focus, then repeat one step at a time. use undo when a reversible content change occurred. practice: compare libreoffice, google workspace, and microsoft 365 for the web using cost, internet, account, privacy, and file-format criteria. basic procedure 2. check accessibility before choosing a program what you will learn: test keyboard access, screen-reader labels, zoom, focus visibility, and help resources in two free programs. before you begin: use a nonprivate practice file and confirm which office program and file format you are testing. do not replace your only original copy. exactly how to do it read the choosing a free office suite manual sections on accessibility, screen readers, file formats, and compatibility. open your selected free office suite and confirm the window title or browser tab, active file, and current account when applicable. navigate the main controls using only the keyboard. record the labels announced by jaws, narrator, or nvda. test keyboard access, screen-reader labels, zoom, focus visibility, and help resources in two free programs. save frequently in the program’s preferred editable format. if working in a browser, confirm that changes are saved before closing. review the work from the beginning using keyboard and screen-reader

entries.title: Cybersecurity for Screen Reader Users Manual
entries.snippet: Cybersecurity for Screen Reader Users Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: cybersecurity for screen reader users manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual cybersecurity for screen reader users manual safer accounts, devices, browsing, and communication independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches practical cybersecurity to people who use screen readers, braille displays, keyboard navigation, or speech access. it assumes no technical security background. core approach: security decisions should not depend on seeing color, logos, icons, hover previews, or visual layout. this guide teaches verification methods that work through accessible text, keyboard commands, screen-reader information, known apps, saved bookmarks, typed addresses, and trusted contact methods. safety principle: urgency is not proof. a legitimate bank, employer, government agency, software company, or family member can be contacted independently. never let a message force you to use only the contact method inside that same message. how to use this manual work through the manual in order. the first sections establish habits used everywhere else. when a message is suspicious, do not click, reply, call the included number, or open the attachment just to investigate. use a known app, saved bookmark, typed website address, statement/card phone number, or trusted contact record to verify independently. treat passwords, recovery codes, one-time codes, passkeys, security questions, and remote-control access as credentials. keep software updated; security updates close known weaknesses. use a password manager and unique passwords where passwords are still required. turn on mfa; prefer passkeys or other phishing-resistant methods where available. if something goes wrong, act quickly: disconnect remote access, secure the account, change credentials, turn on mfa, scan/update devices, and contact the legitimate institution. table of contents part 1 - the four core cybersecurity habits part 2 - what phishing is part 3 - accessible sender verification part 4 - accessible link verification part 5 - suspicious attachments and downloads part 6 - passwords and password managers part 7 - mfa, authenticator apps, and security keys part 8 - passkeys part 9 - one-time codes and mfa fatigue part 10 - browser and website security warnings part 11 - email safety part 12 - text messages, calls, and voicemail scams part 13 - tech-support and remote-access scams part 14 - banking, payment, gift card, and refund scams part 15 - social media, dating, and impersonation scams part 16 - shopping, delivery, and subscription scams part 17 - software updates and safe apps part 18 - backups and ransomware resilience part 19 - public wi-fi, bluetooth, and device privacy part 20 - screen reader and braille privacy part 21 - account recovery and security alerts part 22 - what to do after a scam or account compromise part 23 - work and school security part 24 - accessible security checklists part 25 - practice scenarios part 26 - quick reference part 27 - official security resources part 1 - the four core cybersecurity habits cisa's secure our world guidance centers on four simple habits. this manual expands them for screen-reader users. situation safer action recognize and report phishing do not engage with suspicious messages; verify independently and report/delete them. use strong, unique passwords use a password manager; do not reuse a password across accounts. turn on mfa use the strongest option offered; prefer phishing-resistant methods where available. install software updates apply security updates promptly from official update mechanisms. password length: cisa's current consumer guidance recommends passwords of at least 16 characters, random and unique for each account, with a password manager to create and store them. part 2 - what phishing is phishing is an attempt to make you open a harmful attachment, visit a fake site, reveal information, approve a login, send money, or install software. urgency: 'act in 30 minutes or your account will close.' fear: 'your computer has a virus.' authority: 'this is your bank, boss, police, irs, microsoft, apple, google, or it department.' reward: 'you won a prize/refund.' scarcity: 'only one item left; pay now.' secrecy: 'do not tell anyone.' payment pressure: gift cards, cryptocurrency, wire transfer, payment app, or cash. credential request: password, verification code, recovery code, pin, or remote access. screen-reader-specific warning: a link's spoken text can say one thing while its real destination is different. a sender display name can also be forged or misleading. always verify the actual address/domain when the decision matters. part 3 - accessible sender verification 3.1 verify an email sender what you will learn: check the actual sender address instead of trusting the display name. before you begin: do not reply yet. exactly how to do it open the message without activating links or attachments. move to the from/sender field. use your email program's message-details or sender-details command to read the full email address. spell the domain character by character if necessary. compare the domain with the organization's known official domain. if the message asks for action, leave the message and contact the organization using a known app, saved bookmark, statement/card number, or manually typed official website. what should happen: you know the actual sender address and have verified the request independently. if that does not happen: if your email client hides the full address, open message details/headers or use a different trusted client/device. do not treat a display name as proof. practice: inspect three legitimate messages and identify their full sender domains. 3.2 verify a caller or text sender what you will learn: do not trust caller id or the number in the message. before you begin: a call/text claims to be from an institution or person. exactly how to do it do not provide credentials or money. end the call or stop replying. find the contact through a trusted source you already possess. call back using the trusted number, not the number supplied by the caller/message. for family emergencies, contact the person or another family member through a known number. what should happen: you verify identity through a separate channel. if that does not happen: caller id and message sender names/numbers can be spoofed. practice: practice finding a bank or utility number from an official statement or app. part 4 - accessible link verification 4.1 inspect a link without opening it what you will learn: determine the destination domain first. before you begin: focus the link but do not activate it. exactly how to do it listen to the visible link text. use your screen reader's link-information command or the application's context menu where available. press shift+f10 on windows to open the link context menu. choose copy link address when available instead of open. paste the copied address into a safe text editor such as notepad. read/spell the domain carefully. cancel/delete the pasted text after inspection if it contains a personal token. what should happen: you can examine the destination without visiting it. if that does not happen: some tracking links are long or obscured. if the message is asking you to sign in, skip the link entirely and reach the service through a known app/bookmark/typed address. practice: inspect several trusted links and identify the domain. domain rule: read the registered domain, not just words anywhere in the address. a name such as bank.example.com.evil-site.test is controlled by evil-site.test, not by 'bank.example.com'. 4.2 use the independent-path method what you will learn: avoid link analysis when a safer route exists. before you begin: a message says an account needs attention. exactly how to do it close or leave the message. open the institution's official app, your saved trusted bookmark, or type the kn

entries.text: focus 40 blue manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible braille technology manual focus 40 blue accessible manual a progressive keyboard-and-braille guide for windows and jaws users. all manuals ten focus lessons my progress identify your focus model first this course emphasizes the focus 40 blue fifth generation. a fifth-generation focus has a menu button centered between braille keys 1 and 4. older focus 40 blue models have different controls, ports, features, and firmware. never install firmware until the exact model and generation are confirmed. use the official guide for the assigned device generation. start jaws before connecting the focus to windows. save open work before changing connections or settings. use instructor-provided or fictional files during practice. never submit passwords, pairing codes, serial numbers, protected books, or private workplace information. major controls and features 40 refreshable braille cells: display one line of computer text in braille. cursor router buttons: move the cursor, activate links, and support text selection. perkins-style keyboard and braillein: enter text and windows or jaws commands. panning buttons, rocker bars, and nav rockers: move through text and structured information. usb and bluetooth: connect to computers and supported mobile devices. fifth-generation scratchpad and brf book reader: create notes and read supported files without a computer. basic and advanced how-tos connect the focus to jaws by usb keyboard commands: insert+j opens the jaws window. alt+o opens options, then b opens braille in common jaws versions. start jaws and save open work. connect the focus directly with its usb cable and power it on. wait for the braille cells to refresh. open jaws braille settings and confirm focus is the active display. press a windows key and verify that its result appears in both speech and braille. you should feel: text matching the focused windows control. if that does not happen: confirm the cable, power, jaws driver, and exact focus generation before changing settings. read, pan, and route the cursor device commands: the left and right panning buttons move one display width. a cursor router button moves the cursor to its corresponding braille cell. open a harmless practice document. read the current 40-cell line from left to right. press the right panning button once and confirm the next portion appears. press the left panning button to return. press the cursor router above a known word. type one practice character, verify its location, then undo with ctrl+z. if that does not happen: confirm the active window and editing caret before routing again. use focus keyboard help device command: press space with t-h chord, dots 1-4-5-6, for focus keyboard help. save work and turn keyboard help on. press one unfamiliar focus control. read its description without performing the command. exit help before returning to the document. if that does not happen: with focus connected to jaws, press insert+space followed by j and search jaws command search for the function. switch among saved connections device commands: on fifth-generation focus blue, menu+dot 1 through menu+dot 5 selects a bluetooth connection; menu+dot 8 selects usb. save work on the currently connected device. identify which connection number belongs to the target device. press menu with the assigned dot once. wait for the display to refresh and verify the target device’s focused item. use menu+dot 8 to return to usb when needed. if that does not happen: do not repeat rapidly. confirm pairing and the saved connection number in the focus connections menu. ten-lesson learning path lesson 1: orientation, power, and device identification — create a tactile orientation guide naming the major controls and explaining how to identify the device generation. lesson 2: connect by usb and configure jaws — write a usb connection and jaws verification checklist. lesson 3: pair and manage bluetooth connections — create a credential-free bluetooth pairing and connection-switching guide. lesson 4: read, pan, route the cursor, and select text — submit a command chart for panning, navigation, cursor routing, and text selection. lesson 5: type with braillein and edit text — create focus-lesson-5.txt or docx containing a short corrected workplace note. lesson 6: navigate windows, file explorer, and documents — create a keyboard-and-braille workflow for finding and reading a workplace file. lesson 7: navigate webpages, forms, lists, and tables — document an accessible web-navigation practice session. lesson 8: use scratchpad, brf book reader, and microsd safely — create a local note and a storage-safety checklist; submit only your original note. lesson 9: braille settings, study mode, cleaning, and updates — create a safe settings, cleaning, and firmware checklist. lesson 10: final focus 40 blue workplace project — complete an end-to-end focus 40 blue workplace task and submit only the original summary. safe working routine identify the focus model and generation. confirm power, battery, cable, and connection mode. confirm the active jaws braille display and windows focus. practice on a copy and verify the destination before saving or transferring. restore reversible settings after practice. disconnect, clean, and update only according to the official instructions. official freedom scientific references focus blue fifth-generation user guide focus blue training and jaws features focus 40 blue documentation focus blue quick-start guide start focus 40 blue lesson 1 return to manuals basic and advanced step-by-step procedures these procedures make the manual usable on its own. the separate lessons provide assignments and progress tracking when you want a course experience. basic 1: orientation, power, and device identification basic 2: connect by usb and configure jaws basic 3: pair and manage bluetooth connections basic 4: read, pan, route the cursor, and select text basic 5: type with braillein and edit text advanced 6: navigate windows, file explorer, and documents advanced 7: navigate webpages, forms, lists, and tables advanced 8: use scratchpad, brf book reader, and microsd safely advanced 9: braille settings, study mode, cleaning, and updates advanced 10: final focus 40 blue workplace project basic procedure 1. orientation, power, and device identification what you will learn: create a tactile orientation guide naming the major controls and explaining how to identify the device generation. before you begin: place the device on a stable surface, identify its exact model, and use only nonprivate practice files. save open work before changing connections or settings. exactly how to do it place the focus on a stable surface with the braille cells nearest you. locate the 40 braille cells, cursor router buttons, perkins-style keys, spacebar, shift buttons, panning buttons, nav rockers, rocker bars, selector buttons, and menu button by touch. use the centered menu button to identify a fifth-generation model; older focus models have different controls and firmware. when operating on battery, hold power for about two seconds to turn the display on. press menu to review battery status, then return without changing settings. hold power for about three and one-half seconds to turn off when not connected by usb. jaws and braille tip: use insert+t to confirm the window title, insert+tab to identify focus, and insert+1 for keyboard help. focus commands vary by device generation, jaws settings, application, and connection method; use the official guide linked from the manual when a command differs. what should happen: you can complete the procedure and verify the result using the keyboard, your screen reader, or your braille display. if that does not happen: stop and identify the active device, connection, application, and screen-reader focus. confirm the exact model before repeating a device command or changing firmware or settings. practice: cre

entries.snippet: Gmail Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: gmail manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual gmail manual email, keyboard navigation, labels, filters, attachments, and safety independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual google: use gmail with a screen reader purpose: this manual is written directly to the person learning gmail. it assumes you may be using gmail for the first time and explains what to press, what should happen, what your screen reader should announce, and what to try if the result is different. reference view: this manual uses gmail's current standard view. google retired the old basic html experience, so older instructions may no longer match what you see. screen reader setup: google recommends chrome with nvda or jaws on windows, chromevox on chromeos, and voiceover on macos. gmail works best as a web application when the screen reader is in focus/application mode rather than virtual/browse mode. how to use this manual work through parts 1-10 first if gmail is completely new to you. do one action at a time. stop and listen to what changed before pressing another key. tab and shift+tab move through many controls. enter activates buttons, links, and selected messages. escape closes menus, popups, dialogs, or backs out of temporary interfaces. gmail's own keyboard shortcuts work best when enabled and when your screen reader is in focus/application mode. jaws users: jaws+z toggles virtual pc cursor. gmail's web-app shortcuts generally work when virtual pc cursor is off. nvda users: nvda+space toggles browse and focus mode. gmail's web-app shortcuts generally work in focus mode. voiceover users: turn quick nav/quick keys off when gmail needs to receive letter shortcuts. whenever a command is a sequence, such as g then i, press the second key within about three seconds. table of contents part 1 - what gmail is part 2 - open gmail and sign in part 3 - learn the gmail standard view part 4 - turn on gmail keyboard shortcuts part 5 - read your inbox part 6 - open and read a message part 7 - compose and send email part 8 - reply, reply all, and forward part 9 - attachments part 10 - search part 11 - archive, delete, spam, snooze, and mute part 12 - star, mark read/unread, and importance part 13 - labels and move to part 14 - create filters part 15 - conversation view part 16 - drafts, sent, trash, and spam part 17 - contacts and addressing part 18 - settings, inbox layout, and reading pane part 19 - undo send part 20 - security and phishing part 21 - gmail with jaws part 22 - gmail with nvda part 23 - gmail with voiceover on mac part 24 - gmail with narrator part 25 - gmail on iphone/ipad part 26 - gmail on android part 27 - troubleshooting part 28 - independent practice course part 29 - quick reference keyboard commands part 30 - official google resources part 1 - what gmail is gmail is google's web-based email service. in gmail standard view, the inbox behaves more like a web application than a traditional webpage. gmail has its own keyboard commands for opening, selecting, labeling, archiving, replying to, and searching messages. message: one email. conversation/thread: a group of related replies that gmail can display together. inbox: incoming messages not archived or moved elsewhere. label: gmail's way to organize messages. a message can have more than one label. archive: removes a message from inbox without deleting it. trash: holds deleted messages temporarily. spam: suspicious or unwanted messages filtered by gmail or marked by you. star: a visual/organizational marker for important messages. snooze: temporarily hides a message until a chosen time. draft: an unsent message gmail saves while you compose. part 2 - open gmail and sign in 2.1 open gmail in a browser what you will learn: reach gmail without using a mouse. before you begin: use a supported current browser such as chrome. exactly how to do it press the windows key or command+space on mac and open your browser. move to the address bar with ctrl+l on windows or command+l on mac. type mail.google.com. press enter/return. if google asks you to sign in, enter your gmail or google workspace email address. activate next. enter your password or complete your organization's sign-in/verification process. wait for gmail to finish loading before navigating. what should happen: gmail opens to your account, usually in inbox. if that does not happen: if the wrong google account opens, use the account menu to switch accounts or sign out, then sign in with the intended account. practice: open gmail, identify your account, and return to inbox. part 3 - learn the gmail standard view top area: search mail, google account controls, settings, and help. left navigation: compose, inbox, starred, snoozed, sent, drafts, more, labels, and sometimes chat/meet. message list: sender, subject, snippet, date/time, star, and selection controls. message view: the opened conversation and its actions. compose window: to, cc/bcc, subject, message body, attachments, formatting, and send. right side panel: may contain calendar, keep, tasks, contacts, and add-ons. important: the precise tab order can change based on gmail features, account type, browser, reading pane, side panels, chat/meet visibility, and organization settings. part 4 - turn on gmail keyboard shortcuts 4.1 enable gmail shortcuts from the shortcut dialog what you will learn: turn on gmail's web-application keyboard commands. before you begin: use gmail standard view. put your screen reader in focus/application mode. exactly how to do it press shift+slash, which produces the question mark key. wait for the keyboard shortcuts dialog. press tab once. listen for a link named enable or disable. if it says enable, press enter. if it says disable, shortcuts are already enabled. press escape to close the dialog. press g, then i to go to inbox as a test. what should happen: the inbox receives focus or opens after g then i. if that does not happen: if shift+slash does not open the dialog, make sure you are in standard view and your screen reader is not intercepting the key. you can also enable keyboard shortcuts in settings. practice: enable shortcuts, press g then i, and confirm inbox. sequence rule: for shortcuts written as two keys, such as g then i, press the first key, release it, and press the second within about three seconds. part 5 - read your inbox 5.1 move through conversations what you will learn: move one conversation at a time. before you begin: gmail shortcuts are enabled and the screen reader is in focus/application mode. exactly how to do it press g then i to move to inbox. press j to move to the next conversation. stop and listen to the sender, subject, snippet, and status. press j again. press k to move back to the previous conversation. continue one message at a time until the desired conversation is focused. press enter or o to open it. what should happen: focus moves through conversations and the selected one opens. if that does not happen: if j or k types into a field or does nothing, make sure focus is not inside search or compose and confirm screen-reader mode and gmail shortcuts. practice: move through five messages, then return to the first one. part 6 - open and read a message 6.1 open, read, and return to inbox what you will learn: read a conversation and return without using back repeatedly. before you begin: focus a message in the inbox. exactly how to do it press enter or o to open the conversation. use your screen reader reading commands or gmail navigation to read the sender, recipients, subject, date, and message body. if the conversation contains multiple collapsed messages, move to the desired message and expand it with enter/space when needed. review any attachment names before opening them. when finished, press u to return to the conversation list. press j or k to continue through inbox. what should happen: the message opens, can be read, and u returns you to the list. if that does no

entries.text: google calendar screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual google calendar screen reader manual keyboard-first scheduling independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual google: use google calendar with a screen reader purpose: this manual teaches google calendar from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains exactly what to press, which calendar area or event field should receive focus, what should be announced, and how to recover when the result is different. reference setup: this manual focuses on google calendar on the web in a current chrome browser, with practical iphone/ipad and android sections. screen reader recommendation: google recommends using calendar as a web application. jaws users should generally turn the virtual pc cursor off, nvda users should use focus mode, voiceover users should turn quick nav off, and narrator users may need scan mode off so calendar receives its own shortcuts. how to use this manual work through parts 1-14 before concentrating on your screen reader. those sections teach calendar itself. google recommends schedule view, also called agenda view, for screen-reader users. press a or 5. press c to create a normal event. press shift+c to open the create-type dialog for event, out of office, task, and other available types. press t to return to today. press / to search calendar. press g to go to a specific date. press ctrl+/ on windows or command+/ on mac to review google's current calendar shortcuts. inside an open event, alt+1 through alt+7 on windows can announce specific event information without moving focus. before sending an invitation, verify the guest address, event date/time, time zone, and meeting location/link. table of contents part 1 - what google calendar is part 2 - open calendar and confirm the account part 3 - learn the calendar interface part 4 - turn on and review keyboard shortcuts part 5 - calendar views part 6 - navigate schedule view part 7 - navigate day, week, month, and year views part 8 - go to today and go to a specific date part 9 - create a basic event part 10 - invite guests part 11 - create recurring events part 12 - edit, review, and delete events part 13 - respond to invitations part 14 - search calendar part 15 - notifications and reminders part 16 - google meet and video meetings part 17 - find a time and suggested times part 18 - out of office, focus time, tasks, and working location part 19 - share a calendar part 20 - manage multiple calendars part 21 - calendar settings part 22 - jaws with google calendar part 23 - nvda with google calendar part 24 - narrator with google calendar part 25 - voiceover with google calendar part 26 - braille displays part 27 - iphone/ipad and android part 28 - security and privacy part 29 - troubleshooting part 30 - independent practice course part 31 - quick reference commands part 32 - official google resources part 1 - what google calendar is google calendar is a scheduling application for appointments, meetings, invitations, tasks, working-location information, and shared calendars. it is part of google workspace and integrates with gmail, google meet, google tasks, and google contacts. event: an appointment or meeting on a date/time. all-day event: an event without a specific time block. guest: a person invited to an event. organizer: the person/account that owns the event. calendar: one collection of events. one account can display several calendars. schedule view: chronological list of upcoming events; google recommends this view for screen readers. main drawer: left-side area with create, small calendar, and calendar lists. events area: the main calendar view. banner area: search, settings, view switcher, account, and other controls. right sidebar: tasks, keep, contacts, and other side-panel apps when available. part 2 - open calendar and confirm the account 2.1 open google calendar what you will learn: reach calendar and verify the correct google account. before you begin: use a supported current browser. exactly how to do it open chrome. press ctrl+l. type calendar.google.com. press enter. wait for calendar to load. use tab/f6 or screen-reader navigation to locate the google account/profile control. confirm the correct name or email address before creating or sharing events. use the skip to main content button if it is offered near the top. what should happen: google calendar opens under the intended account. if that does not happen: if the wrong account is active, switch accounts before creating events or inviting people. practice: open calendar and confirm the account. part 3 - learn the calendar interface google documents four major calendar areas: banner area: main drawer toggle, search, help, settings, view switcher, google apps, and account. events area: day/week/month/year/schedule content. main drawer area: create, small calendar, people search, and calendar list. right sidebar: google apps such as tasks, keep, and contacts. 3.1 move between calendar areas what you will learn: recognize which part of calendar currently has focus. before you begin: calendar is open. exactly how to do it press tab repeatedly from the top of the page and listen to the major controls. use shift+tab to move backward. press a to switch to schedule view and place focus in the event-oriented view. press ctrl+alt+period on windows to move toward the right sidebar when it is available. press escape to close a menu/search and return toward the main calendar interface. what should happen: you can tell whether focus is in banner, events, main drawer, or right sidebar. if that does not happen: if single-letter shortcuts type into a field, press escape and ensure your screen reader is in web-application/focus mode. practice: identify all four areas. part 4 - turn on and review keyboard shortcuts 4.1 enable calendar shortcuts in settings what you will learn: make calendar single-letter commands available. before you begin: calendar is open. exactly how to do it press s to open settings if shortcuts are already active. if not, navigate to settings with tab/menus. find the keyboard shortcuts setting. turn enable keyboard shortcuts on. save if the page presents a save control. return to calendar. press ctrl+/ to open the shortcut list. what should happen: calendar's documented keyboard shortcuts are available. if that does not happen: if c, t, a, or other shortcuts do nothing, verify this setting and the screen-reader application mode. practice: enable shortcuts and open the shortcut list. current help shortcut: google documents ctrl+/ on windows/chromeos and command+/ on macos to review calendar shortcuts. some older references use question mark; use google's current shortcut list as the final reference. part 5 - calendar views task command day view 1 or d week view 2 or w month view 3 or m custom view 4 or x schedule/agenda view 5 or a year view 6 or y 5.1 switch views what you will learn: move among calendar's major presentations. before you begin: keyboard shortcuts are enabled. exactly how to do it press a. listen for schedule view. press d. listen for day view. press w. listen for week view. press m. listen for month view. press y. listen for year view. press a to return to schedule view. what should happen: calendar changes view after each command. if that does not happen: if a letter types into search or another field, press escape and restore application/focus mode. practice: cycle through every view and return to schedule. part 6 - navigate schedule view google recommends schedule view for screen-reader users. task command move between days left / right arrow move between events in a day up / down arrow next date range/day n previous date range/day p 6.1 review upcoming events what you will learn: move chronologically through upcoming events. before you begin: press a to enter schedule view. exactly how to do it press up/down arrow to move among

entries.title: Google Chrome Screen Reader Manual
entries.snippet: Google Chrome Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: google chrome screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual google chrome screen reader manual narrator, nvda, and jaws independent self-study guide for web browsing all manuals table of contents start of manual google chrome keyboard shortcuts purpose: this manual teaches google chrome from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains what to press, what browser region or webpage element should receive focus, what your screen reader should announce, and how to recover when the result is different. reference platform: this manual focuses on current google chrome on windows 11. screen readers: core chrome keyboard commands are taught first. narrator, nvda, and jaws are covered separately so browser and screen-reader commands stay distinct. how to use this manual learn chrome itself before memorizing screen-reader quick-navigation keys. ctrl+l, alt+d, or f6 can move focus to the address bar. ctrl+t opens a new tab. ctrl+w closes the current tab. ctrl+shift+t reopens recently closed tabs. f6 cycles focus through chrome's major browser areas. tab and shift+tab move through clickable controls. screen-reader browse/scan modes are used for structural webpage navigation. f7 turns caret browsing on or off. alt+shift+r opens chrome reading mode on windows when supported. ctrl+j opens downloads, ctrl+h opens history, and ctrl+shift+o opens bookmark manager. verify the website domain before entering passwords or sensitive information. table of contents part 1 - what google chrome is part 2 - open chrome and learn the window part 3 - address bar and search part 4 - tabs, windows, and tab groups part 5 - back, forward, reload, and home part 6 - webpage keyboard navigation part 7 - find on page part 8 - bookmarks part 9 - history part 10 - downloads part 11 - forms and interactive controls part 12 - links and context menus part 13 - pdfs in chrome part 14 - reading mode part 15 - caret browsing part 16 - accessibility settings, live caption, and live translate part 17 - zoom and full screen part 18 - profiles, sign-in, and sync part 19 - incognito, privacy, cookies, and passwords part 20 - extensions and accessibility extensions part 21 - security and phishing part 22 - narrator with chrome part 23 - nvda with chrome part 24 - jaws with chrome part 25 - braille displays with chrome part 26 - troubleshooting part 27 - independent practice course part 28 - quick reference commands part 29 - official google resources part 1 - what google chrome is google chrome is a web browser. it displays webpages, web applications, pdfs, downloads, settings, extensions, history, bookmarks, and account/profile features. omnibox/address bar: where you type a website address or web search. tab: one open webpage or browser task. tab strip: area containing open tabs and tab groups. toolbar: browser controls such as back, reload, bookmark, extensions, profile, and chrome menu. web content: the current webpage. bookmarks: saved website shortcuts. history: previously visited pages. downloads: files downloaded through chrome. extensions: optional add-ons that can change chrome behavior. part 2 - open chrome and learn the window 2.1 open google chrome what you will learn: start chrome without using a mouse. before you begin: chrome must be installed. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type chrome. press enter on google chrome. wait for chrome to open. press f6 once. listen to the browser region announced. continue pressing f6 to hear the tab strip, address bar/toolbar, and page area. press shift+f6 to move backward. what should happen: chrome opens and you can identify its major focus areas. if that does not happen: if f6 does not move, press escape to close an open menu or popup and try again. practice: open chrome, cycle focus through the main areas, then return to the webpage. part 3 - address bar and search task command focus address bar ctrl+l, alt+d, or f6 search from anywhere ctrl+k or ctrl+e open typed search/address in new tab alt+enter 3.1 open a website what you will learn: go directly to a known address. before you begin: chrome is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+l. type the website address, for example google.com. press enter. wait for the page to load. use the screen reader to confirm the page title or main heading. what should happen: the website opens in the current tab. if that does not happen: if search results appear, verify the address you typed. practice: open two known websites. 3.2 search the web what you will learn: use the omnibox as a search box. before you begin: chrome is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+l. type a search phrase. press enter. wait for results. use screen-reader heading and link navigation to review results. what should happen: search results appear. if that does not happen: if chrome stays on the previous page, make sure the omnibox received focus before typing. practice: search for three topics. part 4 - tabs, windows, and tab groups task command new tab ctrl+t close current tab ctrl+w reopen closed tab ctrl+shift+t next tab ctrl+tab or ctrl+page down previous tab ctrl+shift+tab or ctrl+page up specific tab 1-8 ctrl+1 through ctrl+8 rightmost tab ctrl+9 new window ctrl+n new incognito window ctrl+shift+n move tab left/right ctrl+shift+page up / ctrl+shift+page down 4.1 open and switch tabs what you will learn: work with several webpages at once. before you begin: chrome is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+t. open a site or search. press ctrl+t and open a second site. press ctrl+tab to move forward through tabs. press ctrl+shift+tab to move backward. listen to each page title. what should happen: the active tab changes. if that does not happen: if only one tab exists, ctrl+tab may appear to do nothing. practice: open three tabs and cycle through all three. 4.2 restore a closed tab what you will learn: recover a tab closed by mistake. before you begin: close a non-important tab. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+t. wait for the restored tab. listen to the page title. what should happen: the most recently closed tab reopens. if that does not happen: press ctrl+shift+t again to restore earlier tabs when available. practice: close and restore two tabs. 4.3 reach tab groups with the keyboard what you will learn: access group controls when your chrome setup uses tab groups. before you begin: at least one tab group exists. exactly how to do it press f6 until the tabs are in focus. press tab or shift+tab to move among tab and group items. focus the tab group header. press spacebar or enter to collapse or expand it. press the menu/application key or shift+f10 to open its context menu. what should happen: the group expands/collapses and the menu can be reached without a mouse. if that does not happen: if no group header is announced, the current window may not contain a tab group. practice: create or use a practice tab group and collapse/expand it. part 5 - back, forward, reload, and home task command back alt+left arrow forward alt+right arrow reload ctrl+r or f5 reload ignoring cache ctrl+shift+r or shift+f5 home page alt+home stop loading escape 5.1 use back and forward what you will learn: move through recent pages in one tab. before you begin: follow at least one link from a starting page. exactly how to do it press alt+left arrow. listen for the previous page. press alt+right arrow. listen for the newer page. what should happen: chrome moves through the tab's history. if that does not happen: if nothing happens, the tab has no backward/forward history. practice: navigate three pages and move backward/forward. part 6 - webpage keyboard navigation 6.1 move through clickable page controls what you will learn: use only chrome keyboard focus navigation. before you begin: open a page with several links or form controls. exactly how to do it press tab. listen to the focused link, button, field, or control. press tab again. press shift+tab to move backward

entries.title: Google Docs Screen Reader Manual
entries.snippet: Google Docs Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: google docs screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual google docs screen reader manual keyboard-first document creation and collaboration independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches google docs from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains exactly what to press, what should receive focus, what the screen reader should announce, and how to recover when the result is different. reference setup: google docs works best as a web application in a current chrome browser. google recommends current screen readers and current chrome for best results. screen reader modes: jaws users should generally edit with the virtual pc cursor off. nvda users should generally edit in focus mode. voiceover users should turn quick nav off. narrator users may need scan mode off while editing. how to use this manual start with parts 1-12 even if you already know a screen reader. those sections teach google docs itself. press ctrl+alt+z on windows to enable or verify screen reader support. on mac, press command+option+z. google docs behaves like a web application rather than a normal webpage while editing. use alt+/ to search menus and commands when you know what you want but not where it is. use ctrl+/ to open google docs keyboard shortcuts. use ctrl+alt+h on windows or command+option+h on mac to enable braille support. use headings, lists, comments, and tables structurally rather than only visually. save is automatic in google docs, but you still need to verify the correct google account and document name. before sharing, verify both the recipient and the permission level. table of contents part 1 - what google docs is part 2 - open a blank document part 3 - turn on screen reader support part 4 - learn the google docs interface part 5 - enter and edit text part 6 - move through a document part 7 - format text and paragraphs part 8 - headings and document structure part 9 - bulleted and numbered lists part 10 - tables part 11 - links, images, and alt text part 12 - find, replace, and explore part 13 - comments and suggestions part 14 - sharing and collaboration part 15 - version history part 16 - download, print, and export part 17 - jaws with google docs part 18 - nvda with google docs part 19 - narrator with google docs part 20 - voiceover with google docs part 21 - braille displays part 22 - accessibility and document design part 23 - troubleshooting part 24 - independent practice course part 25 - quick reference commands part 26 - official google resources part 1 - what google docs is google docs is a browser-based word processor. documents are stored in google drive and can be edited, commented on, suggested, shared, and downloaded in other formats. document body: the editable text area. menu bar: file, edit, view, insert, format, tools, extensions, help, and accessibility-related commands. toolbar: common formatting and document controls. comments: discussion attached to selected text or locations. suggesting mode: proposed edits that can be accepted or rejected. share dialog: controls who can view, comment, or edit. version history: earlier saved states of the document. part 2 - open a blank document 2.1 create a new google doc what you will learn: open a blank document quickly. before you begin: sign in to the intended google account first. exactly how to do it open chrome. press ctrl+l. type docs.new. press enter. wait for the document to load. listen for a message such as screen reader support enabled or the document editing area. type: google docs practice document. what should happen: a new untitled document opens and text appears in the editing area. if that does not happen: if another account opens the document, switch accounts before continuing. if focus stays in browser controls, press f6/tab until the editor is active. practice: create a new document and type one sentence. part 3 - turn on screen reader support 3.1 enable screen reader support what you will learn: make docs expose its accessibility commands and announcements. before you begin: a google doc is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+alt+z on windows or command+option+z on mac. listen for confirmation that screen reader support is enabled. if you prefer the menu, open tools with alt+shift+t on windows or control+option+t on mac. choose accessibility settings. check turn on screen reader support. close the dialog. what should happen: google docs announces screen-reader-aware editing information and accessibility commands become available. if that does not happen: if ctrl+alt+z performs another system action, use the tools > accessibility settings method. practice: turn support off and back on once so you recognize the announcement. part 4 - learn the google docs interface 4.1 move between major areas what you will learn: identify menus, toolbar, and document body. before you begin: a document is open with screen reader support enabled. exactly how to do it press alt+/. listen for the search menus field. press escape. use tab/shift+tab to move among top-level buttons and controls. use alt+shift+f on windows when you need to focus the menu bar, then use left/right arrow through menus. press escape to return toward the document. move back to the editing area and type one character, then undo with ctrl+z. what should happen: you can distinguish the docs chrome from the document editing area. if that does not happen: if typing activates a menu command, focus is not in the document body. press escape and return to the editor. practice: move to menu bar, toolbar, and document body without a mouse. menu shortcut tip: google docs exposes many commands through alt+/ search menus. this is often easier than memorizing a long menu path. part 5 - enter and edit text task command move character left/right arrow move word ctrl+left/right arrow move line up/down arrow line start/end home/end document start/end ctrl+home/ctrl+end select text shift with navigation keys undo/redo ctrl+z / ctrl+y 5.1 type and correct text what you will learn: edit text with standard windows commands. before you begin: place the cursor in the document body. exactly how to do it type a short paragraph. press ctrl+left arrow to move backward by word. press left/right arrow to move by character. press backspace or delete to remove incorrect text. type the correction. use ctrl+home and ctrl+end to confirm beginning/end navigation. what should happen: text is corrected at the cursor location. if that does not happen: if arrows move browser focus instead of text, return to the document editing area and make sure the screen reader is in editing/focus mode. practice: create three errors and correct them. part 6 - move through a document 6.1 announce cursor location what you will learn: ask docs where the cursor is. before you begin: screen reader support is enabled. exactly how to do it hold ctrl+alt. press a, then l. release the keys. listen for docs to announce the cursor location. what should happen: docs announces location information appropriate to the context. if that does not happen: if the sequence does not work, make sure screen reader support is enabled and the browser/keyboard layout is not intercepting ctrl+alt. practice: use the command in three different paragraphs. 6.2 read from the cursor what you will learn: have docs verbalize content starting from the current location. before you begin: place the cursor in a paragraph. exactly how to do it hold ctrl+alt. press a, then r. release the keys. listen to the document content from the cursor. what should happen: docs verbalizes content from the current position. if that does not happen: if no speech occurs, verify screen reader support and focus. practice: read from two different cursor locations. part 7 - format text and paragraphs task command bold ctrl+b italic ctrl+i underline ctrl+u clear formatting ctrl+\ align left ctrl+shift+l center

entries.snippet: Google Drive Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: google drive screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual google drive screen reader manual files, folders, sharing, and cloud storage independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches google drive from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains exactly what to press, what should receive focus, what the screen reader should announce, and how to recover when the result is different. reference setup: this manual focuses on google drive on the web in a current browser, plus practical drive for desktop and mobile basics. screen-reader approach: google recommends using drive as a web application rather than as a normal web page. jaws users generally work with virtual pc cursor off; nvda users generally work in focus mode; narrator users may need scan mode off; voiceover users should turn quick nav off when drive needs to receive its own keyboard commands. how to use this manual start with parts 1-12 before concentrating on your screen reader. those sections teach drive itself. use alt+n on windows to open the new menu. use slash (/) to begin a drive search. use alt+g, then i to move to the items view. use alt+g, then n to move to the navigation panel. use ctrl+/ to open google's current drive keyboard-shortcuts list. use alt+shift+a for actions that apply to the current folder. use spacebar to select or clear selection on an item in the items view. use enter to open a selected folder or file. before sharing, verify both the person and the permission level. table of contents part 1 - what google drive is part 2 - open drive and identify the account part 3 - learn the drive interface part 4 - navigate my drive and folders part 5 - select files and folders part 6 - create folders and google files part 7 - upload files and folders part 8 - open and preview files part 9 - download files part 10 - rename, move, copy, and create shortcuts part 11 - star, recent, shared with me, and activity part 12 - search google drive part 13 - share files and folders part 14 - permissions and link sharing part 15 - version history and file details part 16 - trash, restore, and delete permanently part 17 - shared drives and organizational content part 18 - offline access and drive for desktop part 19 - jaws with google drive part 20 - nvda with google drive part 21 - narrator with google drive part 22 - voiceover with google drive part 23 - braille displays part 24 - iphone/ipad and android basics part 25 - security and privacy part 26 - troubleshooting part 27 - independent practice course part 28 - quick reference commands part 29 - official google resources part 1 - what google drive is google drive is google's cloud file-storage and collaboration service. it stores files and folders, connects to google docs/sheets/slides, supports sharing and collaboration, and can synchronize files with a computer. my drive: files, folders, and shortcuts you created or added to your drive. shared with me: files and folders other people shared directly with you. recent: items you accessed recently. starred: items you marked for quick access. trash/bin: items you deleted but have not yet permanently removed. shared drives: organization-owned storage used by teams in eligible google workspace accounts. shortcut: a reference to another file or folder; it is not an independent copy. drive for desktop: google's windows/macos synchronization application. part 2 - open drive and identify the account 2.1 open google drive what you will learn: reach your drive from the browser. before you begin: use the intended google account. exactly how to do it open chrome or another supported browser. press ctrl+l. type drive.google.com. press enter. wait for drive to load. use f6/tab or the screen reader to locate the google account/profile control. confirm the account name or email address before opening or sharing files. what should happen: google drive opens under the intended account. if that does not happen: if the wrong account is active, switch google accounts before creating, uploading, or sharing anything. practice: open drive and identify the active account. part 3 - learn the drive interface drive has several major regions. google documents dedicated keyboard commands to move directly among them. task command navigation panel alt+g, then n folders list alt+g, then f items view alt+g, then i page content alt+g, then c details pane alt+g, then d top of application / google bar alt+g, then t download status alt+g, then a upload status alt+g, then u 3.1 move directly to the items view what you will learn: reach the file/folder list without tabbing through the whole page. before you begin: drive is open. exactly how to do it press alt+g. release the keys. press i. listen for the items view and the currently focused file/folder. use arrow keys through the items. what should happen: focus moves directly to the drive items area. if that does not happen: if the shortcut is intercepted, place the screen reader in application/focus mode and try again. practice: move to items, navigation, and details using the alt+g sequences. part 4 - navigate my drive and folders 4.1 open my drive what you will learn: move from anywhere in drive to your main drive storage. before you begin: drive is open. exactly how to do it press alt+g, then n. use up/down arrow through the navigation panel. stop on my drive. press enter. press alt+g, then i to move to its items. what should happen: my drive opens and the items view contains its files/folders. if that does not happen: if my drive is already selected, pressing enter may simply refresh focus; use alt+g then i afterward. practice: open my drive and identify three items. 4.2 open and leave a folder what you will learn: enter a folder and return to its parent. before you begin: focus a folder in the items view. exactly how to do it press enter. wait for the folder to open. use arrow keys through its contents. to return, move to the drive breadcrumb/current folder path with tab/f6 or use browser back with alt+left arrow when appropriate. confirm the parent folder name after returning. what should happen: the folder opens and you can return to the parent location. if that does not happen: if enter previews instead of opens, confirm the focused item is actually a folder. practice: open two folder levels and return. part 5 - select files and folders 5.1 select one item what you will learn: select a file/folder without opening it. before you begin: focus is in the items view. exactly how to do it use arrow keys to move to the desired item. press spacebar. listen for selected status. press spacebar again to clear selection if needed. what should happen: the item is selected without opening. if that does not happen: if spacebar opens a preview or scrolls, verify the items view has application focus. practice: select and deselect three items. 5.2 select multiple items what you will learn: select several items for one action. before you begin: focus the first item. exactly how to do it press spacebar to select it. move with arrow keys to another item. press spacebar to add it to the selection. repeat for a third item. use the available actions only after confirming the selected count. press escape or clear selections when finished. what should happen: multiple items are selected. if that does not happen: if moving clears the first selection in your current view, use ctrl/shift selection methods available in the shortcuts list or act on one item at a time. practice: select two practice items and clear selection. part 6 - create folders and google files 6.1 create a new folder what you will learn: create a named folder without using the mouse. before you begin: open the drive location where the folder should be created. exactly how to do it press alt+n. listen for the new menu. use arrow keys to folder. press enter. type the folder name. press enter. wait f

entries.title: Google Drive, Gmail, Forms, and Classroom Manual
entries.course: Google Drive, Gmail, Forms, and Classroom
entries.snippet: Step-by-step keyboard manual for Google Drive, Gmail, Forms, and Classroom.
entries.text: google services manual - accessible learning center skip to main content google applications google drive, gmail, forms, and classroom manual complete common google tasks with the keyboard and a screen reader. basic how-tos advanced how-tos command list basic how-tos google drive: open a file what you will learn: complete google drive: open a file independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: tab and shift+tab move among controls. arrow keys move within a file list. enter opens the selected item. open drive.google.com and confirm the google account. use your screen reader’s heading command to find my drive or shared with me. press tab until the file list is announced. use arrow keys to select a file and listen for its name, type, owner, and modified date. press enter to open it. what should happen: a file-list item followed by the file’s name and details. if that does not happen: press escape once to leave an open menu, then navigate by headings or landmarks back to the file area. practice: repeat google drive: open a file with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. google drive: upload a file what you will learn: complete google drive: upload a file independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: use heading and button navigation to find new, then choose file upload. open the drive folder that should receive the file. find and activate the new button. choose file upload. in the file picker, type the complete path or navigate to the file. select it and press enter. wait for the upload-complete announcement, then locate the file in drive. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: do not upload again immediately. search the folder for the filename and check for an upload-status alert. practice: repeat google drive: upload a file with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. gmail: read and reply what you will learn: complete gmail: read and reply independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: tab moves through controls. enter opens a focused message. ctrl+enter may send only when that gmail confirmation setting is enabled. open gmail and confirm the correct account and inbox. navigate to the message list and select the intended sender and subject. press enter and read the full message. find and activate reply. write the response and review quoted content. find the send button and activate it. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: navigate by headings and buttons. do not rely on single-letter shortcuts until gmail keyboard shortcuts are enabled in settings. practice: repeat gmail: read and reply with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. gmail: compose a new message what you will learn: complete gmail: compose a new message independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard command: c opens compose only after gmail keyboard shortcuts are enabled. activate compose by its labeled button, or press c if shortcuts are enabled. enter the recipient, press tab, and enter the subject. move to the message body and write the message. locate any attachment and verify its filename. review recipients, subject, and body, then activate send. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: use tab and shift+tab to locate each labeled field. escape may close the compose window while saving a draft. practice: repeat gmail: compose a new message with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. advanced how-tos google drive: share with one person what you will learn: complete google drive: share with one person independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard command: shift+f10 opens the selected file’s context menu in supported browsers and configurations. select the exact file and hear its complete name. press shift+f10 and choose share. enter the person’s email address. choose viewer, commenter, or editor deliberately. review the recipient and permission, then send the invitation. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: cancel the dialog and locate the labeled share button. never choose “anyone with the link” by accident. practice: repeat google drive: share with one person with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. google forms: create and test a question what you will learn: complete google forms: create and test a question independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: tab and shift+tab move among editor controls; space activates a focused button or checkbox. create a blank form and enter a descriptive title and instructions. find add question and activate it. enter a complete question, then choose the correct response type. turn required on only when necessary. open preview, navigate the form by keyboard, submit practice answers, and verify the confirmation message. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: confirm whether focus is in the editor, question text, toolbar, or preview before continuing. practice: repeat google forms: create and test a question with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. google classroom: submit an assignment what you will learn: complete google classroom: submit an assignment independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: navigate by headings, links, and buttons; enter or space activates the focused control. open the class and verify the assignment heading. read all instructions, due information, and attached resources. find your work, then add or create. add the correct drive file or upload a file. hear the attached filename, then activate turn in. read the confirmation dialog and confirm only when correct. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: return to the assignment heading and inspect controls in reading order. verify whether the work says assigned, turned in, or returned.
