or activate space: activate a button or change a checkbox escape: close a menu or dialog shift+f10: context menu ctrl+f: browser find, not drive search c in gmail: compose, when gmail shortcuts are enabled r in gmail: reply, when gmail shortcuts are enabled return to manuals

entries.title: Google Gemini Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible keyboard-first Google Gemini manual for blind and low-vision learners.
entries.text: google gemini manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible google gemini course google gemini manual practical, responsible ai skills for work, learning, and independent problem-solving. basics prompting verification privacy screen readers lessons what generative ai does generative ai predicts and creates text or other content from patterns in training data and the information supplied in a conversation. it can help brainstorm, organize, explain, summarize, and draft. it does not understand a situation the way a person does, and it can produce confident but incorrect or invented information. use ai as an assistant, not as the final decision-maker. a person remains responsible for checking accuracy, appropriateness, accessibility, and compliance with workplace rules. a reliable prompt pattern task: state exactly what you want. context: explain the audience and purpose using nonprivate information. constraints: give length, tone, reading level, deadline, or other limits. format: request headings, bullets, a numbered procedure, or a simple table. checks: ask the tool to identify uncertainty and provide sources when appropriate. continue the conversation with specific follow-ups. for example: “shorten this to 150 words,” “explain the second step,” or “which statements need verification?” verify before using the result open original sources instead of trusting an ai summary or citation. confirm names, dates, quotations, calculations, contact details, laws, policies, and software instructions. prefer current primary sources from the organization responsible for the information. compare important claims with a second reliable source. test instructions safely before giving them to another person. rewrite the final result in your own voice and keep a record of corrections. privacy and workplace rules do not enter client records, medical or disability details, passwords, financial account information, private addresses, confidential workplace material, copyrighted documents you are not permitted to share, or information that identifies another person. use fictional or public information in these lessons. follow the employer’s approved-tool, retention, disclosure, and human-review requirements. a personal free account is not automatically approved for organizational data. never allow ai to make an employment, benefit, medical, legal, financial, safety, or accommodation decision for a person. accessible output ask for descriptive headings, short paragraphs, meaningful link text, numbered steps, and simple tables. ask for image descriptions when an image matters, but verify the description with a trusted person when accuracy is important. avoid layouts that communicate meaning only through color, position, or visual formatting. jaws, narrator, and nvda ai interfaces change often. use tab and shift+tab to move among controls, enter or space to activate a control, and the screen reader’s heading, landmark, link, button, edit-field, and browse-mode commands to review the page. use browser find to locate words such as “sources,” “copy,” or part of your prompt. jaws: h moves by heading, b by button, e by edit field, insert+f7 opens links, and insert+f5 opens form fields. nvda: h moves by heading, b by button, e by edit field, nvda+f7 opens the elements list, and nvda+space switches browse and focus modes. narrator: use caps lock or insert with arrow keys for scan mode navigation; press caps lock+space to toggle scan mode when needed. after sending a prompt, allow time for the response to finish. move by heading or paragraph and confirm whether focus changed. product-specific keyboard behavior may change after updates. free-course rule these lessons can be completed with an available free ai service or by studying the examples without creating an account. do not start a paid trial, enter payment information, or purchase a subscription for this course. official references official gemini apps help google: verify responses from gemini apps basic and advanced step-by-step procedures these procedures make the manual usable on its own. the separate lessons provide assignments and progress tracking when you want a course experience. basic 1: open gemini and navigate the chat interface basic 2: write prompts with purpose, context, and format basic 3: refine a response through follow-up prompts basic 4: create clear workplace checklists and plans basic 5: summarize public web information and verify it advanced 6: draft content for google docs and gmail advanced 7: plan calendar tasks and spreadsheet information advanced 8: review sources, bias, and missing information advanced 9: use gemini with jaws, narrator, or nvda advanced 10: final google gemini workplace project basic procedure 1. open gemini and navigate the chat interface what you will learn: identify the prompt field, send control, new-chat control, response area, and account controls. before you begin: use a free or approved ai service and only fictional or public information. do not enter private workplace, client, medical, financial, or account information. exactly how to do it open the google gemini manual and review the prompting, verification, privacy, and screen-reader sections. open an available ai tool in a regular browser tab. if an account or feature is unavailable, study the sample prompt and write the expected process instead. navigate by headings and form controls. find the prompt edit field and confirm its label before typing. use this practice prompt or adapt it without adding private information: act as an accessible workplace skills coach. help me identify the prompt field, send control, new-chat control, response area, and account controls. use fictional or public information only. organize the response with descriptive headings and numbered steps. identify anything i must verify. read the complete response by heading, paragraph, list item, and link. do not assume the first answer is correct. send at least one follow-up prompt that improves clarity, accuracy, accessibility, or completeness. verify important claims using the original source or another authoritative source. record unsupported statements and corrections. edit the final result in your own words. remove generic, inaccurate, biased, or unnecessary content. create a short process note naming the tool, prompts used, facts checked, changes made, and remaining uncertainty. save the assignment as gemini-lesson-1.txt . screen-reader help: jaws and nvda users can press h for headings, b for buttons, and e for edit fields in browse mode. narrator users can navigate with scan mode. press tab and shift+tab for interactive controls. because ai interfaces change frequently, listen to each control’s current accessible name. what should happen: you can complete the procedure and verify the result using the keyboard, your screen reader, or your braille display. if that does not happen: confirm focus is in the intended edit field or control. review the page by headings and buttons, shorten the request, and never solve an interface problem by entering private information or starting a paid trial. practice: identify the prompt field, send control, new-chat control, response area, and account controls. basic procedure 2. write prompts with purpose, context, and format what you will learn: request a fictional workplace procedure with an audience, length limit, and numbered format. before you begin: use a free or approved ai service and only fictional or public information. do not enter private workplace, client, medical, financial, or account information. exactly how to do it open the google gemini manual and review the prompting, verification, privacy, and screen-reader sections. open an available ai tool in a regular browser tab. if an account or feature is unavailable, study the sample prompt and write the expected process instead. navigate by headings and form controls. find the prompt edit field and confirm its label before typ

entries.snippet: Google Meet Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: google meet screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual google meet screen reader manual keyboard-first online meetings independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual google: use google meet with a screen reader purpose: this manual teaches google meet from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains exactly what to press, what should receive focus, what the screen reader should announce, and how to recover when the result is different. reference setup: this manual focuses on google meet on a computer in a current chrome browser, with practical mobile sections. feature availability: some meet features depend on google account type, workspace edition, administrator settings, host controls, meeting size, or rollout status. if a button is missing or disabled, that does not always mean you are using meet incorrectly. how to use this manual work through parts 1-14 before concentrating on your screen reader. those sections teach meet itself. use ctrl+d on windows/chromeos to mute or unmute your microphone. use ctrl+e to turn your camera on or off. use ctrl+alt+c to open or close meeting chat. use ctrl+alt+p to open or close the people/participants sidebar. use ctrl+alt+h to raise or lower your hand. use ctrl+alt+s to hear who is currently speaking. use ctrl+alt+i to hear current room/meeting information. use ctrl+alt+x to hear recently received reactions. press ctrl+/ to open the meet shortcut dialog. press escape to close a meet sidebar or dialog when appropriate. before presenting your screen, close confidential windows and verify exactly what will be shared. table of contents part 1 - what google meet is part 2 - open meet and join a meeting part 3 - the pre-call screen part 4 - learn the in-meeting layout part 5 - microphone and camera part 6 - speaker, microphone, and camera settings part 7 - captions part 8 - people and participants part 9 - meeting chat part 10 - raise and lower your hand part 11 - reactions part 12 - present your screen part 13 - stop presenting and recover focus part 14 - leave a meeting part 15 - meeting details, links, and joining information part 16 - sidebars and dialogs part 17 - host controls and moderation part 18 - picture-in-picture and companion mode part 19 - jaws with google meet part 20 - nvda with google meet part 21 - narrator with google meet part 22 - voiceover with google meet part 23 - braille displays part 24 - iphone/ipad and android part 25 - accessibility and communication practices part 26 - security and privacy part 27 - troubleshooting part 28 - independent practice course part 29 - quick reference commands part 30 - official google resources part 1 - what google meet is google meet is google's video-meeting service. a meeting can include audio, video, captions, participants, chat, reactions, hand raising, screen sharing, host controls, and other activities depending on the account and meeting. pre-call screen: the page before you enter the meeting. in-meeting control bar: microphone, camera, captions, hand raise, presentation, more options, and leave controls. people sidebar: participant list and raised hands. chat sidebar: meeting messages. activities sidebar: polls, q&a, breakout rooms, and other features when available. host controls sidebar: moderation controls for eligible hosts/co-hosts. dialog: temporary window such as settings, shortcuts, or troubleshooting. presentation: a shared tab, window, full screen, or supported camera source. part 2 - open meet and join a meeting 2.1 join from a calendar or email link what you will learn: open the correct meeting and reach the pre-call screen. before you begin: have the legitimate meeting invitation available. exactly how to do it open the meeting invitation. move to the google meet link. read the link or surrounding event information to verify it is the expected meeting. press enter. wait for meet.google.com to open. confirm you are signed in with the intended google account if the meeting requires it. wait for the pre-call screen before pressing join. what should happen: the meeting's pre-call screen opens. if that does not happen: if the page asks for permission to use microphone/camera, allow only if you intend to use those devices and trust the meeting. practice: open a test meeting link and stop at the pre-call screen. 2.2 join with a meeting code what you will learn: enter a code without needing a calendar event. before you begin: know the meeting code or nickname and that you are authorized to join. exactly how to do it open meet.google.com. move to the field for entering a code or link. type or paste the meeting code. activate join. wait for the pre-call screen. what should happen: meet opens the requested meeting. if that does not happen: if the code is invalid or expired, verify it with the organizer rather than guessing variants. practice: practice entering a known safe meeting code. part 3 - the pre-call screen 3.1 review microphone and camera before joining what you will learn: enter the meeting in the state you intend. before you begin: the pre-call screen is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+d and listen for whether the microphone is muted or unmuted. press ctrl+e and listen for whether the camera is on or off. choose the state you want before joining. use tab through the pre-call controls. locate settings if you need to change speaker, microphone, or camera. locate join now or ask to join. review your own displayed account/name if available. activate join now or ask to join only when ready. what should happen: you enter with the intended microphone and camera state. if that does not happen: if the microphone/camera shortcut does not respond, browser permission may be blocked or another application may be using the device. practice: practice reaching join without activating it. good default: when joining a group meeting, entering muted reduces accidental background audio unless the meeting expects immediate speaking. part 4 - learn the in-meeting layout google's current desktop layout keeps the main call controls in a bottom bar. meeting details, people, chat, and activities are grouped toward the lower-right area; exact control order can vary by account and feature availability. 4.1 explore without activating controls what you will learn: learn where the current meet controls are. before you begin: join a safe meeting. exactly how to do it press tab once. listen to the focused control. continue pressing tab slowly. listen for microphone, camera, captions, hand raise, present now, more options, and leave call. continue to meeting-details/people/chat/activities controls. press shift+tab to move backward. do not press space or enter unless you intend to activate a control. what should happen: you can identify the control bar and side-panel controls. if that does not happen: if focus enters another browser region, use shift+tab/f6 or screen-reader focus navigation to return to the meet controls. practice: tab through the main controls twice without changing anything. leave button safety: google deliberately separates the leave call button from microphone/camera controls to reduce accidental hangups, but keyboard users should still listen to the focused button name before pressing enter. part 5 - microphone and camera task command mute/unmute microphone - windows/chromeos ctrl+d camera on/off - windows/chromeos ctrl+e mute/unmute microphone - macos command+d camera on/off - macos command+e 5.1 mute and unmute what you will learn: control whether other participants can hear you. before you begin: you are in a meeting. exactly how to do it press ctrl+d. listen for the new microphone state. press ctrl+d again. listen for the opposite state. leave the microphone in the state you intend. what should happen: meet changes the microphone state. if that does not happen: if the microphone is unavailable, check meet settings, browser permission

entries.title: iPhone and iPad VoiceOver Manual
entries.snippet: iPhone and iPad VoiceOver Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: iphone and ipad voiceover manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual iphone and ipad voiceover manual touch gestures, navigation, typing, and apps independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches iphone and ipad from the beginning to a person using voiceover. it explains where controls are physically located, what gesture to use, what voiceover should announce, how to recover when the result is different, and how to practice each skill independently. reference version: the manual is based on apple's current ios 26 and ipados 26 voiceover guidance. some screens and feature names can vary by device model, carrier, region, and installed apps. device differences: iphone models with face id use the side button and edge gestures. older iphone models and some ipads have a physical home button. ipads may use a top button with touch id or face id depending on model. how to use this manual practice new gestures first in settings > accessibility > voiceover > voiceover practice so a mistake does not activate something unexpectedly. voiceover changes ordinary touch gestures. a single tap selects and speaks an item; a double-tap activates the selected item. swipe right moves to the next item. swipe left moves to the previous item. a two-finger scrub means move two fingers back and forth quickly three times in a z shape. it commonly means back, cancel, or dismiss. a two-finger double-tap is the magic tap. its action depends on context, such as answering/hanging up a call or starting/stopping media or dictation. three-finger swipes scroll pages and lists. four-finger gestures move quickly to screen edges or among apps. the rotor changes what an up/down swipe does. learn the rotor early; it is central to efficient voiceover use. if you become disoriented, touch the screen to hear what is under your finger, then swipe left/right to rebuild context. for passwords or other sensitive information, use headphones or silent braille input when privacy matters. table of contents part 1 - physical orientation: iphone and ipad part 2 - turn voiceover on and off part 3 - voiceover practice and core gestures part 4 - select, activate, and explore by touch part 5 - scroll, go home, and switch apps part 6 - lock screen and unlocking part 7 - status bar, control center, and notifications part 8 - home screen, app library, and search part 9 - the voiceover rotor part 10 - onscreen keyboard and typing modes part 11 - edit, select, copy, and paste text part 12 - dictation, siri, and magic tap part 13 - safari and web navigation part 14 - messages part 15 - phone and facetime on iphone part 16 - mail part 17 - settings and voiceover customization part 18 - screen curtain and privacy part 19 - voiceover recognition and image descriptions part 20 - braille screen input part 21 - refreshable braille displays part 22 - braille access part 23 - external keyboards part 24 - files, downloads, and sharing part 25 - app-specific actions and the actions rotor part 26 - ipad multitasking and dock part 27 - safety and privacy part 28 - troubleshooting part 29 - independent practice course part 30 - quick reference gestures part 31 - official apple resources part 1 - physical orientation: iphone and ipad 1.1 iphone with face id hold the iphone with the screen facing you and the charging/data port at the bottom. the side button is on the right edge. it wakes/locks the phone and is used for the accessibility shortcut when configured. volume up and volume down are on the left edge. the action button or ring/silent control is also on the left edge, depending on model. the front-facing camera/sensor area is near the top of the screen. the speaker/earpiece is near the top edge. the charging port is centered on the bottom edge on current models; speakers/microphones are also along the bottom edge. 1.2 iphone with home button the home button is centered below the screen. press it to go home; double-click it for the app switcher. the side or top sleep/wake button is used to lock/wake the phone, depending on model. volume controls are on the left edge. 1.3 ipad hold the ipad with the screen facing you. the charging port is centered on one short edge; exact speaker positions depend on model. the top button is on an outer edge and wakes/locks the ipad. on some models it also contains touch id. volume controls are near the top button on current models, but position varies by ipad generation. some ipads have a physical home button centered below the screen; newer models do not. because hardware layouts vary, identify your specific model in settings > general > about before memorizing physical positions. part 2 - turn voiceover on and off 2.1 turn voiceover on in settings what you will learn: enable the built-in screen reader. before you begin: you can currently see or have sighted assistance for the initial setup. exactly how to do it open settings. choose accessibility. choose voiceover. turn voiceover on. after voiceover starts, remember that one tap selects and a double-tap activates. what should happen: voiceover begins speaking the selected control. if that does not happen: if voiceover does not speak, raise media volume and verify voiceover is actually on. practice: turn it on and navigate back one screen. 2.2 use siri what you will learn: turn voiceover on/off without navigating settings. before you begin: siri is enabled. exactly how to do it activate siri with the side/top/home button or by voice if configured. say, turn on voiceover. to turn it off later, ask siri, turn off voiceover. what should happen: siri changes the voiceover state. if that does not happen: if siri cannot change the setting, use settings or the accessibility shortcut. practice: practice asking siri for voiceover status. 2.3 configure the accessibility shortcut what you will learn: toggle voiceover with a hardware-button triple-click. before you begin: voiceover is already configured enough to navigate settings. exactly how to do it open settings > accessibility. move to accessibility shortcut near the bottom. activate it. select voiceover. on iphone with face id, triple-click the side button. on devices with a home button, triple-click the home button. on ipad without home button, triple-click the top button. what should happen: voiceover toggles on/off or the shortcut menu appears if more than one accessibility feature is selected. if that does not happen: if nothing happens, verify voiceover is checked in accessibility shortcut and click quickly three times. practice: toggle voiceover with the shortcut once. part 3 - voiceover practice and core gestures 3.1 open voiceover practice what you will learn: learn gestures without triggering real actions. before you begin: voiceover is on. exactly how to do it open settings > accessibility > voiceover. find voiceover practice. double-tap to open it. try one-, two-, three-, and four-finger taps, double taps, triple taps, and swipes. listen to voiceover describe each gesture. activate done and double-tap to exit. what should happen: gestures are announced without performing their normal action. if that does not happen: if a gesture performs a real action, you may not be in voiceover practice. return to settings and reopen it. practice: spend at least five minutes practicing flicks and multifinger gestures. task gesture / action select/speak item single tap activate selected item double-tap next item swipe right previous item swipe left scroll one page three-finger swipe read from top two-finger swipe up read from current item two-finger swipe down pause/resume speech two-finger tap back/dismiss two-finger scrub magic tap two-finger double-tap first item on screen four-finger tap near top last item on screen four-finger tap near bottom part 4 - select, activate, checker when available, but also perform a keyboard and screen-reader review. keep an original editable file before exporting pdf or converting formats. native and exchange formats libreoffice native formats odt for writer, ods for calc, and odp for impress preserve libreoffice editing features. microsoft exchange formats docx, xlsx, and pptx are often required by employers or instructors using microsoft 365. other formats csv carries plain spreadsheet data without formulas or formatting. pdf is useful for fixed-layout review but may be harder to edit and must be checked for accessibility. save the native version first. then save or download a separate exchange copy and review it in the receiving program whenever possible. jaws, narrator, and nvda interfaces vary by program and update. nvda+t for the title, nvda+tab for focus, and nvda+1 for input help. narrator: use caps lock+t for the title and caps lock+1 for input learning. toggle scan mode only when the application or webpage requires it. browser-based editors may have their own screen-reader-support setting and keyboard shortcuts. read the current official help before changing screen-reader modes. compatibility review exchange copy. never promise perfect compatibility without testing the actual document in the receiving software. privacy, accounts, and sharing use fictional or public information in these lessons. entries.title: Mantis Q40 Detailed Instructor Training Manual
entries.snippet: Mantis Q40 Detailed Instructor Training Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: mantis q40 detailed instructor training manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual mantis q40 detailed instructor training manual teaching, setup, troubleshooting, and advanced operation instructor reference guide all manuals table of contents start of manual official humanware mantis q40 support purpose: this is a teaching manual. it is written so an instructor can answer how at every step: which control to locate, which key to press, what the learner should hear or feel, what to do next, and how to verify independent performance. source note: humanware currently provides mantis user guide 2.6, getting started, ios, jaws, android, chromebook, mac connection, faq, release notes, and firmware 2.6.0 build 5120 resources on its support page. copyright note: this manual is original instructional material and is not a word-for-word reproduction of humanware documentation. how to use this manual do not tell the learner only what to do. always demonstrate how. name the system before the command: mantis, mac, voiceover, windows, jaws, nvda, ios, or android. after every action, tell the learner what they should feel in braille or hear from the screen reader. use guided practice first, then remove prompts. a learner has mastered a skill only when they can repeat it accurately without instructor cues. command labels used throughout system action what to press / do mantis device command a command performed on the mantis q40 itself. mac standard mac command a normal macos keyboard shortcut. voiceover apple screen-reader command vo means control+option by default, or caps lock if configured. screen reader jaws/nvda/narrator a command whose behavior comes from the computer's screen reader. table of contents 1. physical orientation and controls 2. power, charging, and startup 3. basic mantis navigation 4. main menu and context menu 5. braille display reading skills 6. cursor-routing buttons 7. editor: create, type, edit, save, open 8. library: open and read files 9. brf/brl and file management 10. wi-fi 11. firmware update 12. bluetooth pairing concepts 13. connect mantis to a mac 14. voiceover navigation on mac - exact how 15. voiceover text editing with mantis 16. connect mantis to iphone/ipad 17. jaws connection and teaching workflow 18. nvda connection and teaching workflow 19. chromebook / android overview 20. troubleshooting decision procedures 21. instructor lesson plans 22. mastery checklists 23. quick reference commands 24. official resources 1. physical orientation and controls lesson 1.1 - learn the device by touch what you will learn: complete lesson 1.1 - learn the device by touch independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it goal: identify the major parts of the mantis without visual assistance. why this matters: efficient braille use begins with reliable hand placement and tactile orientation. instructor explanation: explain that the mantis combines a full qwerty keyboard with 40 refreshable braille cells. the learner should be able to return to a known physical reference point whenever they become disoriented. how - step-by-step place the mantis flat on a table with the braille cells closest to the learner. have the learner place both hands lightly on the qwerty keyboard. find the f and j home-row keys by touch. move both hands forward toward the learner until the 40-cell braille display is located. slide one index finger slowly from the leftmost braille cell to the rightmost cell. explain that each cell can raise and lower pins. move the fingertip immediately above the braille cells to locate the row of cursor-routing buttons. locate the thumb/navigation controls near the front edge. do not press them yet; simply identify them. locate the power and connection areas by touch. explain which ports are used for charging/usb. return hands to the home-row position. repeat the route from home row to braille cells and back three times. instructor check: the learner can point to the keyboard, braille cells, routing buttons, and navigation controls without prompting. guided practice: ask the learner to close their eyes or work nonvisually and identify each control you name. common mistakes: reaching too quickly and pressing controls while exploring. teach light touch first. mastery check: the learner identifies all major controls correctly two times in a row. 2. power, charging, and startup what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: press escape, confirm the active window and focus, and repeat one numbered step at a time. practice: repeat lesson 1.1 - learn the device by touch with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. lesson 2.1 - power on and recognize startup what you will learn: complete lesson 2.1 - power on and recognize startup independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it goal: turn the mantis on and recognize when startup is complete. why this matters: clients need a reliable starting procedure before any other task. instructor explanation: explain that the braille cells may change during startup. the learner should wait for the device to finish loading before beginning navigation. how - step-by-step make sure the mantis has been charged or connected to power. locate the mantis power control by touch. press and hold the power control as required for normal startup, then release it. place one hand on the braille display and wait for the cells to initialize. read the information that appears on the braille display after startup. if a menu item is displayed, tell the learner this is the current focus. do not type until startup is complete. instructor check: the learner can tell you when the mantis has finished startup and what item is currently displayed. guided practice: power the device off and on again and have the learner repeat without verbal prompting. common mistakes: pressing keys repeatedly during startup or assuming a blank display means failure immediately. mastery check: the learner powers on, waits appropriately, and identifies the first displayed item independently. 3. basic mantis navigation teach these commands before any application. humanware documentation uses the thumb/navigation controls for movement and standard qwerty keys for activation and menus. system action what to press / do mantis move to previous menu item press the previous thumb/navigation key once. mantis move to next menu item press the next thumb/navigation key once. mantis activate/open current item press enter. a cursor-routing button on the displayed item can also be used in supported contexts. mantis pan braille left press the left thumb/navigation key. mantis pan braille right press the right thumb/navigation key. mantis open context menu press ctrl+m. mantis return to main menu use the documented main-menu shortcut for the installed firmware; windows/home-related commands may be available depending on context. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: press escape, confirm the active window and focus, and repeat one numbered step at a time. practice: repeat lesson 2.1 - power on and recognize startup with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. lesson 3.1 - move through a menu what you will learn: complete lesson 3.1 - move through a menu independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it goal: move one item at a time and activate

entries.title: Mantis Q40 Independent Self-Study Manual
entries.snippet: Mantis Q40 Independent Self-Study Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: mantis q40 independent self-study manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual mantis q40 independent self-study manual braille display and qwerty keyboard operation independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual firmware 2.6 reference edition open humanware's official mantis q40 support page how this manual is different: this manual is written directly to you, the mantis user. it assumes you may be touching the device for the first time. every procedure tells you what to find, exactly what to press, what should happen, and what to try if it does not. reference version: humanware currently lists mantis user guide 2.6 and firmware 2.6.0 build 5120. menus or behavior can change in later firmware, so use the official humanware support link above whenever your screen differs from this manual. copyright: this is original training material. it summarizes and teaches use of the device without reproducing humanware's manual word-for-word. how to read this manual you do not need to memorize the entire manual. work through it in order the first time. later, use the headings and quick-reference sections to look up a task. whenever you see mantis, the command is performed on the mantis q40. whenever you see mac, it is a standard macos keyboard command. whenever you see voiceover, it is an apple voiceover command. vo means the voiceover modifier. by default, vo is control+option held together. caps lock can also be configured as vo. when you see 'press', press and release the key unless the instruction says to hold it. when you see a combination such as ctrl+m, hold ctrl, press m once, then release both keys. read the 'what should happen' paragraph after every procedure. it tells you how to confirm you succeeded. if your result is different, follow the 'if that does not happen' instructions before trying unrelated settings. table of contents part 1 — meet the mantis q40 part 2 — power, charging, startup, and shutdown part 3 — learn the basic navigation controls part 4 — understand the main menu and context menus part 5 — read braille on a 40-cell display part 6 — use cursor-routing buttons part 7 — use the built-in editor part 8 — open and read books and files in library part 9 — understand brf, brl, docx, txt, and other files part 10 — work with storage and file organization part 11 — connect to wi-fi part 12 — check and update firmware part 13 — understand bluetooth and terminal mode part 14 — connect the mantis to a mac part 15 — learn voiceover navigation from the beginning part 16 — type and edit on a mac with mantis part 17 — connect to iphone or ipad part 18 — connect to windows with jaws part 19 — connect to windows with nvda part 20 — narrator, chromebook, and android part 21 — braille settings and translation part 22 — battery, care, and safe transport part 23 — troubleshooting part 24 — practice course: beginner to independent part 25 — quick reference part 26 — official resources part 1 — meet the mantis q40 the mantis q40 is unusual because it combines two devices in one: a full qwerty keyboard and a 40-cell refreshable braille display. you can use it by itself for several tasks, or connect it to another device and use it as a braille display and keyboard. 40 refreshable braille cells display text tactually. a row of cursor-routing buttons lets you move directly to a braille position. the qwerty keyboard lets you type the same way you would on a conventional computer keyboard. navigation/thumb controls let you move through menus and pan the braille display. bluetooth and usb can connect the mantis to computers and mobile devices. standalone applications include tools such as editor, library, online library, terminal, calculator, and date/time depending on firmware and configuration. supported files: humanware lists doc, docx, txt, brf, and brl for the editor, and brf, pef, txt, html, docx, niso, and rtf for the library. 1.1 orient the mantis by touch what you will learn: find the keyboard, braille cells, routing buttons, and navigation controls without relying on sight. before you begin: put the mantis on a table with the braille display edge closest to your body. exactly how to do it rest both hands lightly on the qwerty keyboard. find the familiar typing area and the home-row keys. move both hands toward your body until your fingertips reach the long horizontal row of 40 braille cells. move one index finger slowly from the far-left braille cell to the far-right braille cell. do not press hard. refreshable braille pins are designed to be read with light fingertip pressure. move your fingertip slightly above the braille cells. feel for the small cursor-routing buttons positioned above the cells. return your hands to the front edge and locate the thumb/navigation controls. these controls are used frequently for moving and panning. move your hands back to the qwerty keyboard. repeat the route keyboard → braille display → routing buttons → navigation controls → keyboard until you can find each area without searching. what should happen: you can name and locate the keyboard, 40 braille cells, routing buttons, and navigation controls. if that does not happen: if you become disoriented, stop pressing keys. return both hands to the qwerty home row and begin the tactile route again. practice: with the mantis turned off, locate all four areas three times in a row. part 2 — power, charging, startup, and shutdown 2.1 charge the mantis what you will learn: connect the mantis to power safely. before you begin: use the charging equipment supplied with or approved for the mantis. exactly how to do it locate the charging/usb connection on the mantis. insert the appropriate charging cable gently. do not force the connector. if it does not enter easily, verify orientation. connect the other end to the appropriate power source. leave the mantis connected long enough to obtain a useful charge before long sessions. before disconnecting, hold the plug rather than pulling on the cable. what should happen: the device charges and can be powered on normally. if that does not happen: if the device will not charge, try a known-good cable/power source that is appropriate for the device. inspect the port for debris without inserting metal objects. if charging still fails, contact humanware support. practice: practice locating the charging port with the device powered off. 2.2 turn the mantis on what you will learn: power on the device and recognize when startup is complete. before you begin: make sure the battery is charged or the device is connected to power. exactly how to do it locate the power control. press and hold the power control for normal startup, then release it. place your reading fingers lightly on the braille display. wait while the braille cells initialize. do not repeatedly press keyboard keys while the device is starting. when text or a menu item appears on the braille display, read it. pause before doing anything else. the displayed item is the current focus. what should happen: the braille display initializes and a menu/status item becomes readable. if that does not happen: if nothing happens, connect power and try again. if the display briefly changes but then becomes blank, allow additional startup time before assuming failure. practice: power the device on from a completely off state two times. 2.3 turning the mantis off use the normal power/shutdown procedure rather than disconnecting power or forcing a restart. save open files first. if an application asks whether to save changes, choose the option that preserves your work before shutting down. important: a forced power-off should be reserved for an unresponsive device after normal exit/shutdown methods fail. part 3 — learn the basic navigation controls most standalone mantis tasks follow the same pattern: move to an item, read it in braille, then activate it. do not activate an item simply because you think you know where you are

entries.title: Microsoft Copilot Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible keyboard-first Microsoft Copilot manual for blind and low-vision learners.
entries.text: microsoft copilot manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible microsoft copilot course microsoft copilot manual practical, responsible ai skills for work, learning, and independent problem-solving. basics prompting verification privacy screen readers lessons what generative ai does generative ai predicts and creates text or other content from patterns in training data and the information supplied in a conversation. it can help brainstorm, organize, explain, summarize, and draft. it does not understand a situation the way a person does, and it can produce confident but incorrect or invented information. use ai as an assistant, not as the final decision-maker. a person remains responsible for checking accuracy, appropriateness, accessibility, and compliance with workplace rules. a reliable prompt pattern task: state exactly what you want. context: explain the audience and purpose using nonprivate information. constraints: give length, tone, reading level, deadline, or other limits. format: request headings, bullets, a numbered procedure, or a simple table. checks: ask the tool to identify uncertainty and provide sources when appropriate. continue the conversation with specific follow-ups. for example: “shorten this to 150 words,” “explain the second step,” or “which statements need verification?” verify before using the result open original sources instead of trusting an ai summary or citation. confirm names, dates, quotations, calculations, contact details, laws, policies, and software instructions. prefer current primary sources from the organization responsible for the information. compare important claims with a second reliable source. test instructions safely before giving them to another person. rewrite the final result in your own voice and keep a record of corrections. privacy and workplace rules do not enter client records, medical or disability details, passwords, financial account information, private addresses, confidential workplace material, copyrighted documents you are not permitted to share, or information that identifies another person. use fictional or public information in these lessons. follow the employer’s approved-tool, retention, disclosure, and human-review requirements. a personal free account is not automatically approved for organizational data. never allow ai to make an employment, benefit, medical, legal, financial, safety, or accommodation decision for a person. accessible output ask for descriptive headings, short paragraphs, meaningful link text, numbered steps, and simple tables. ask for image descriptions when an image matters, but verify the description with a trusted person when accuracy is important. avoid layouts that communicate meaning only through color, position, or visual formatting. jaws, narrator, and nvda ai interfaces change often. use tab and shift+tab to move among controls, enter or space to activate a control, and the screen reader’s heading, landmark, link, button, edit-field, and browse-mode commands to review the page. use browser find to locate words such as “sources,” “copy,” or part of your prompt. jaws: h moves by heading, b by button, e by edit field, insert+f7 opens links, and insert+f5 opens form fields. nvda: h moves by heading, b by button, e by edit field, nvda+f7 opens the elements list, and nvda+space switches browse and focus modes. narrator: use caps lock or insert with arrow keys for scan mode navigation; press caps lock+space to toggle scan mode when needed. after sending a prompt, allow time for the response to finish. move by heading or paragraph and confirm whether focus changed. product-specific keyboard behavior may change after updates. free-course rule these lessons can be completed with an available free ai service or by studying the examples without creating an account. do not start a paid trial, enter payment information, or purchase a subscription for this course. official references official microsoft copilot help and learning microsoft copilot on windows basic and advanced step-by-step procedures these procedures make the manual usable on its own. the separate lessons provide assignments and progress tracking when you want a course experience. basic 1: open copilot and understand its main controls basic 2: write clear prompts for microsoft work tasks basic 3: refine responses with follow-up instructions basic 4: draft and improve professional messages basic 5: summarize public documents and verify key points advanced 6: create word, excel, and powerpoint planning content advanced 7: research with citations and check original sources advanced 8: protect organizational data and follow permissions advanced 9: use copilot with jaws, narrator, or nvda advanced 10: final microsoft copilot workplace project basic procedure 1. open copilot and understand its main controls what you will learn: locate the prompt field, send control, conversation history, response actions, and account area. before you begin: use a free or approved ai service and only fictional or public information. do not enter private workplace, client, medical, financial, or account information. exactly how to do it open the microsoft copilot manual and review the prompting, verification, privacy, and screen-reader sections. open an available ai tool in a regular browser tab. if an account or feature is unavailable, study the sample prompt and write the expected process instead. navigate by headings and form controls. find the prompt edit field and confirm its label before typing. use this practice prompt or adapt it without adding private information: act as an accessible workplace skills coach. help me locate the prompt field, send control, conversation history, response actions, and account area. use fictional or public information only. organize the response with descriptive headings and numbered steps. identify anything i must verify. read the complete response by heading, paragraph, list item, and link. do not assume the first answer is correct. send at least one follow-up prompt that improves clarity, accuracy, accessibility, or completeness. verify important claims using the original source or another authoritative source. record unsupported statements and corrections. edit the final result in your own words. remove generic, inaccurate, biased, or unnecessary content. create a short process note naming the tool, prompts used, facts checked, changes made, and remaining uncertainty. save the assignment as copilot-lesson-1.txt . screen-reader help: jaws and nvda users can press h for headings, b for buttons, and e for edit fields in browse mode. narrator users can navigate with scan mode. press tab and shift+tab for interactive controls. because ai interfaces change frequently, listen to each control’s current accessible name. what should happen: you can complete the procedure and verify the result using the keyboard, your screen reader, or your braille display. if that does not happen: confirm focus is in the intended edit field or control. review the page by headings and buttons, shorten the request, and never solve an interface problem by entering private information or starting a paid trial. practice: locate the prompt field, send control, conversation history, response actions, and account area. basic procedure 2. write clear prompts for microsoft work tasks what you will learn: create a prompt for a fictional microsoft 365 workplace task with a specific audience and format. before you begin: use a free or approved ai service and only fictional or public information. do not enter private workplace, client, medical, financial, or account information. exactly how to do it open the microsoft copilot manual and review the prompting, verification, privacy, and screen-reader sections. open an available ai tool in a regular browser tab. if an account or feature is unavailable, study the sample prompt and write the expected process instead. navigate by headings and form controls. fi

entries.title: Microsoft Edge Screen Reader Manual
entries.snippet: Microsoft Edge Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft edge screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft edge screen reader manual narrator, nvda, and jaws independent self-study guide for web browsing all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft edge accessibility features purpose: this manual teaches microsoft edge from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains exactly what to press, what browser region or webpage element should receive focus, what your screen reader should announce, and how to recover when the result is different. reference platform: this manual focuses on current microsoft edge on windows 11. screen readers: core edge keyboard commands are taught first. narrator, nvda, and jaws are covered separately so browser commands and screen-reader commands are not mixed together. how to use this manual learn the browser itself before memorizing screen-reader-specific web commands. ctrl+l or alt+d moves directly to the address bar. ctrl+t opens a new tab. ctrl+w closes the current tab. ctrl+shift+t reopens the last closed tab. f6 moves focus among major edge panes. shift+f6 moves backward. ctrl+f6 moves directly to the web content pane. tab and shift+tab move among focusable page controls and browser controls. screen-reader browse/scan modes control how you move through webpage structure. do not type passwords into pages you reached from suspicious email links. use ctrl+s only when you intentionally want to save a webpage or file. use ctrl+j to review downloads and ctrl+h to review history. table of contents part 1 - what microsoft edge is part 2 - open edge and learn the window part 3 - address bar and web search part 4 - tabs and windows part 5 - back, forward, reload, and home part 6 - webpage keyboard navigation part 7 - find on page part 8 - favorites part 9 - history part 10 - downloads part 11 - forms, buttons, checkboxes, and combo boxes part 12 - links and opening new tabs part 13 - pdfs in edge part 14 - read aloud and immersive reader part 15 - caret browsing part 16 - accessibility settings part 17 - zoom, full screen, and focus visibility part 18 - profiles, sign-in, and sync part 19 - privacy, cookies, passwords, and inprivate part 20 - security and phishing part 21 - narrator with edge part 22 - nvda with edge part 23 - jaws with edge part 24 - braille displays with edge part 25 - troubleshooting part 26 - independent practice course part 27 - quick reference commands part 28 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what microsoft edge is microsoft edge is the web browser built into windows 11. it displays webpages, web applications, pdfs, downloads, settings, favorites, history, and browser extensions. address bar: where you type a website address or search query. tab: one open webpage or browser task. toolbar: browser controls such as back, refresh, favorites, profile, and settings and more. web content pane: the current webpage. favorites: saved website shortcuts. history: previously visited pages. downloads: files downloaded through edge. profile: optional microsoft account sign-in and sync settings. part 2 - open edge and learn the window 2.1 open microsoft edge what you will learn: start the browser without using a mouse. before you begin: be at the windows keyboard. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type edge. press enter on microsoft edge. wait for the browser window. press f6 once. listen to the region announced. press f6 several more times to hear different edge panes. press ctrl+f6 to move to the web content pane. what should happen: edge opens and keyboard focus can move among the browser's major regions. if that does not happen: if f6 seems trapped in one area, press escape to close any open popup/menu and try again. practice: open edge, cycle through panes, and return to web content. part 3 - address bar and web search task command address bar ctrl+l or alt+d search from address bar ctrl+e open typed address/search in new tab alt+enter 3.1 open a website by address what you will learn: navigate directly to a known website. before you begin: edge is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+l. type the full website address, for example microsoft.com. press enter. wait for the page to load. use your screen reader to read the page title or first heading. what should happen: the requested website opens in the current tab. if that does not happen: if search results appear instead, check whether the address was typed correctly. practice: open two known websites by address. 3.2 search the web from the address bar what you will learn: perform a web search without opening a search engine first. before you begin: edge is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+l. type a search phrase such as accessible pdf keyboard navigation. press enter. wait for search results. use your screen reader's heading/link commands to review results. what should happen: search results appear in the current tab. if that does not happen: if a previous address remains, ctrl+l should select it automatically; typing replaces it. practice: search for three topics. part 4 - tabs and windows task command new tab ctrl+t close current tab ctrl+w reopen closed tab ctrl+shift+t next tab ctrl+tab or ctrl+page down previous tab ctrl+shift+tab or ctrl+page up specific tab 1-8 ctrl+1 through ctrl+8 last tab ctrl+9 new window ctrl+n new inprivate window ctrl+shift+n 4.1 open and switch tabs what you will learn: work with more than one webpage. before you begin: edge is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+t. type a search or address. press enter. press ctrl+t again and open another page. press ctrl+tab to move to the next tab. press ctrl+shift+tab to move back. listen to the page title after each switch. what should happen: you can keep multiple webpages open and identify which tab is active. if that does not happen: if ctrl+tab appears to do nothing, only one tab may be open. practice: open three tabs and cycle through them. 4.2 recover a closed tab what you will learn: restore a tab closed by mistake. before you begin: close a non-important tab with ctrl+w. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+t. wait for the tab to reopen. listen for the restored page title. what should happen: the most recently closed tab reopens. if that does not happen: if a different tab opens, repeated ctrl+shift+t can restore earlier closed tabs. practice: close and restore two practice tabs. part 5 - back, forward, reload, and home task command back alt+left arrow forward alt+right arrow reload ctrl+r or f5 hard reload/ignore cached content ctrl+shift+r or shift+f5 home page alt+home 5.1 move back and forward what you will learn: return to recently visited pages within one tab. before you begin: open one page, then follow a link to another. exactly how to do it press alt+left arrow. listen for the previous page title. press alt+right arrow. listen for the newer page title. what should happen: edge moves backward and forward through that tab's history. if that does not happen: if nothing happens, there may be no previous/forward page in that tab. practice: navigate through three pages and use back/forward. part 6 - webpage keyboard navigation screen readers add structural webpage navigation, while edge itself provides focus navigation with tab and shift+tab. 6.1 move through focusable controls what you will learn: navigate links, buttons, and form fields without using screen-reader quick keys. before you begin: open a webpage with several controls. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f6 to ensure focus is in web content. press tab. listen for the link, button, field, or other control. press tab again. press shift+tab to move backward. press enter on a link/button when you intentionally want to activate it. use spacebar on many checkboxes and buttons. what should happen: focus moves among interactive page elements. if that does not happen: if tab moves through browser controls rather than the page, press ctrl+f6 first. practice:

entries.snippet: Microsoft Excel Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft excel screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft excel screen reader manual narrator, nvda, and jaws independent self-study guide for excel on windows all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft screen reader support for excel purpose: this manual teaches microsoft excel from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains exactly what to press, what cell or control should receive focus, what your screen reader should announce, and how to recover when the result is different. reference version: the manual is written primarily for excel for microsoft 365 on windows. many commands also work in excel 2024, 2021, 2019, and 2016, though ribbon labels and newer features can vary. screen readers: core excel commands are taught first. narrator, nvda, and jaws are covered separately later so commands are not mixed together. how to use this manual work through parts 1-15 before concentrating on your screen reader. those sections teach excel itself. always know the active cell address. a screen reader often announces both the cell reference and its value. arrow keys move one cell at a time unless you are editing inside a cell. enter normally moves down one cell after data entry. tab normally moves right one cell. f2 puts the current cell into edit mode. escape cancels an unfinished edit. ctrl+arrow jumps to an edge of the current data region. use it carefully on large sheets. ctrl+g opens go to and is one of the safest ways to reach an exact cell. ctrl+page up and ctrl+page down switch worksheets. use real excel tables with headers when data belongs in a structured table. save often with ctrl+s. table of contents part 1 - what excel is part 2 - workbooks, worksheets, cells, rows, and columns part 3 - open excel and create a workbook part 4 - move around a worksheet part 5 - enter, edit, and clear cell data part 6 - select cells, rows, columns, and ranges part 7 - save, open, close, and rename part 8 - formulas and functions part 9 - copy, fill, paste, and autosum part 10 - worksheets: add, rename, move, and navigate part 11 - excel tables part 12 - sort and filter part 13 - find and replace part 14 - formatting numbers, text, alignment, and columns part 15 - comments and notes part 16 - charts and visual objects part 17 - accessibility and accessible spreadsheet design part 18 - print and page setup part 19 - narrator with excel part 20 - nvda with excel part 21 - jaws with excel part 22 - large worksheets and efficient navigation part 23 - braille displays with excel part 24 - excel for the web part 25 - troubleshooting part 26 - independent practice course part 27 - quick reference commands part 28 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what excel is microsoft excel is a spreadsheet application. it organizes information into a grid of rows and columns. the point where a row and column meet is a cell. a workbook is the excel file. a worksheet is one sheet/tab inside the workbook. columns use letters such as a, b, c, and aa. rows use numbers such as 1, 2, and 100. a cell address combines column and row, such as a1, c12, or aa250. a range is a group of cells, such as a1:c10. a formula begins with an equals sign. a function is a built-in formula such as sum or average. part 2 - workbooks, worksheets, cells, rows, and columns 2.1 understand cell addresses what you will learn: use cell references as your primary orientation system. before you begin: open a blank workbook. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g. type a1. press enter. listen for your screen reader to announce cell a1. press right arrow once; you should move to b1. press down arrow once; you should move to b2. press left arrow once; you should move to a2. what should happen: you can predict the current cell address after each move. if that does not happen: if your screen reader announces only values and not addresses, adjust its excel verbosity or use its current-cell command. practice: move to c5 using arrows, then return to a1 with ctrl+g. part 3 - open excel and create a workbook 3.1 open excel what you will learn: start excel without a mouse. before you begin: excel must be installed. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type excel. use up/down arrow if multiple results appear. press enter on microsoft excel. wait for the excel start screen. what should happen: excel opens. if that does not happen: if excel does not appear in search, microsoft 365/excel may not be installed. practice: open excel twice with windows search. 3.2 create a blank workbook what you will learn: open a worksheet ready for data entry. before you begin: excel is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+n. wait for a new workbook. listen for the active cell, normally a1. type name. press tab. type score. press enter. what should happen: a new workbook contains headings in a1 and b1, and the active cell moves according to excel's entry behavior. if that does not happen: if ctrl+n opens a start page, choose blank workbook with tab/enter. practice: create a workbook with name and score headings. part 4 - move around a worksheet task command one cell arrow keys next cell to right tab previous cell to left shift+tab next row/down after entry enter previous row/up shift+enter edge of current data region ctrl+arrow go to exact cell ctrl+g beginning of row home cell a1 ctrl+home last used cell/region end ctrl+end 4.1 go to an exact cell what you will learn: reach a known address safely on a large worksheet. before you begin: open any worksheet. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g. type d25. press enter. listen for d25. type test. press ctrl+g. type a1. press enter. what should happen: you can jump directly without counting rows/columns. if that does not happen: if go to stays open, press enter again or tab to ok. practice: jump to z100, then back to a1. 4.2 use ctrl+arrow carefully what you will learn: move to the edge of a data block. before you begin: create a small block of data first. exactly how to do it place focus inside the data. press ctrl+right arrow. listen to the cell address and value. press ctrl+down arrow. listen again. use ctrl+left arrow and ctrl+up arrow to return toward the upper-left edge. what should happen: focus jumps to the edge of contiguous data. if that does not happen: if excel jumps very far, there may be blank cells or unexpected used cells in the sheet. use ctrl+g to recover. practice: practice within a 5-by-5 block. part 5 - enter, edit, and clear cell data 5.1 enter data into a cell what you will learn: type a value and commit it. before you begin: focus an empty cell. exactly how to do it type a word or number. press enter. listen for focus to move down one cell. press up arrow to return and confirm the value. what should happen: the value is stored in the cell. if that does not happen: if typing starts a ribbon command, the worksheet may not have focus. press escape/f6 until a cell is active. practice: enter five names in column a. 5.2 edit existing cell content what you will learn: change only part of a cell value. before you begin: focus a cell containing text. exactly how to do it press f2. listen for edit mode or the cell contents. use left/right arrow to move within the text. use backspace/delete to remove characters. type the correction. press enter to save the edit. what should happen: the same cell contains the corrected value. if that does not happen: if arrow keys move to another cell, f2 did not enter edit mode. return and press f2 again. practice: correct three deliberate spelling errors. 5.3 clear a cell without deleting the row what you will learn: remove content only. before you begin: focus a non-important practice cell. exactly how to do it press delete. listen for the cell to become blank. move away and back to verify. what should happen: the cell remains in place but its content is cleared. if that does not happen: if a delete dialog opens, you may have used a different delet

entries.snippet: Microsoft OneDrive Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft onedrive screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft onedrive screen reader manual cloud storage with keyboard and screen readers independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft screen reader support for onedrive purpose: this manual teaches onedrive from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains where onedrive appears, what to press, what should receive focus, what the screen reader should announce, and how to recover when the result is different. reference platform: the main workflows are onedrive on windows 11 and onedrive on the web. work/school and personal accounts are both discussed because labels and sharing rules can differ. key distinction: onedrive on the web is a browser application. synced onedrive in windows behaves like a normal file explorer location. learn both because the same cloud file can be reached in either place. how to use this manual work through parts 1-12 first if onedrive is new to you. in onedrive for the web, use ctrl+f6/f6 to move between browser and onedrive regions, then tab and arrow keys within regions. in the onedrive web content grid, arrow keys move between items, spacebar toggles selection, enter opens, f2 renames, delete deletes, s shares, and i toggles the details pane in supported onedrive for work or school contexts. in windows file explorer, onedrive files use normal windows commands such as arrow keys, enter, f2, delete, ctrl+c, ctrl+v, and alt+up arrow. files on-demand means some files may be cloud-only until opened or marked available offline. before deleting, moving, or renaming a synced file, remember the change can sync to the cloud and other devices. before sharing, verify the recipient, permission, and whether the link is restricted or broadly accessible. save important work before experimenting with sync, move, or delete commands. table of contents part 1 - what onedrive is part 2 - personal vs work or school onedrive part 3 - find onedrive in windows 11 part 4 - onedrive status and sync icons part 5 - navigate onedrive in file explorer part 6 - create, rename, copy, move, and delete files part 7 - files on-demand and offline access part 8 - open onedrive on the web part 9 - navigate onedrive on the web part 10 - upload and download part 11 - search part 12 - share files and folders part 13 - link permissions and access safety part 14 - version history part 15 - recycle bin and restore part 16 - sync setup and sync problems part 17 - folder backup part 18 - shared and recent items part 19 - narrator with onedrive part 20 - nvda with onedrive part 21 - jaws with onedrive part 22 - voiceover on mac part 23 - braille displays part 24 - iphone/ipad and android part 25 - security and privacy part 26 - troubleshooting part 27 - independent practice course part 28 - quick reference commands part 29 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what onedrive is onedrive is microsoft cloud storage. a file stored in onedrive can be available through onedrive.com and, when sync is configured, through a onedrive folder in windows file explorer. changes made in one location can synchronize to the other. onedrive folder: the synced cloud-storage location in file explorer. my files: the main file area in onedrive on the web. shared: items other people shared with you or that you shared, depending on view. recent: recently opened or changed items. recycle bin: deleted cloud items that have not yet been permanently removed. files on-demand: controls whether a file is cloud-only, locally cached, or always available on the computer. sync: keeps cloud and local versions aligned when online. part 2 - personal vs work or school onedrive personal onedrive uses a microsoft account. onedrive for work or school uses an organization account and may be governed by administrator policies. work/school sharing, retention, external access, storage, and sync options can be restricted by the organization. the windows file explorer name may appear as onedrive - personal or onedrive - organization name. practical rule: before changing a file, identify which onedrive account/location contains it. the same filename can exist in personal and work onedrive at the same time. part 3 - find onedrive in windows 11 3.1 open the onedrive folder in file explorer what you will learn: reach synced onedrive files using normal windows navigation. before you begin: onedrive must be signed in and configured on the computer. exactly how to do it press windows+e to open file explorer. press f6 or shift+f6 until the navigation pane is announced. use up/down arrow through locations. stop on onedrive, onedrive - personal, or onedrive - your organization name. press enter. press f6 until the file list is announced. use arrow keys through files and folders. what should happen: the onedrive file list opens in file explorer. if that does not happen: if onedrive is missing, the app may not be signed in, running, or configured. open the onedrive app from windows search and sign in. practice: open onedrive and identify three items. part 4 - onedrive status and sync icons onedrive uses status information to indicate whether files are cloud-only, available locally, always available, syncing, or experiencing an error. a screen reader may announce the status in file explorer depending on the current view and column information. cloud-only: stored in onedrive and downloaded when opened. locally available: downloaded to the computer after use and may be removable by windows/onedrive when space is needed. always available: intentionally kept on the computer for offline access. syncing: changes are being uploaded/downloaded. error/attention needed: onedrive could not complete a sync action. 4.1 review a file's onedrive status what you will learn: determine whether a file is available offline. before you begin: open the onedrive folder in file explorer. exactly how to do it move to a file. use shift+f10 to open its context menu. listen for onedrive commands such as always keep on this device or free up space. if always keep on this device is offered, the file can be marked for offline availability. if free up space is offered, a local copy may currently exist. what should happen: the available onedrive command helps identify the file state. if that does not happen: if onedrive commands are absent, verify the item is actually inside a synced onedrive location. practice: inspect three files without changing their status. part 5 - navigate onedrive in file explorer task command open file/folder enter rename f2 delete delete copy/cut/paste ctrl+c / ctrl+x / ctrl+v new folder ctrl+shift+n parent folder alt+up arrow properties alt+enter context menu shift+f10 5.1 open a folder and return what you will learn: navigate onedrive like a normal windows folder. before you begin: focus a onedrive folder. exactly how to do it press enter to open the folder. use up/down arrow through items. press alt+up arrow to return to the parent folder. listen to the current folder name. what should happen: you can move into and out of onedrive folders. if that does not happen: if alt+up arrow changes browser history instead, file explorer is not the active app. practice: open two folder levels and return. part 6 - create, rename, copy, move, and delete files 6.1 create a new folder what you will learn: create a folder that will sync to onedrive. before you begin: open the intended onedrive location in file explorer. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+n. type a clear folder name. press enter. wait briefly for onedrive to sync the new folder. what should happen: the folder appears locally and then in onedrive online. if that does not happen: if the folder cannot be created, check permission and storage/sync status. practice: create a folder named onedrive practice. 6.2 rename a synced item what you will learn: rename a cloud-synced file safely. before you begin: us
