entries.snippet: Microsoft OneNote Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft onenote screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft onenote screen reader manual notes, notebooks, pages, and organization independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft screen reader support for onenote purpose: this manual teaches current microsoft onenote from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains what to press, where focus should move, what should be announced, and how to recover when the result is different. reference version: the main procedures are written for the current onenote desktop app included with microsoft 365 on windows. separate sections cover onenote for the web, macos/voiceover, mobile, and braille. important version note: the former onenote for windows 10 app reached end of support in october 2025. this guide therefore focuses on the current desktop onenote app rather than the retired windows 10 app. how to use this manual learn onenote's structure first: notebook, section, page, page title, and content block. use ctrl+g to move to the notebook picker, ctrl+shift+g to move to sections, and ctrl+alt+g to move to pages. press ctrl+t to create a section and ctrl+n to create a page in the current section. press tab from a page title to move into the page content area. onenote pages can contain several independent note containers; screen readers may announce them as content blocks. use ctrl+e to search all notebooks and ctrl+f to search the current page. use ctrl+1 through ctrl+9 for common note tags; ctrl+0 removes note tags from selected notes. use f9 to synchronize all shared notebooks and shift+f9 to synchronize the current shared notebook. save is normally automatic because onenote synchronizes notebook changes. before sharing, verify which notebook you are sharing and whether it contains private sections/pages. table of contents part 1 - what onenote is part 2 - open onenote and learn the structure part 3 - switch notebooks part 4 - create and navigate sections part 5 - create and navigate pages part 6 - page titles and content blocks part 7 - type, edit, and format notes part 8 - lists and outlines part 9 - note tags part 10 - tables part 11 - links, files, pictures, and alt text part 12 - search onenote part 13 - audio notes part 14 - move, copy, rename, and delete pages/sections part 15 - section groups part 16 - sharing and collaboration part 17 - sync and offline behavior part 18 - accessibility checker and accessible notebook design part 19 - narrator with onenote part 20 - nvda with onenote part 21 - jaws with onenote part 22 - voiceover and onenote for mac part 23 - onenote for the web part 24 - braille displays part 25 - iphone/ipad and android part 26 - security and privacy part 27 - troubleshooting part 28 - independent practice course part 29 - quick reference commands part 30 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what onenote is onenote is a digital notebook application. information is organized in a hierarchy rather than as separate files for every note. notebook: the top-level collection of notes. section: a major category within a notebook. section group: an optional folder-like grouping of sections. page: one note page inside a section. subpage: a page visually/structurally nested beneath another page. page title: the page's name and a key navigation cue. content block: a note container on the page. one page can contain several. tag: a marker such as to do, important, question, or contact. shared notebook: a notebook stored where other authorized people can collaborate. part 2 - open onenote and learn the structure 2.1 open onenote what you will learn: start onenote without using a mouse. before you begin: onenote must be installed. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type onenote. press enter on microsoft onenote. wait for the app to open. press ctrl+g. listen for the current notebook. press ctrl+shift+g. listen for the current section. press ctrl+alt+g. listen for the current page. what should happen: you can identify the notebook, section, and page layers. if that does not happen: if one shortcut does not move focus, press escape to close menus/dialogs and try again. practice: open onenote and identify notebook, section, and page. focus map: notebook, section, page, page title, and page content are separate focus locations. when a command behaves unexpectedly, identify which layer currently has focus. part 3 - switch notebooks 3.1 switch to another open notebook what you will learn: move between notebooks without hunting through the interface. before you begin: have more than one notebook open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g. use up/down arrow through the notebook list. listen to each notebook name. press spacebar on the notebook you want. wait for its last visited page to open. press ctrl+shift+g to verify its sections. what should happen: the selected notebook becomes active. if that does not happen: if only one notebook is listed, another notebook has not been opened/synced into this onenote profile. practice: switch between two notebooks and return. part 4 - create and navigate sections 4.1 create a section what you will learn: add a major category to the current notebook. before you begin: open the notebook where the section belongs. exactly how to do it press ctrl+t. listen for the new section name text box. type a descriptive section name. press enter. what should happen: a new section is created and named. if that does not happen: if a new page appears unexpectedly, confirm you pressed ctrl+t rather than ctrl+n. practice: create a section named practice. 4.2 navigate sections what you will learn: move directly through section tabs. before you begin: the notebook has multiple sections. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+g. use up/down arrow through sections as announced in your current layout. stop on the desired section. press spacebar or enter if necessary to activate it. press ctrl+alt+g to move to that section's pages. what should happen: the selected section becomes active and its pages are available. if that does not happen: if arrows move within page text, ctrl+shift+g did not move focus to sections. practice: move through every section once. part 5 - create and navigate pages 5.1 create a page what you will learn: add a new note page to the current section. before you begin: select the correct section first. exactly how to do it press ctrl+n. listen for a new untitled page and page-title field. type a descriptive page title. press enter. begin typing page content. what should happen: a new page is created at the end of the current section. if that does not happen: if a new application window opens, verify the onenote window had focus. practice: create pages named meeting notes and ideas. 5.2 navigate pages what you will learn: move among pages without searching. before you begin: the section has several pages. exactly how to do it press ctrl+alt+g. use up/down arrow through page titles. press spacebar or enter on the desired page. listen for the page title. press tab once to move into the content area. what should happen: the desired page opens and you can reach its notes. if that does not happen: if ctrl+alt+g does not move to pages, close any dialog and try again. practice: move among five pages and return to the first. part 6 - page titles and content blocks 6.1 jump to the page title what you will learn: rename or review the page's title. before you begin: a page is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+t. listen for the page title. edit the title if needed. press enter. press tab to move into the page content. what should happen: focus moves to the page title and then back to content. if that does not happen: if ctrl+shift+t affects selected text instead, make sure onenote—not a browser—is active. practice: rename a practice page and rename it back. 6.2 move between content blocks what you will learn: understand onenote's free

entries.title: Microsoft Outlook Manual
entries.snippet: Microsoft Outlook Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft outlook manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft outlook manual email, calendar, contacts, narrator, nvda, and jaws independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft outlook accessibility support purpose: this manual is written directly to the person learning microsoft outlook. it assumes little or no prior outlook experience and explains exactly what to press, what should happen, and how to recover if the result is different. current interface: this manual uses new outlook for windows as its primary reference. microsoft still supports other outlook versions, so some controls and shortcuts differ in classic outlook, outlook on the web, mac, ios, and android. screen readers: microsoft documents new outlook with narrator, jaws, and nvda. the windows keyboard steps in this manual work regardless of screen reader, while screen-reader-specific notes are labeled separately. how to use this manual work through parts 1-12 first if outlook is completely new to you. do one action at a time and listen to the result before pressing another key. tab moves forward through controls; shift+tab moves backward. arrow keys move within lists, menus, and message lists. enter opens the selected message, event, link, or control. escape closes menus, dialogs, or reading panes in many contexts. ctrl+f6 moves between major outlook regions in new outlook and outlook on the web. microsoft recommends turning the reading pane off for some screen-reader workflows because it simplifies focus movement. when a command differs between new outlook and classic outlook, this manual prioritizes new outlook and labels classic behavior separately where useful. table of contents part 1 - what outlook is part 2 - open outlook and identify your version part 3 - learn the outlook window part 4 - essential keyboard navigation part 5 - mail: open the inbox and read messages part 6 - create and send a new email part 7 - reply, reply all, and forward part 8 - attach files and open attachments part 9 - search for email part 10 - organize the inbox part 11 - folders and moving messages part 12 - delete, archive, flag, mark read/unread part 13 - junk, phishing, and safe email habits part 14 - contacts and people part 15 - calendar basics part 16 - open and navigate calendar events part 17 - create an appointment part 18 - schedule a meeting and invite people part 19 - respond to meeting invitations part 20 - join teams/online meetings from outlook part 21 - recurring meetings part 22 - search and filter calendar part 23 - notifications and reminders part 24 - settings and accessibility part 25 - spell check, formatting, and accessible email part 26 - narrator with outlook part 27 - nvda with outlook part 28 - jaws with outlook part 29 - outlook on the web part 30 - outlook mobile basics part 31 - troubleshooting part 32 - independent practice course part 33 - quick reference commands part 34 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what outlook is microsoft outlook combines email, calendar, contacts/people, search, and microsoft 365 communication tools in one application. new outlook for windows has a modern interface similar to outlook on the web. mail contains your inbox, folders, sent items, drafts, junk, deleted items, and other mail folders. calendar contains appointments, meetings, and online-meeting links. people/contacts stores contact information when available. search finds messages, people, events, and other outlook content. the folder/message list and reading/composition areas are separate regions of the interface. part 2 - open outlook and identify your version 2.1 open outlook from windows search what you will learn: launch outlook without a mouse. before you begin: outlook must be installed or provisioned for your account. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type outlook. use up/down arrow if more than one outlook result appears. press enter on outlook. wait for the outlook window to load. if sign-in is requested, follow your organization or microsoft account sign-in process. what should happen: outlook opens to mail or the last-used outlook module. if that does not happen: if outlook does not appear in windows search, use outlook on the web or contact your organization about installation. practice: close and reopen outlook once. 2.2 identify new outlook vs classic outlook what you will learn: know which instructions apply to your interface. before you begin: outlook is open. exactly how to do it use tab or ctrl+f6 to move through major interface regions. listen for a command such as try the new outlook if you are in classic outlook. if you hear command toolbar and do not hear try the new outlook, you are likely already using the newer outlook experience. you can also inspect outlook help/about if your organization allows it. what should happen: you know whether you are using new or classic outlook. if that does not happen: if you are unsure, use microsoft's what version of outlook do i have guidance or compare the current interface with your organization documentation. practice: identify the version before learning many shortcuts. part 3 - learn the outlook window app/navigation area: switches among mail, calendar, people, and other microsoft 365 apps. folder pane: inbox, sent items, drafts, deleted items, junk email, and custom folders. message list: shows messages in the selected folder. reading pane: can show the selected message without opening a separate window. command toolbar/ribbon: new mail, delete, archive, move, flag, and other commands. search: finds mail, contacts, and calendar items. 3.1 explore the window with ctrl+f6 what you will learn: move among major outlook regions efficiently. before you begin: outlook is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f6 once. listen to the region name. press ctrl+f6 again. continue cycling through the major outlook regions. within a region, use tab, shift+tab, and arrow keys. press escape if you enter a temporary menu or dialog. what should happen: focus cycles through major outlook landmarks/regions. if that does not happen: if ctrl+f6 behaves differently, verify that outlook rather than your browser has focus. in outlook on the web, ctrl+f6 is also the expected region-navigation key. practice: cycle through all major regions twice. part 4 - essential keyboard navigation task command new email ctrl+n reply ctrl+r reply all ctrl+shift+r forward ctrl+f send ctrl+enter search ctrl+e calendar ctrl+2 mail ctrl+1 move among major regions ctrl+f6 mark read ctrl+q mark unread ctrl+u delete selected message delete important: shortcut behavior can vary between new outlook, classic outlook, and outlook on the web. if a shortcut differs, check microsoft's current keyboard-shortcut page linked at the end of this manual. part 5 - mail: open the inbox and read messages 5.1 open the inbox and move through messages what you will learn: read messages from the message list. before you begin: outlook is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+1 to move to mail. use ctrl+f6 until the folder pane or message list is reached. if focus is in the folder pane, use up/down arrow until inbox is selected and press enter if needed. move to the message list with tab or ctrl+f6. press up/down arrow through messages. listen to sender, subject, date/time, read/unread status, attachment status, and flag information when your screen reader announces it. press enter to open the selected message. read the message using your screen reader's normal reading commands. press escape to return to the message list when appropriate. what should happen: you can choose a message, open it, read it, and return to the list. if that does not happen: if enter moves focus into a reading pane rather than a separate message, use ctrl+f6/tab to locate message content or turn the reading pane off in settings for a simpler screen-reader workflow. practice: read three messages and return

entries.title: Microsoft PowerPoint Accessible Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible Microsoft PowerPoint manual for Microsoft 365 desktop on Windows with JAWS and keyboard-first instruction.
entries.text: microsoft powerpoint manual - accessible learning center skip to main content keyboard-first microsoft 365 training microsoft powerpoint accessible manual create, review, and present accessible slide decks with jaws and the keyboard. keyboard quick reference accessible slide practices course lessons about this manual this manual targets powerpoint in microsoft 365 desktop on windows. powerpoint contains several work areas, including the thumbnails pane, slide editing area, notes pane, and ribbon. press f6 to move among these areas and tab or shift+tab to move among objects on a slide. use built-in slide layouts whenever possible. layout placeholders provide structure that is easier to navigate and maintain than manually positioned text boxes. give every slide a unique, descriptive title. keyboard quick reference common powerpoint commands used in this course task command move among powerpoint panes f6 or shift+f6 move among slide objects tab or shift+tab create a new slide ctrl+m duplicate a selected slide or object ctrl+d move to next or previous slide in thumbnails down arrow or up arrow edit text in a selected placeholder enter or f2 exit text editing and select the object escape insert or edit a hyperlink ctrl+k save ctrl+s save as f12 start slide show from beginning f5 start slide show from current slide shift+f5 advance during slide show right arrow, spacebar, or page down move backward during slide show left arrow, backspace, or page up end slide show escape temporarily show a black screen b search office commands alt+q search jaws commands insert+spacebar, then j accessible slide practices use built-in slide layouts and give every slide a unique title. keep text concise and use real bulleted or numbered lists. maintain strong contrast and do not use color as the only way to communicate meaning. add concise alternative text to meaningful pictures, charts, shapes, and other visual objects. mark objects decorative only when they add no information. use the reading order pane to arrange objects logically, with the title before related content. use simple tables with a designated header row. avoid merged or split cells. for charts, retain source values and add a plain-text summary of the important result. use meaningful link text that identifies the destination. add speaker-note prompts to describe visuals aloud during a presentation. avoid flashing content and unnecessary animation. run check accessibility and test the entire deck with the keyboard. reading order screen readers follow the slide's object order, which may differ from the visual arrangement. open the reading order pane through alt+q or an accessibility checker recommendation, then move objects into a logical sequence. test that sequence by pressing tab through the slide. images, tables, and charts alt text should explain why a visual matters in the presentation. it should be concise, specific, and based on the presentation context. a chart needs alt text plus access to exact source values and a short text summary. a table needs clear headers and a simple structure. presenting accessibly start the slide show with f5, move with the arrow keys, and press escape to finish. speak important information shown in images, charts, and demonstrations. do not ask the audience to identify information only by color, position, or appearance. basic and advanced step-by-step procedures these procedures make the manual usable on its own. the separate lessons provide assignments and progress tracking when you want a course experience. basic 1: powerpoint basics: slides, placeholders, and saving basic 2: slide layouts, titles, and organizing a presentation basic 3: text, bullets, and clear slide content basic 4: images, alternative text, and decorative objects basic 5: reading order and keyboard navigation advanced 6: accessible tables and charts advanced 7: meaningful links and contact information advanced 8: color, contrast, fonts, and accessible design advanced 9: speaker notes and presenting with the keyboard advanced 10: final accessible workplace presentation basic procedure 1. powerpoint basics: slides, placeholders, and saving what you will learn: create a basic presentation, move among slide placeholders with the keyboard, and save the file. before you begin: open the application and a fictional, instructor-provided, or nonprivate practice file. save a separate working copy before making major changes. exactly how to do it open microsoft powerpoint and create a blank presentation. press f6 several times and listen as jaws moves among the slide area, thumbnails pane, notes pane, and ribbon. return to the slide area. press tab to move between the title and subtitle placeholders. type workplace technology training in the title placeholder. move to the subtitle placeholder and type prepared by followed by a fictional name. press ctrl+m to create a new slide. type training goals in the title placeholder. in the content placeholder, enter learn keyboard commands, practice accessible documents, and complete workplace assignments as separate lines. press page up and page down in the thumbnails pane to review both slides. press ctrl+s and save the presentation as powerpoint-lesson-1.pptx. keyboard help: press alt+q to search powerpoint commands when ribbon keytips differ. for jaws help, press insert+spacebar, then j, and search for the task. what should happen: you can complete the procedure and verify the result using the keyboard, your screen reader, or your braille display. if that does not happen: press escape to leave an unexpected menu or dialog, confirm the active window and keyboard focus, then repeat one step at a time. use undo when a reversible content change occurred. practice: create a two-slide workplace technology training presentation with a title slide and a training goals slide. basic procedure 2. slide layouts, titles, and organizing a presentation what you will learn: use built-in slide layouts and meaningful titles to create a clear presentation structure. before you begin: open the application and a fictional, instructor-provided, or nonprivate practice file. save a separate working copy before making major changes. exactly how to do it open powerpoint-lesson-1.pptx. press ctrl+m to add a third slide. press alt+q, type slide layout, and choose title and content. title slide 3 training schedule and add three fictional schedule items. add slide 4 and title it contact information. add a fictional department email and telephone extension. press f6 until jaws announces the thumbnails pane. use up arrow and down arrow to review slide titles. select the contact information slide. press ctrl+x, move to the position after the title slide, and press ctrl+v to place it second. review the new order by moving through the thumbnails pane. confirm that every slide has a unique title. save a copy as powerpoint-lesson-2.pptx. keyboard help: press alt+q to search powerpoint commands when ribbon keytips differ. for jaws help, press insert+spacebar, then j, and search for the task. what should happen: you can complete the procedure and verify the result using the keyboard, your screen reader, or your braille display. if that does not happen: press escape to leave an unexpected menu or dialog, confirm the active window and keyboard focus, then repeat one step at a time. use undo when a reversible content change occurred. practice: expand and reorganize the training presentation so it contains four slides, uses built-in layouts, and has a unique title on every slide. basic procedure 3. text, bullets, and clear slide content what you will learn: create concise, structured slide text that works for screen-reader users and visual audiences. before you begin: open the application and a fictional, instructor-provided, or nonprivate practice file. save a separate working copy before making major changes. exactly how to do it create a new presentation with the title accessible customer service. add a slide

entries.title: Microsoft Teams Manual
entries.snippet: Microsoft Teams Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft teams manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft teams manual meetings, chat, channels, files, calls, and screen readers independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft teams accessibility support purpose: this manual is written directly to the person learning microsoft teams. it assumes you may be using teams for the first time. every procedure explains where to go, what to press or select, what should happen, and what to try if the result is different. important: microsoft teams changes frequently and organizations can customize which apps appear and in what order. if a numbered app shortcut differs from this manual, use the app's current position in your teams app bar or use search/keyboard navigation instead. accessibility focus: the manual includes mouse/visual instructions where useful and detailed keyboard/screen-reader methods for windows and mac. microsoft documents teams with narrator, jaws, nvda, and voiceover. how to use this manual work through parts 1-8 first if you are completely new to teams. do one action at a time. after each action, stop and confirm what changed. tab moves forward through many controls. shift+tab moves backward. enter usually activates the focused button, link, chat, or menu item. spacebar often toggles switches and checkboxes. escape usually closes a menu, returns focus to a list, or backs out of a temporary interface. windows shortcut labels in this manual refer to the teams desktop app unless the section specifically says web. mac shortcuts use command where microsoft documents a mac-specific equivalent. screen-reader users should listen to both the control name and control type before activating it. teams may use combined chats and channels or separate list views. this manual explains both concepts. table of contents part 1 - what microsoft teams is part 2 - install, open, and sign in part 3 - learn the teams window and app bar part 4 - essential keyboard navigation part 5 - search part 6 - chat: find, read, start, and send messages part 7 - chat formatting, attachments, reactions, and mentions part 8 - chats and channels: combined and separate views part 9 - teams and channels part 10 - files part 11 - calendar part 12 - schedule a meeting part 13 - join a meeting part 14 - meeting controls: microphone, camera, people, chat, and leave part 15 - captions, transcription, reactions, raise hand, and accessibility part 16 - share your screen or content part 17 - calls part 18 - activity and notifications part 19 - status, profile, and settings part 20 - audio and video device settings part 21 - screen reader navigation on windows part 22 - voiceover navigation on mac part 23 - teams on the web part 24 - mobile teams basics part 25 - troubleshooting part 26 - independent practice course part 27 - quick reference keyboard commands part 28 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what microsoft teams is microsoft teams is a communication and collaboration application. depending on your account and organization, you can use it for individual and group chat, team/channel conversations, meetings, calls, calendar events, file sharing, and connected microsoft 365 apps. chat is usually best for direct or small-group conversations. channels organize ongoing discussions and files around a team, department, class, project, or topic. calendar shows teams meetings and connected microsoft 365 calendar events. meetings include audio/video, participant controls, meeting chat, captions, reactions, and content sharing. calls can be person-to-person or group calls when calling is enabled for your account. files shared through teams may be stored in onedrive or sharepoint depending on where they are shared. terminology: a 'team' is a larger workspace or membership group. a 'channel' is a subject or working area inside a team. a 'chat' is a direct conversation that is not necessarily tied to a channel. part 2 - install, open, and sign in 2.1 open teams on windows what you will learn: open the teams desktop app using the keyboard. before you begin: microsoft teams must already be installed. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type teams. wait for microsoft teams to appear in search results. press enter. wait for the teams window to open. if a sign-in screen appears, move to the account/email field with tab if necessary. type your work, school, or microsoft account email address. press tab until next/sign in is focused and press enter. follow the authentication prompts. type your password, approve a verification request, or choose the required sign-in method. after sign-in, wait for the main teams window to finish loading before pressing additional navigation keys. what should happen: the main teams interface opens and your account is signed in. if that does not happen: if teams does not appear in windows search, it may not be installed or your organization may use the web version. if sign-in fails, confirm the account and authentication method with your organization. practice: close teams, reopen it from windows search, and confirm that you return to the main interface. 2.2 open teams on a mac what you will learn: open the teams desktop app without using the mouse. before you begin: microsoft teams must already be installed. exactly how to do it press command+space to open spotlight. type microsoft teams. press return. wait for teams to open. if a sign-in screen appears, use tab or voiceover navigation to move to the email/account field. type your account email address. activate next/sign in. follow password and verification prompts until teams opens. what should happen: the teams main window opens. if that does not happen: if spotlight does not find teams, check the applications folder or use teams on the web if permitted. practice: quit teams, reopen it from spotlight, and confirm you are signed in. part 3 - learn the teams window and app bar the teams window is divided into regions. exact names and order can vary, but the same ideas are consistent: an app/navigation area, a list area, and a content/conversation area. app bar: gives access to activity, chat, teams/channels, calendar, calls, and other installed apps. list pane: shows chats, channels, meetings, contacts, or other items for the current app. main content pane: shows the selected conversation, channel, calendar, meeting details, or file. top area: includes search and account/settings controls. right-side panes: can open for people, meeting chat, details, or other contextual information. numbered app shortcuts: microsoft notes that app-number shortcuts depend on the sequential position of the app on your app bar. if you or your organization reorder apps, the number changes. 3.1 explore the window with tab what you will learn: learn where focus moves before relying on shortcuts. before you begin: teams is open and no menu/dialog is active. exactly how to do it press tab once. listen to or visually identify the focused control. press tab again and note the next control. continue through several controls. press shift+tab to move backward. when focus enters a list, use up arrow and down arrow to move among list items if teams exposes the list that way. press escape if focus enters a temporary control or pane you want to leave. repeat until you can identify the app/navigation area, current list, and conversation/content area. what should happen: focus moves predictably among teams controls. if that does not happen: if tab seems trapped in one section, press escape once and try tab again. if a list is active, use arrow keys inside the list rather than repeatedly pressing tab. practice: explore for two minutes without activating anything; simply identify controls. part 4 - essential keyboard navigation task windows desktop mac desktop show keyboard shortcuts ctrl+period (.) or alt+/ command+period (.) go to search ctrl+e command+e open settings ctrl+comma (,) command+co

entries.snippet: Microsoft Word Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft word screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft word screen reader manual narrator, nvda, and jaws independent self-study guide for word on windows all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft screen reader support for word purpose: this manual is written directly to a person learning microsoft word with a screen reader. it assumes little or no prior word experience and explains what to press, what should happen, what your screen reader should announce, and how to recover when the result is different. reference version: the manual is written primarily for word for microsoft 365 on windows. many commands also work in word 2024, 2021, 2019, and 2016, but ribbon wording can differ. screen readers: core word keyboard commands are taught first. narrator, nvda, and jaws are covered separately so screen-reader commands are not mixed together. how to use this manual work through parts 1-12 before focusing on your screen reader. those sections teach word itself. do one action, stop, and listen to what changed before pressing another key. word uses both direct shortcuts and the ribbon. direct shortcuts are usually faster once memorized. alt activates ribbon keytips. after pressing alt, use the letters word announces for the tab and command you want. f6 cycles among major word regions such as document, ribbon, status bar, and panes. tab and shift+tab move between controls in dialogs and panes. arrow keys move through text, menus, lists, and ribbon controls depending on context. narrator, nvda, and jaws all work with standard windows text-editing keys. use word's built-in styles instead of making headings look like headings only with bold and larger font. save often with ctrl+s. table of contents part 1 - what microsoft word is part 2 - open word and create a document part 3 - learn the word window and ribbon part 4 - type, move, select, and edit text part 5 - save, save as, open, and close part 6 - find and replace part 7 - character and paragraph formatting part 8 - headings, styles, and navigation pane part 9 - bulleted and numbered lists part 10 - tables part 11 - links, pictures, alt text, headers, and footers part 12 - spelling, grammar, and editor part 13 - comments part 14 - track changes part 15 - accessibility checker and accessible document design part 16 - print, export to pdf, and share part 17 - narrator with word part 18 - nvda with word part 19 - jaws with word part 20 - reading long documents part 21 - braille displays with word part 22 - word online part 23 - troubleshooting part 24 - independent practice course part 25 - quick reference commands part 26 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what microsoft word is microsoft word is a word-processing application for creating, reading, editing, formatting, reviewing, and sharing documents. word documents commonly use the docx format. document body: the main area where text is typed and edited. ribbon: a set of tabs such as home, insert, layout, references, review, and view. status bar: reports information such as page number, word count, and view. navigation pane: lets you search the document and move among headings. comments pane: contains collaboration comments. review features: track changes, accept/reject, comments, compare, spelling, and accessibility tools. part 2 - open word and create a document 2.1 open word from windows search what you will learn: start microsoft word without using a mouse. before you begin: word must be installed. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type word. use up/down arrow if more than one result appears. press enter on microsoft word. wait for word to open. what should happen: the word start screen or a document window opens. if that does not happen: if word does not appear in search, microsoft 365/word may not be installed or may use a different organization deployment. practice: open word twice using search. 2.2 create a blank document what you will learn: start a new editable document. before you begin: word is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+n. wait for a blank document. type: this is my first word practice document. press enter twice. type a second sentence. what should happen: text appears in the new document. if that does not happen: if ctrl+n opens a start screen instead of a blank file, choose blank document with tab/enter. practice: create a new document and type two short paragraphs. part 3 - learn the word window and ribbon 3.1 move between word regions with f6 what you will learn: understand where keyboard focus is. before you begin: open a document. exactly how to do it press f6 once. listen to the region or control announced. press f6 again. continue several times. use shift+f6 to move backward through the regions. stop when focus returns to the document body. what should happen: focus cycles through word's major regions. if that does not happen: if f6 seems to do nothing, make sure word is the active application and no modal dialog is open. practice: cycle through all regions once. 3.2 use ribbon keytips what you will learn: reach a ribbon command by keyboard. before you begin: be in a word document. exactly how to do it press alt. listen for ribbon keytips. press h for home. listen as focus enters the home tab. use tab/shift+tab or arrow keys through controls. press escape to leave the ribbon and return toward the document. what should happen: the home ribbon tab becomes active. if that does not happen: if pressing alt opens an application menu from another program, word may not have focus. practice: open home, insert, and review tabs using alt key sequences. part 4 - type, move, select, and edit text task command character left/right left / right arrow word left/right ctrl+left / ctrl+right line up/down up / down arrow start/end of line home / end start/end of document ctrl+home / ctrl+end select character shift+left / shift+right select word ctrl+shift+left / ctrl+shift+right select line/paragraph portions shift with navigation keys select all ctrl+a delete previous character backspace delete next character delete undo ctrl+z redo/repeat ctrl+y 4.1 correct a typing error what you will learn: move the insertion point to an exact location and replace text. before you begin: type a sentence containing one deliberate error. exactly how to do it press ctrl+left arrow to move backward one word at a time. use left/right arrow to move one character at a time. press backspace or delete to remove the incorrect character. type the correct character. use your screen reader's line or word reading command to verify the correction. what should happen: the correction occurs at the intended position. if that does not happen: if text changes in the wrong location, press ctrl+home or ctrl+end to establish a known position and navigate again. practice: create three errors and correct all three. 4.2 select and replace a word what you will learn: select text with the keyboard. before you begin: place the caret next to a word. exactly how to do it hold ctrl+shift. press left or right arrow to select the word. release the keys. type the replacement word. what should happen: the selected word is replaced. if that does not happen: if extra punctuation or spaces are selected, undo with ctrl+z and select more carefully. practice: replace three words using selection. part 5 - save, save as, open, and close task command save ctrl+s save as f12 or ctrl+shift+s depending word version/configuration open ctrl+o close document ctrl+w exit word alt+f4 5.1 save a new document what you will learn: choose a filename and location. before you begin: have an unsaved document open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+s. if the save as area appears, navigate to the desired folder/location. move to the file name field. type a descriptive filename without typing .docx unless word requires it. move to save. press enter. wait for word to return to the document. what should happen: the d

entries.title: NLS Braille eReader Accessible Manual
entries.snippet: Detailed NLS Braille eReader manual covering both HumanWare and Zoomax models.
entries.text: nls braille ereader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible technology manual nls braille ereader accessible manual a step-by-step guide for both humanware and zoomax nls braille ereaders. all manuals ten nls braille ereader lessons my progress purpose and setup this manual supports independent practice with nls braille ereader on windows. use the exact software version, device model, account permissions, and workplace policy available to you. commands and labels can change after updates. start jaws before opening the application or connecting a braille device. use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focus, and insert+1 for keyboard help. practice with fictional, public, instructor-provided, or redacted information only. never submit passwords, recovery codes, government identifiers, protected books, or private workplace data. save a backup before changing, deleting, converting, or remediating a file. identify your model before using commands zoomax: has six display keys labeled d1 through d6, four system keys labeled s1 through s4, and five navigation keys. s1 opens the main menu. humanware: uses four thumb keys for menu movement and does not use the zoomax s1 through s4 arrangement. important: both models have 20 braille cells and perkins-style keys, but their navigation and file commands are not interchangeable. humanware model: basic and advanced how-tos keyboard commands: humanware ereader commands use braille chords, thumb keys, enter, and backspace as described in each task. return to the main menu and open a book device commands: space with m, dots 1-3-4, opens the main menu. up and down thumb keys move through items. enter opens the selected item. press space with m. move to book reader and press enter. open book list. use the thumb keys to find the intended title. press enter and use the panning keys to read. you should feel: the selected title followed by its opening text. if that does not happen: press space with m once and confirm whether book reader stopped or another message is displayed. navigate, search, and identify your position device commands: space+dot 1 or space+dot 4 moves by paragraph; space+dot 2 or space+dot 5 moves by page; space+f, dots 1-2-4, searches; space with the w-h sign, dots 1-5-6, gives where am i. open a practice book. move forward and backward by paragraph, then by page. press space+f, type a word, and press enter. use space+n for the next result or space+p for the previous result. press space with dots 1-5-6 to confirm the location. if that does not happen: check spelling and whether the search started after the current position. insert and return to a bookmark device commands: enter+b, dots 1-2, inserts a quick bookmark. enter+j, dots 2-4-5, opens the bookmark list. move to a passage you want to save. press enter+b and note the bookmark confirmation. move several pages away. press enter+j, enter the bookmark number if requested, and press enter. use where am i to verify the restored position. if that does not happen: open the bookmark menu with enter+m and inspect saved bookmark numbers. find and download a bard title connect to a trusted wi-fi network. press space+m and open online services, then nls bard. open search collection, enter a title, author, or keyword, and press enter. move through results and press enter for title information. choose download or download then open. wait for completion, return to book reader, and confirm the title in book list. if that does not happen: check the wi-fi and bard status. never include bard credentials in a lesson file. manage a file without losing it device commands: space+d selects a drive; space+i gives information; backspace+c copies; backspace+x cuts; backspace+v pastes. open file manager and press space+d to select the drive. use thumb keys to select the file and press space+i to confirm its name and location. use backspace+c to preserve the original or backspace+x only when moving it. open the verified destination and press backspace+v. confirm both source and destination before deleting anything. if that does not happen: preserve every copy and check available storage with space+i. zoomax model: basic and advanced how-tos return to the main menu and open a book device commands: s1 or space with m, dots 1-3-4, opens the main menu. navigate up or down with n-up, n-down, d1, d3, d4, or d6. dot 8, n-center, or a cursor router activates the selected item. press s1. move to book reader and press enter. open book list. move through titles until the intended book is displayed. press enter and use d2 or the left panning key to pan left; use d5 or the right panning key to pan right. you should feel: the selected title followed by its opening text. if that does not happen: press s1 once and check for a startup, storage, or error message before reopening book reader. navigate and identify your reading position device commands: dot 1 moves to the previous paragraph and dot 4 to the next paragraph. dot 2 moves to the previous page and dot 5 to the next page. space with the w-h sign, dots 1-5-6, gives the current position. open a practice book. move forward and backward by paragraph. move forward and backward by page. press space with dots 1-5-6. read the reported page, volume, and position information. if that does not happen: confirm that focus is inside the open book rather than book list or a menu. search for text device commands: space with f, dots 1-2-4, opens find. space with n, dots 1-3-4-5, finds the next occurrence; space with p, dots 1-2-3-4, finds the previous occurrence. move to a known point in the book. press space+f, type the search term, and press enter. read the surrounding line to confirm the match. press space+n for the next match or space+p to move backward. use where am i to record the result’s location. if that does not happen: check spelling, braille grade, and whether the search begins from the current position. create and return to a bookmark device approach: press s3 for the context menu, then select the bookmark command shown for the current book. move to the passage you want to save. press s3 and find set bookmark. activate it and confirm the bookmark message. move several pages away. open the context menu again, choose go to bookmark, select the bookmark, and press enter. use where am i to verify the restored position. if that does not happen: confirm that the book supports bookmarks and that the bookmark was created in the current title. find and download a bard title device command: space with a, dot 1, opens bard from anywhere after the device is configured. connect to trusted wi-fi and press space+a. choose a title, author, subject, or keyword search. enter the search text and press enter. move through results, open the intended title, and review its information. choose download or the current download-and-open option. wait for completion, then open book list and verify the title. if that does not happen: check wi-fi and bard sign-in status without putting credentials in a lesson file. use file manager safely device commands: space with f, dots 1-2-4, opens file manager. s2 opens the application menu; s3 opens the context menu. press space+f and identify the current drive and folder. move to the file and confirm its complete name. press s3 and choose copy when the original must remain, or move only when relocation is intended. navigate to the destination folder and use its context or application menu to paste. verify both locations before deleting anything. if that does not happen: preserve every copy and check available storage before repeating the operation. connect the zoomax ereader as a braille display device commands: space with t, dots 2-3-4-5, toggles bluetooth. the power on quick menu also offers bluetooth and usb modes. save current reading position and work. choose bluetooth or usb mode on the ereader. on the computer or mobile device, open the screen reader’s braille-display settings. sele

entries.title: NLS Braille eReader EMZ-20 Manual
entries.snippet: NLS Braille eReader EMZ-20 Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: nls braille ereader emz-20 manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual nls braille ereader emz-20 manual zoomax 20-cell refreshable braille ereader independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual model emz-20 • nls talking book program official nls braille ereader zoomax user guide purpose: this manual is written directly to the person learning the nls braille ereader model emz-20. it assumes you may be touching the device for the first time. every procedure identifies exactly where a button or port is located, what to press, what should appear on the 20-cell braille display, and what to do if the result is different. device identity: the emz-20 is the zoomax version of the nls braille ereader. nls also distributes a different humanware 20-cell ereader. the button layout and commands are not interchangeable. official reference: this manual is original training material based on the current nls braille ereader zoomax user guide and getting started information from the national library service for the blind and print disabled, library of congress. how to use this manual begin with parts 1 through 7 even if you already know braille. they teach the physical layout and command system used throughout the rest of the device. orient the device with the 20 braille cells closest to your body unless a procedure says otherwise. dot 7 is the backspace key. dot 8 is the enter key. the six display keys are d1, d2, d3 on the left and d4, d5, d6 on the right. the four system keys are s1 and s2 on the far-left front area, and s3 and s4 on the far-right front area. the two large rectangular front keys are bl and br. they act like space for many commands and act as panning keys while reading a book. the five center navigation keys are n-left, n-up, n-right, n-down, and n-center. do one action, then stop and read the display before pressing another key. when you forget a command, use s3 to open the context menu or open help from the main menu. table of contents part 1 - identify the emz-20 and what it does part 2 - physical layout: top surface part 3 - physical layout: front controls part 4 - physical layout: left and right sides part 5 - charging the battery part 6 - power on, power off, and suspend part 7 - learn the braille keyboard part 8 - main menu part 9 - menu navigation and first-letter navigation part 10 - context menu and global commands part 11 - reading 20-cell braille and panning part 12 - book reader basics part 13 - book navigation by line, paragraph, page, volume, and article part 14 - where am i, autoscroll, word wrap, and reflow part 15 - bard: wi-fi and first login part 16 - bard: browse, search, download, and wish list part 17 - nfb-newsline part 18 - file manager part 19 - nls cartridge, usb flash drive, and sd card part 20 - settings part 21 - braille settings and grade part 22 - wi-fi part 23 - battery, device information, and help part 24 - bluetooth mode part 25 - connect to iphone or ipad part 26 - connect to mac with voiceover part 27 - connect to windows or mac by usb part 28 - use with jaws and nvda part 29 - keyboard lock and common recovery skills part 30 - troubleshooting part 31 - care and safe handling part 32 - independent practice course part 33 - quick reference commands part 34 - official nls resources part 1 - identify the emz-20 and what it does the emz-20 is the zoomax nls braille ereader. it is a 20-cell refreshable braille display and standalone electronic braille reader distributed through nls network libraries. it can read electronic braille and other supported documents, download nls content through bard, use external storage, and function as a braille display for compatible computers and apple mobile devices. 20 refreshable braille cells with a routing button behind each cell. eight-key perkins-style braille keyboard: dots 1 through 8. three space-key locations: the center space key plus bl and br for many chord commands. six display keys: d1 through d6. four system keys: s1 through s4. five navigation keys: n-left, n-up, n-right, n-down, and n-center. usb-c for charging and computer connection. usb-a for nls cartridge cable or usb flash drive. sd-card slot for external storage. wi-fi for bard and nfb-newsline. bluetooth for compatible external screen-reader devices. part 2 - physical layout: top surface 2.1 orient the device correctly what you will learn: place the emz-20 in the correct position before learning any buttons. before you begin: place the device on a stable surface. exactly how to do it find the long row of 20 refreshable braille cells. rotate the device until those cells are closest to your body. keep the device in that orientation for all physical descriptions in this manual. place both index fingers lightly on the braille cells and move from the leftmost cell to the rightmost cell. move your fingertips slightly toward the back of the device. directly behind each braille cell is a small round cursor-routing button. move farther toward the back to locate the perkins-style braille keyboard. what should happen: the braille cells are along the front/top edge closest to you, routing buttons are immediately behind them, and the braille keyboard is farther back. if that does not happen: if you cannot identify the row of 20 cells, do not press keys. rotate the unit until the long line of braille cells is nearest you. practice: with the unit powered off, find cells, routing buttons, and keyboard three times. 2.2 learn the perkins keyboard by touch layout: from the center toward the left are dots 1, 2, 3, and dot 7. from the center toward the right are dots 4, 5, 6, and dot 8. dot 7 also serves as backspace; dot 8 also serves as enter. the space key is centered below/between the braille input groups. left-hand group from inner to outer: dot 1, dot 2, dot 3, dot 7. right-hand group from inner to outer: dot 4, dot 5, dot 6, dot 8. dot 7 = backspace. dot 8 = enter. center space is used by itself and in chord commands. part 3 - physical layout: front controls along the angled front panel closest to you are eleven controls. learn them by moving from the outside edges toward the center. control where it is main purpose s1 far-left outer small round system key main menu s2 second small round key from far-left menu for the current application bl large rectangular key left of center acts as space for many chords; pans backward while reading a book n-left left directional navigation key in center cluster move left/backward in books or hierarchy n-up upper directional navigation key move up in menus/lists; previous line in a book n-center middle of navigation cluster select/activate in supported contexts n-right right directional navigation key move right/forward in books or hierarchy n-down lower directional navigation key move down in menus/lists; next line in a book br large rectangular key right of center acts as space for many chords; pans forward while reading a book s3 second small round key from far-right context menu s4 far-right outer small round key open current book at last reading position keyboard lock: pressing s1 and s4 together toggles keyboard lock. when locked, the display reads keyboard locked. press s1+s4 again, or use the power on button as described by nls, to unlock. part 4 - physical layout: left and right sides 4.1 left side with the braille cells closest to you, feel along the left side from front to back. front corner: lanyard attachment point. behind the lanyard point: sd-card slot. the braille letters “sd” are above the sd-card slot. 4.2 right side with the braille cells closest to you, feel along the right side from front to back. the order is critical because this is where power and charging are located. front corner: lanyard attachment point. immediately behind it: small round power on button. braille “on” is above it. immediately behind power on: small round power off button. braille “off” is above it. behind the power b
