entries.snippet: Step-by-step keyboard manual for NotebookLM, Be My AI, and AI-assisted access.
entries.text: ai-assisted access manual - accessible learning center skip to main content artificial intelligence notebooklm, be my eyes, and ai-assisted access manual use ai access tools by keyboard, verify their answers, and protect private information. basic how-tos advanced how-tos command list basic how-tos navigate an ai website what you will learn: complete navigate an ai website independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: tab and shift+tab move through controls. enter activates links and buttons. space changes checkboxes. h moves by heading and b moves by button in jaws and nvda browse mode. open the tool and confirm its name and active account. press h to review page headings. press e or f in supported screen readers to find an edit field. type a short prompt using only public, fictional, or authorized information. submit it, then return to headings or browse mode to locate the response. read the complete response before acting. what should happen: a named prompt field, a submit control, and a structured response. if that does not happen: press escape once, check the focused control with insert+tab or nvda+tab, and navigate by landmarks or headings. practice: repeat navigate an ai website with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. ask for a useful image description what you will learn: complete ask for a useful image description independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: find upload, add image, or take picture by button navigation. remove private documents, addresses, faces, credentials, and medical information unless sharing is authorized. activate the image control and choose the intended image. verify the filename before submitting. ask a focused question such as, “describe the controls from top to bottom,” or “read the expiration date and state any uncertainty.” save the answer only after checking important details another way. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: cancel the upload and confirm the image format, connection, and permissions. practice: repeat ask for a useful image description with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. create a notebooklm notebook and add a source what you will learn: complete create a notebooklm notebook and add a source independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: use h for headings, b for buttons, and tab or shift+tab through dialogs. open notebooklm and activate create new notebook. enter a descriptive notebook name. activate add source. choose the source type and select only an authorized document or public link. wait for processing and verify that the source name appears in the source list. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: do not add the source again until you check the source list and any processing alert. practice: repeat create a notebooklm notebook and add a source with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. advanced how-tos verify a notebooklm answer against its source what you will learn: complete verify a notebooklm answer against its source independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: use heading and link navigation to move between an answer, its citation links, and the source viewer. ask one specific question. read the entire answer and note names, dates, numbers, and claims. open each citation. read enough text before and after the cited passage to understand context. mark each claim supported, unsupported, or uncertain. use only supported claims in your work. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: treat the answer as unverified and search the original source directly. practice: repeat verify a notebooklm answer against its source with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. compare two sources what you will learn: complete compare two sources independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: use the source-selection controls before asking the question. add two authorized sources and confirm both names. select only those sources if the tool permits source selection. ask for agreements, differences, and direct citations. open the citations for each claimed difference. create your own short comparison using verified facts. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: ask separate questions about each source and compare the verified answers yourself. practice: repeat compare two sources with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. use ai for visual access without overtrusting it what you will learn: complete use ai for visual access without overtrusting it independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: return to the prompt field and ask follow-up questions that isolate one detail at a time. ask the tool to separate visible observations from interpretation. ask where an item is located using clock-face or top-to-bottom language. ask it to repeat exact text, numbers, or colors and state uncertainty. verify medication, money, identity, navigation, safety, and legal information with a trusted person or authoritative source. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: state what remains unknown. never convert an uncertain ai description into a confident instruction. practice: repeat use ai for visual access without overtrusting it with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. write a safer prompt what you will learn: complete write a safer prompt independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard command: ctrl+a selects the current prompt text; ctrl+c copies; ctrl+v pastes. state the task and desired format. supply only the minimum authorized context. ask the tool to identify assumptions and uncertainty. request citations when the answer depends on sources. review the prompt for private information before submitting. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: shorten the request and ask one question at a time. practice: repeat write a safer prompt with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. quick command list tab / shift+tab: next or previous control enter: activate or submit escape: close a menu or dialog h: next heading in jaws or nvda browse mode b: next button in jaws or nvda browse mode e: next edit field in jaws or nvda browse mode insert+tab / nvda+tab: identify focused control ctrl+a / ctr

entries.title: OneDrive, Dropbox, and Cloud Sharing Manual
entries.snippet: Step-by-step keyboard manual for OneDrive, Dropbox, and cloud sharing.
entries.text: cloud storage manual - accessible learning center skip to main content cloud storage onedrive, dropbox, and cloud sharing manual save, organize, synchronize, share, and recover files safely. basic how-tos advanced how-tos command list basic how-tos find your synchronized folder what you will learn: complete find your synchronized folder independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: windows+e opens file explorer. alt+d focuses the address bar. alt+up arrow moves to the parent folder. press windows+e. use the navigation pane or address bar to open onedrive or dropbox. press alt+d and have the screen reader read the location. press escape to return to the file list. select a file and hear its complete name and status. what should happen: onedrive or dropbox in the current path. if that does not happen: a similarly named local folder may not synchronize. confirm the service is signed in before saving important work there. practice: repeat find your synchronized folder with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. create a folder and save a file in it what you will learn: complete create a folder and save a file in it independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: ctrl+shift+n creates a folder in file explorer. f2 renames it. open the correct onedrive or dropbox location. press ctrl+shift+n. type a descriptive folder name and press enter. open the folder and save or paste a practice file into it. wait for synchronization, then verify the file is listed. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: press escape, recheck the current path, and confirm you have permission to create folders. practice: repeat create a folder and save a file in it with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. copy or move a file what you will learn: complete copy or move a file independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: ctrl+c copies, ctrl+x moves, and ctrl+v pastes. select one file and read its name. press ctrl+c to keep the original, or ctrl+x to move it. open the destination and confirm its path. press ctrl+v once. verify the result and wait for synchronization. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: do not paste repeatedly. check both locations for duplicates, conflicts, or a permission alert. practice: repeat copy or move a file with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. advanced how-tos share a file with named people what you will learn: complete share a file with named people independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard command: shift+f10 or the application key opens a context menu in many windows configurations. select the file and verify its name and owner. press shift+f10 and choose share. enter the intended email addresses. choose can view or can edit. review recipients and permission before sending. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: cancel and use the service’s labeled share command. sharing may open a web dialog. practice: repeat share a file with named people with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. create and check a sharing link what you will learn: complete create and check a sharing link independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: open share, then locate link settings with tab or button navigation. choose specific people or people you choose whenever possible. turn editing off unless collaborators must change the file. set an expiration date if available and useful. copy the link. test it in a private browser window without exposing private data. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: remove the link or stop sharing and create a narrower permission. practice: repeat create and check a sharing link with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. recover an earlier version what you will learn: complete recover an earlier version independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: select the file, open its context menu, and find version history. confirm the file and current owner. open version history and review dates, times, and editors. preview or download the older version when possible. make a backup of the current version. restore only after confirming what will be replaced. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: keep the current file and ask the owner or administrator whether version history is available. practice: repeat recover an earlier version with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. resolve a synchronization conflict what you will learn: complete resolve a synchronization conflict independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: f2 renames a selected file; alt+enter opens properties. stop editing both copies. compare filenames, modified dates, sizes, and locations. rename each copy clearly instead of overwriting either one. open and compare their content. keep the correct copy, then archive or delete the other only after verification. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: preserve both copies and ask for help. never guess which conflict copy is current. practice: repeat resolve a synchronization conflict with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. quick command list windows+e: file explorer alt+d: address bar ctrl+shift+n: new folder f2: rename ctrl+c / ctrl+x / ctrl+v: copy / move / paste shift+f10: context menu alt+enter: properties ctrl+z: undo the most recent supported file action return to manuals

entries.title: Screen Readers: JAWS, Narrator, and NVDA
entries.course: Screen Readers: JAWS, Narrator, and NVDA
entries.snippet: Accessible screen-reader manual comparing JAWS, Windows Narrator, and NVDA.
entries.text: screen readers manual - accessible learning center skip to main content foundational assistive technology manual screen readers: jaws, narrator, and nvda choose one screen reader and learn the same workplace skills with product-specific commands. all manuals ten screen readers lessons my progress choose the screen reader available to you three windows screen-reader choices screen reader best reason to choose it for this course important note jaws choose jaws when it is installed and licensed by you, your school, or your workplace. includes jaws-specific tools such as fscompanion and picture smart ai when available. windows narrator choose narrator when you need the screen reader built into windows 11. start or stop it with windows+ctrl+enter. its scan mode and views differ from jaws. nvda choose nvda when it is already installed or your organization approves the free, open-source windows screen reader. its browse mode and nvda modifier commands differ from jaws and narrator. use one primary screen reader at a time. running several simultaneously can produce overlapping speech and conflicting commands. an instructor may demonstrate a second product after the student can safely start, stop, and recover the primary choice. what stays the same windows and application commands such as tab, shift+tab, arrow keys, enter, spacebar, ctrl+c, ctrl+v, alt+tab, and windows+l usually stay the same. screen-reader commands differ when you request information, change reading modes, open element lists, adjust speech, or use product settings. equivalent concepts with different names screen-reader key: jaws key, narrator key, or nvda key. web-reading mode: jaws virtual cursor, narrator scan mode, or nvda browse mode. typing in forms: jaws forms mode, narrator with scan mode off, or nvda focus mode. command discovery: jaws keyboard help, narrator input learning, or nvda input help. ten-lesson learning path lesson 1: choose, start, and stop a screen reader — choose jaws, narrator, or nvda and start and stop it safely. lesson 2: keyboard help, speech control, and basic information — use keyboard help and control speech without losing focus. lesson 3: read by character, word, line, paragraph, and continuously — read and review text at several levels with the chosen screen reader. lesson 4: navigate windows, dialogs, and controls — move reliably through windows applications and identify focus. lesson 5: browse webpages by headings, links, lists, and landmarks — navigate structured webpages efficiently with the selected screen reader. lesson 6: complete forms and manage input modes — enter fictional information in web forms while controlling reading and typing modes. lesson 7: navigate tables, lists, and structured information — read relationships in tables and lists without losing row or column context. lesson 8: read, edit, and review workplace documents — use shared editing commands and screen-reader feedback in word or another document editor. lesson 9: help, settings, updates, braille, and jaws ai — find trustworthy help, make reversible settings changes, and understand product-specific advanced features. lesson 10: final screen-reader workplace project — complete a realistic windows, web, form, document, and troubleshooting workflow with the chosen screen reader. official references freedom scientific: navigating web pages with jaws freedom scientific: jaws reading commands microsoft: complete guide to narrator microsoft: narrator keyboard commands nv access: current nvda user guide nv access: current nvda commands quick reference progress preservation: this course replaces the former jaws-only presentation. existing jaws lesson submissions remain recognized in student progress. start screen readers lesson 1 return to manuals basic and advanced step-by-step procedures these procedures make the manual usable on its own. the separate lessons provide assignments and progress tracking when you want a course experience. basic 1: choose, start, and stop a screen reader basic 2: keyboard help, speech control, and basic information basic 3: read by character, word, line, paragraph, and continuously basic 4: navigate windows, dialogs, and controls basic 5: browse webpages by headings, links, lists, and landmarks advanced 6: complete forms and manage input modes advanced 7: navigate tables, lists, and structured information advanced 8: read, edit, and review workplace documents advanced 9: help, settings, updates, braille, and jaws ai advanced 10: final screen-reader workplace project basic procedure 1. choose, start, and stop a screen reader what you will learn: choose jaws, narrator, or nvda and start and stop it safely. before you begin: open a harmless practice document or webpage. confirm which screen reader is running and save open work before changing settings. exactly how to do it choose one primary screen reader for this course. do not run multiple screen readers at the same time unless an instructor directs you. confirm that the computer’s speakers or headset are connected and the volume is safe. start the selected screen reader using its method in the comparison table. open notepad and type one short sentence. confirm the screen reader announces the application, focus, and typed text. save the note and stop the screen reader using its documented method. what should happen: you can complete the procedure and verify the result using the keyboard, your screen reader, or your braille display. if that does not happen: press escape to leave an unexpected menu or dialog, confirm the active window and keyboard focus, then repeat one step at a time. use undo when a reversible content change occurred. practice: create a one-page choice report naming the selected screen reader, why it fits the practice computer, and how to start and stop it. basic procedure 2. keyboard help, speech control, and basic information what you will learn: use keyboard help and control speech without losing focus. before you begin: open a harmless practice document or webpage. confirm which screen reader is running and save open work before changing settings. exactly how to do it open the screen reader selected in lesson 1. use its keyboard-help command and press several harmless keys to hear their descriptions. exit keyboard help before returning to work. press ctrl while speech is talking to stop speech. use the current-focus command to identify the selected control. use the window-title command to confirm the active application. what should happen: you can complete the procedure and verify the result using the keyboard, your screen reader, or your braille display. if that does not happen: press escape to leave an unexpected menu or dialog, confirm the active window and keyboard focus, then repeat one step at a time. use undo when a reversible content change occurred. practice: create a command card for keyboard help, stopping speech, current focus, and window title. basic procedure 3. read by character, word, line, paragraph, and continuously what you will learn: read and review text at several levels with the chosen screen reader. before you begin: open a harmless practice document or webpage. confirm which screen reader is running and save open work before changing settings. exactly how to do it open an instructor-provided text document and move to the beginning with ctrl+home. use left and right arrow to review characters in editable text. use ctrl+left arrow and ctrl+right arrow to move by word. use up and down arrow to move by line or paragraph as supported by the application. use the screen reader’s continuous-reading command. stop speech with ctrl and summarize the passage. what should happen: you can complete the procedure and verify the result using the keyboard, your screen reader, or your braille display. if that does not happen: press escape to leave an unexpected menu or dialog, confirm the active window and keyboard focus, then repeat one step at a time. use undo when a reversible con

entries.title: Screen-Reader Troubleshooting and Recovery Manual
entries.snippet: Step-by-step keyboard manual for screen-reader troubleshooting and recovery.
entries.text: screen-reader recovery manual - accessible learning center skip to main content foundations and recovery screen-reader troubleshooting and recovery manual identify focus, mode, application, audio, and computer problems before restarting. basic how-tos advanced how-tos command list basic how-tos identify the active window what you will learn: complete identify the active window independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: jaws: insert+t. nvda: nvda+t. narrator: narrator key+t. stop typing so you do not change unknown content. press the command for your screen reader. listen for the application, document, or dialog title. if it is wrong, press alt+tab once and check the title again. what should happen: a useful window or document title. if that does not happen: test speech in another safe window before closing anything. practice: repeat identify the active window with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. identify the focused control what you will learn: complete identify the focused control independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: jaws: insert+tab. nvda: nvda+tab. narrator: narrator key+tab reads the current item in common configurations. press the focus-information command. decide whether focus is in text, a button, a list, browser content, or a dialog. press tab once. request focus information again and compare the result. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: check for a modal dialog, protected screen, or screen-reader mode intercepting keys. practice: repeat identify the focused control with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. use keyboard help without performing commands what you will learn: complete use keyboard help without performing commands independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: jaws: insert+1. nvda: nvda+1. narrator input learning: narrator key+1. turn keyboard help on. press the command you are unsure about. listen to its name or description. press the keyboard-help command again to turn help off. what should happen: key descriptions without the normal actions occurring. if that does not happen: stop pressing uncertain commands and open the screen reader’s commands or help documentation. practice: repeat use keyboard help without performing commands with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. recover when speech stops what you will learn: complete recover when speech stops independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: windows+ctrl+enter toggles narrator. ctrl+alt+n starts nvda when its desktop shortcut is configured. jaws can be started from its desktop shortcut or start menu. press a volume key and confirm the computer is not muted. check headphones, speakers, bluetooth, and the selected output device. try the screen reader’s start command once. wait at least ten seconds and test with a safe key such as windows. use a second screen reader temporarily if necessary. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: save work with ctrl+s where safe, then ask for sighted or remote assistance before restarting. practice: repeat recover when speech stops with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. advanced how-tos switch between browse and forms interaction what you will learn: complete switch between browse and forms interaction independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: jaws: insert+z toggles the virtual cursor. nvda: nvda+space toggles browse and focus modes. request focus information and identify the web control. use browse mode to read headings, links, and surrounding instructions. move to the edit field or interactive control. switch to focus/forms interaction only when needed. return to browse mode after completing the control. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: press escape once, check focus, and avoid repeatedly toggling modes without listening for confirmation. practice: repeat switch between browse and forms interaction with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. recover from a trapped dialog what you will learn: complete recover from a trapped dialog independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: tab and shift+tab inspect controls. escape cancels many dialogs. alt+f4 closes the active window. read the window title and focused control. move through the dialog once with tab and shift+tab. choose cancel if available. press escape only when canceling is safe. use alt+f4 only after deciding whether unsaved work or a confirmation may appear. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: do not hold keys down. use alt+tab to check whether a hidden confirmation opened behind another window. practice: repeat recover from a trapped dialog with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. restart in the safest order what you will learn: complete restart in the safest order independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: ctrl+s saves in many applications. alt+f4 closes the active application. windows+x, u, r restarts windows. save work and confirm the filename and location. restart only the affected application first. if the problem continues everywhere, restart the screen reader. restart windows only after files are saved and applications are closed. after restart, test one simple task before reopening everything. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: stop before repair or reinstall. back up settings and record the error, application, and steps that caused it. practice: repeat restart in the safest order with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. collect useful information for support what you will learn: complete collect useful information for support independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: windows+v opens clipboard history when enabled. windows+shift+s opens snipping tool for a helper when visual capture is appropriate. write the application and screen-reader names and versions. record the exact task and commands used. copy the complete error message. state what was expected and what happened instead. list the safe troubleshooting already attempted. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and ca

entries.title: Social Media Accessibility Screen Reader Manual
entries.snippet: Social Media Accessibility Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: social media accessibility screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual social media accessibility screen reader manual keyboard and mobile screen-reader instruction independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches how to use major social-media platforms with a screen reader and how to create posts that are accessible to other people. it assumes no prior social-media experience. platforms: facebook, linkedin, youtube, and x. interfaces change frequently, so the manual teaches stable navigation patterns first and then platform-specific controls. screen readers: desktop guidance applies to narrator, nvda, jaws, and voiceover where appropriate. mobile guidance applies to voiceover on iphone/ipad and talkback on android. how to use this manual use headings, landmarks, buttons, links, edit fields, and lists rather than tabbing through every item on long feeds. when a platform introduces a new layout, identify the main navigation region, search field, feed/timeline, post composer, notifications, profile, and settings before learning platform-specific shortcuts. use screen-reader application/focus mode only when the web app requires direct keyboard commands; return to browse/virtual mode for ordinary webpage navigation. before posting media, add meaningful alt text to images and accurate captions to video when the platform supports them. write hashtags in camelcase, avoid long strings of emoji, and avoid decorative unicode characters that screen readers may announce one symbol at a time. before changing privacy or audience settings, have the screen reader repeat the selected audience or account name. do not trust direct messages that ask for passwords, codes, gift cards, crypto, remote access, or urgent money transfers. table of contents part 1 - social media with a screen reader part 2 - screen reader navigation patterns part 3 - writing accessible social posts part 4 - image descriptions and alt text part 5 - video captions and audio description part 6 - hashtags, emoji, and links part 7 - facebook: orientation and feed part 8 - facebook: posting, comments, groups, and messages part 9 - linkedin: orientation and feed part 10 - linkedin: profile, posts, networking, and jobs part 11 - youtube: search and watching videos part 12 - youtube: player shortcuts and captions part 13 - youtube: comments, subscriptions, playlists, and uploading part 14 - x: orientation and timeline part 15 - x: keyboard shortcuts part 16 - x: posting, replies, direct messages, and alt text part 17 - mobile social media with voiceover part 18 - mobile social media with talkback part 19 - privacy, security, and scam safety part 20 - troubleshooting part 21 - independent practice course part 22 - quick reference part 23 - official resources part 1 - social media with a screen reader most social platforms are dynamic web applications. new posts load without a full page refresh, menus open in dialogs, buttons change labels after activation, and feeds can contain repeated controls. the key skill is maintaining context. main navigation: home/feed, search, notifications, messages, profile, settings. feed/timeline: a long list of posts. each post can contain author, time, text, media, reaction controls, comment/reply controls, and menus. composer: edit field/dialog for creating a post. post details: a focused page/dialog for one post and its replies/comments. notifications: activity related to your account. direct messages: private conversations; not automatically trustworthy merely because they appear inside a social platform. part 2 - screen reader navigation patterns task command / method next heading h in many screen readers/browsers next button b next link k in nvda/jaws; vo rotor on mac/ios next edit field e next landmark/region d or r depending on screen reader next list l screen-reader elements list nvda+f7 / jaws+f3 or insert+f7 / vo rotor command warning: screen-reader single-letter commands work only in browse/virtual mode. if typing h, b, or e enters characters into a post field, exit the edit field or return to browse mode. 2.1 rebuild context on any platform what you will learn: recover when focus gets lost in a dynamic feed. before you begin: a social-media webpage is open. exactly how to do it press escape once or twice to close an open menu/dialog if appropriate. use your screen reader to move to the page title or first heading. move by landmarks/regions to find navigation or main content. use headings or buttons to find the feed, search, notifications, or composer. have the screen reader repeat the focused item before activating it. what should happen: you regain a known location without refreshing or signing out. if that does not happen: if the page remains confused, use the browser address bar and reload the known platform homepage, then navigate again. practice: practice getting lost intentionally and recovering. part 3 - writing accessible social posts use sentence case rather than all capitals. keep important information in text, not only inside an image. break long posts into short paragraphs. put emoji at natural points and avoid repeating the same emoji many times. use descriptive link wording when the platform allows it. use camelcase hashtags: #screenreaderusers rather than #screenreaderusers. do not use decorative mathematical/script unicode characters as fake fonts; screen readers may announce them poorly or character by character. if a post depends on a chart, screenshot, flyer, or meme, add the essential information in alt text or the post body. part 4 - image descriptions and alt text alt text should communicate the image information needed to understand the post. describe purpose and key content, not every pixel. good: “three coworkers seated around a conference table reviewing a tactile diagram.” better for text-heavy image: include the important visible words in the post itself, then describe the visual context. avoid starting every description with “image of” unless the platform does not already identify it as an image. do not use auto-generated alt text as a substitute for reviewing important images. 4.1 add alt text before posting what you will learn: make an uploaded image understandable to screen-reader users. before you begin: a social platform supports author-supplied alt text. exactly how to do it upload/select the image in the post composer. move through the image editing controls until you find alt text, alt, edit, accessibility, or image description. open that control. type a concise description of the image’s important content and purpose. save/done the description. return to the post composer and review the audience and post text before publishing. what should happen: the platform stores your description with the image. if that does not happen: if the platform does not expose an alt-text control in the current app, put the essential image description in the post text and try the desktop/web composer if practical. practice: add alt text to a harmless test image. part 5 - video captions and audio description captions provide text access to speech and meaningful audio. auto-captions are useful but should be reviewed for names, jargon, numbers, and punctuation when you control the video. burned-in/on-screen captions are not always exposed as text to screen readers, but they still help many viewers; platform caption tracks are preferable when available. audio description narrates important visual information that is not obvious from dialogue/sound. if audio description is not supported as a separate track, include essential visual context in narration or the description/post text. part 6 - hashtags, emoji, and links example accessibility note #accessibletech good camelcase hashtag #accessibletech harder to parse as separate words ✅ new update available usually concise ✅✅✅✅✅✅✅ repetitive speech noise click here weak link text read the

entries.title: Victor Reader Stream 3 Manual
entries.snippet: Victor Reader Stream 3 Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: victor reader stream 3 manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual victor reader stream 3 manual keys, navigation, books, audio, and online features independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches the victor reader stream 3 from the beginning. it assumes no prior experience with the device and gives physical orientation, exact key sequences, expected speech feedback, troubleshooting, practice, and independent-use checklists. reference: this guide is based on humanware's current stream 3 support materials and user guide version 1.6, with nls/bard information cross-checked against current nls resources. terminology: this manual calls the # key confirm and the * key cancel, matching the device's spoken/manual terminology. how to use this manual keep the stream upright with the numeric keypad facing you and the speaker holes on the bottom edge. learn the physical layout before trying online services. use key describer mode when you forget a key. use key 1 to move among bookshelves and keys 4/6 to move among books on a bookshelf. use keys 2/8 to choose a navigation level and keys 4/6 to move backward/forward at that level. press play/stop to begin or pause reading. press key 5 for where am i? information. press key 0 for device/book information. press and hold key 1 to open the built-in user guide. do not enter bard or bookshare credentials when another person can hear them unless you are comfortable with that privacy risk. table of contents part 1 - what the victor reader stream 3 is part 2 - physical orientation part 3 - charging, power, and battery part 4 - key describer mode part 5 - the bookshelf system part 6 - basic playback part 7 - navigation by heading, page, time, and text part 8 - go to commands part 9 - where am i and info part 10 - sleep timer and clock part 11 - bookmarks part 12 - managing books and files part 13 - sd card and computer file transfer part 14 - text, epub, brf, music, podcasts, and notes part 15 - wi-fi and airplane mode part 16 - bluetooth part 17 - nls bard part 18 - bookshare, nfb-newsline, internet radio, podcasts, and tunein part 19 - recording and audio notes part 20 - settings and software updates part 21 - nls authorization part 22 - troubleshooting part 23 - independent practice course part 24 - quick reference part 25 - official resources part 1 - what the victor reader stream 3 is the victor reader stream 3 is a pocket-size talking-book and media player from humanware. it supports daisy and nls digital talking books, electronic text, braille files, music, podcasts, online book services, internet radio, recording, wi-fi, bluetooth, an sd card, and internal storage. offline bookcase: books and files stored in internal memory or on the sd card. online bookcase: wi-fi services such as nls bard, bookshare, podcasts, radio, and other configured services. bookshelf: one category of content inside a bookcase. navigation level: chapter, heading, page, time jump, paragraph, line, word, character, or another structure supported by the current book. confirm: the # key. cancel: the * key. part 2 - physical orientation 2.1 front face hold the stream upright with the keypad facing you. at the very top of the front face are three special keys. left: square go to key. center: round online key. right: diamond-shaped bookmark key. just above the go to key is a tiny hole for the built-in mono microphone. below those three keys is a telephone-style 12-key numeric pad. key 5 has two raised dots. keys 2, 4, 6, and 8 have tactile raised edges. below the numeric pad are four playback keys. rewind is bottom-left and has a raised edge. fast forward is bottom-right and has a raised edge. play/stop is centered between them. sleep is directly above play/stop. 2.2 left side near the top-left side is the power/toggle button. directly below power is the status led. below the led is a rocker-style up/down control. it changes whichever setting power/toggle has selected: volume, speed, tone, or pitch. at the bottom-left side is a stereo microphone/line-in jack. 2.3 right, top, bottom, and back right side near the top: record button, identified by a raised red circle. top edge: sd-card slot under a small silicone cover. bottom edge center: usb-c port for charging and computer connection. bottom edge left of usb-c: headphone/external-speaker jack. bottom edge right of usb-c: four small holes for the built-in speaker. back: model and serial-number label surrounded by a rubber outline. orientation practice: without powering on the device, locate go to, online, bookmark, 5, play/stop, sleep, power, up/down, record, sd slot, usb-c, headphones, and speaker. part 3 - charging, power, and battery 3.1 charge the stream what you will learn: connect power safely. before you begin: use the supplied usb-c cable and a suitable usb power adapter. exactly how to do it locate the usb-c port at the bottom center. insert the usb-c plug without forcing it. connect the other end to the power adapter. plug the adapter into ac power. leave the stream charging. a full ac charge can take up to about three hours. what should happen: when the player is off and charging, the led blinks. when it is on while charging, the led stays steady. if that does not happen: if it does not charge, try the supplied adapter/cable and another outlet. computer usb charging can be slower or insufficient. practice: charge the device and check battery status. 3.2 turn on or off what you will learn: power the device intentionally. before you begin: the stream has some battery charge. exactly how to do it locate power on the upper-left side. press and hold it until the stream starts. wait for spoken startup feedback. to power off, press and hold power again until shutdown begins. what should happen: the stream starts or shuts down with speech feedback. if that does not happen: if the unit is unresponsive, connect ac power and retry. if necessary use the documented power-button reset procedure. practice: turn the stream on, identify the active bookshelf, then shut it down. battery status: press and hold confirm (#), or press info (0), to hear battery/charging status. part 4 - key describer mode 4.1 learn keys safely what you will learn: have the stream announce keys without carrying out normal actions. before you begin: the stream is on. exactly how to do it press and hold info (0) to enter key describer mode. press any front key. listen to its name/function. try the side controls and playback keys. press and hold info (0) again to exit. what should happen: keys are described instead of performing their ordinary command. if that does not happen: if the stream performs commands, key describer mode was not entered; retry the long press. practice: identify every key without looking at a printed guide. part 5 - the bookshelf system task key / control move to next bookshelf 1 previous/next book on shelf 4 / 6 play selected book play/stop online/offline bookcase online key built-in user guide press and hold 1 5.1 choose a bookshelf and book what you will learn: find content by category. before you begin: the stream contains at least one book/file. exactly how to do it press 1. listen to the bookshelf name. press 1 repeatedly until the desired bookshelf is announced. press 4 or 6 to move backward/forward through books. listen to each title. press play/stop on the desired book. what should happen: the selected book begins where you last stopped, when resume information is available. if that does not happen: if a bookshelf says zero books, choose another shelf or add content. practice: locate three different shelves and one title on each. 5.2 switch online and offline what you will learn: move between local and internet content. before you begin: wi-fi may be needed for online services. exactly how to do it tap the round online key above number 2. listen for online or offline bookcase. press 1 to hear the

entries.snippet: VoiceOver Manual for Mac: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: voiceover manual for mac - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual voiceover manual for mac macos keyboard commands, navigation, and applications independent self-study guide for mac all manuals table of contents start of manual apple voiceover user guide purpose: this manual is written directly to the person learning voiceover. it explains exactly what to press, what should happen, and how to recover when the result is different. vo: vo means the voiceover modifier. by default, use control+option together. caps lock can also be configured as the voiceover modifier. function keys: apple notes that voiceover commands using f1-f12 may also require fn depending on your mac keyboard settings. table of contents part 1 - what voiceover is part 2 - turn voiceover on and off part 3 - voiceover modifier and keyboard help part 4 - move through the mac interface part 5 - interact with groups part 6 - activate controls part 7 - desktop, dock, and menu bar part 8 - finder and spotlight part 9 - apps and windows part 10 - voiceover rotor and item chooser part 11 - quick nav part 12 - web navigation part 13 - read and edit text part 14 - tables and structured content part 15 - notifications and screen sharing part 16 - braille displays and braille access part 17 - trackpad gestures part 18 - voiceover utility part 19 - speech, pronunciation, verbosity, and punctuation part 20 - customize commands and activities part 21 - troubleshooting part 22 - independent practice course part 23 - quick reference commands part 24 - official apple resources part 1 - what voiceover is voiceover is the screen reader built into macos. it speaks and can display in braille the item currently selected by the voiceover cursor. you can control the mac with keyboard commands, trackpad gestures, or a connected braille display. voiceover cursor: the item voiceover is currently describing. keyboard focus: the control receiving keyboard input. interaction: entering a group, toolbar, table, web area, or other container so you can move through its contents. activation: performing the action of the selected control. rotor: a navigation tool that lets you choose categories such as headings, links, or form controls. item chooser: a searchable list of items available in the current context. part 2 - turn voiceover on and off 2.1 turn voiceover on what you will learn: start voiceover. before you begin: be at the mac keyboard. exactly how to do it hold command. press f5 once. release both keys. if your mac requires fn for function keys, try command+fn+f5. listen for voiceover speech. what should happen: voiceover announces that it is on and begins speaking the focused item. if that does not happen: if nothing happens, open system settings > accessibility > voiceover and turn voiceover on there. practice: turn voiceover off and on twice. task command turn voiceover on/off command+f5 alternative on touch id mac hold command and quickly press touch id three times part 3 - voiceover modifier and keyboard help 3.1 learn the vo modifier what you will learn: use voiceover commands correctly. before you begin: voiceover is on. exactly how to do it place one finger on control and one on option. hold both keys together. while holding them, press right arrow once. release all keys. repeat using left arrow. what should happen: voiceover moves to the next or previous item. if that does not happen: if nothing changes, make sure both control and option were held while the arrow key was pressed. practice: move forward five items and backward five items. 3.2 use keyboard help what you will learn: safely learn what keys and commands do. before you begin: voiceover is on. exactly how to do it press vo+k. press a key or voiceover command you want to identify. listen to voiceover describe it. try several commands. press escape to leave keyboard help. what should happen: voiceover identifies commands without carrying them out normally. if that does not happen: if the command performs an action instead, keyboard help may not have opened; press vo+k again. practice: identify vo+space, vo+right arrow, vo+left arrow, and vo+shift+down arrow. part 4 - move through the mac interface task command next item vo+right arrow previous item vo+left arrow read from current position vo+a read from top vo+b pause/resume speech control 4.1 move one item at a time what you will learn: navigate without using a mouse. before you begin: voiceover is on. exactly how to do it press vo+right arrow once. stop and listen to the item name and type. press vo+right arrow again. press vo+left arrow once and confirm you returned. continue one item at a time. what should happen: voiceover describes a different item after each move. if that does not happen: if movement seems stuck, you may be inside a group or control. press vo+shift+up arrow to move outward, then try again. practice: explore ten items on the current screen without activating them. part 5 - interact with groups task command interact with group vo+shift+down arrow stop interacting vo+shift+up arrow 5.1 enter and leave a group what you will learn: reach controls that are inside toolbars, tables, web areas, and other containers. before you begin: voiceover is focused on a group or container. exactly how to do it listen for voiceover to announce a group, toolbar, table, or similar container. press vo+shift+down arrow. press vo+right arrow to move through items inside it. when finished, press vo+shift+up arrow. continue vo+right arrow at the outer level. what should happen: you can move inside the group and then return to its parent level. if that does not happen: if voiceover skips controls you expect to be inside a group, interact with it. if you feel trapped, press vo+shift+up arrow more than once. practice: enter a toolbar, inspect three items, then leave it. part 6 - activate controls task command activate selected control vo+space 6.1 activate a button or link what you will learn: perform the action of the selected item. before you begin: voiceover is focused on the desired control. exactly how to do it use vo+right/left arrow until voiceover announces the exact button, link, checkbox, or other control. stop and confirm the name. press vo+space. listen for what changed before pressing another key. what should happen: the button activates, link opens, checkbox toggles, or control performs its action. if that does not happen: if the wrong action occurs, you activated the wrong item. return and confirm the control name before pressing vo+space. practice: find a harmless button and activate it deliberately. part 7 - desktop, dock, and menu bar task command move to dock vo+d open apple menu vo+shift+m 7.1 open an app from the dock what you will learn: use the dock without a mouse. before you begin: voiceover is on. exactly how to do it press vo+d. use vo+right/left arrow through dock items. stop when the desired app is announced. press vo+space. what should happen: the application opens or comes to the front. if that does not happen: if the dock does not appear, make sure voiceover is active and try vo+d again. practice: open finder or another safe app from the dock. 7.2 use the menu bar what you will learn: open menus and choose commands. before you begin: an app is active. exactly how to do it press vo+m or use the appropriate voiceover menu-bar navigation command for your configuration. move through menu headings. open the desired menu with vo+space. use arrow keys or vo navigation through menu items. press enter/vo+space on the command. press escape to close without choosing. what should happen: the selected menu command runs. if that does not happen: if focus remains inside the application, use the apple menu shortcut vo+shift+m as a reliable starting point. practice: open the apple menu and close it with escape. part 8 - finder and spotlight 8.1 open spotlight what you will learn: find an app, file, or setting quickly. before you begin: be an

entries.title: Windows 11 Accessibility Manual
entries.snippet: Windows 11 Accessibility Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: windows 11 accessibility manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual windows 11 accessibility manual narrator, nvda, and jaws independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches the built-in accessibility features of windows 11. it is designed to stand alone and assumes no previous experience with windows accessibility settings. scope: this guide focuses on accessibility features built into current windows 11: magnifier, text and pointer settings, color filters, contrast themes, narrator overview, live captions, audio accessibility, hearing devices, voice access, voice typing, on-screen keyboard, sticky/filter/toggle keys, mouse keys, eye control, focus and notification settings, and accessibility shortcuts. core shortcut: press windows+u at any time to open settings > accessibility. how to use this manual change one accessibility setting at a time, test it, and then decide whether to keep it. press windows+u to return to the accessibility settings hub. use tab and shift+tab to move among controls; use arrow keys in lists and spacebar to toggle many switches. keep a written record of settings that make the computer easier to use. some features depend on hardware, language, windows edition, or device capability. built-in accessibility features can be combined; for example, magnifier can be used with narrator, and sticky keys can be used with keyboard shortcuts. do not disable an accessibility feature that another person depends on without their permission. if a shortcut triggers something unexpected, press escape and return to windows+u before changing more settings. table of contents part 1 - windows 11 accessibility overview part 2 - open and navigate accessibility settings part 3 - text size and visual effects part 4 - mouse pointer and touch part 5 - text cursor part 6 - magnifier part 7 - magnifier reading part 8 - color filters part 9 - contrast themes part 10 - narrator overview part 11 - live captions part 12 - audio, mono audio, and visual alerts part 13 - hearing devices part 14 - voice access part 15 - voice typing part 16 - on-screen keyboard part 17 - sticky keys, filter keys, and toggle keys part 18 - mouse keys part 19 - touch and pen accessibility part 20 - eye control part 21 - focus, notifications, and visual clutter part 22 - accessibility flyout and sign-in screen part 23 - windows hello and easier sign-in part 24 - combining features safely part 25 - privacy and security part 26 - troubleshooting part 27 - independent practice course part 28 - quick reference part 29 - official microsoft resources part 1 - windows 11 accessibility overview windows 11 groups accessibility settings into broad areas for vision, hearing, and interaction. microsoft also provides tools for focus and cognitive accessibility. vision: text size, visual effects, mouse pointer and touch, text cursor, magnifier, color filters, contrast themes, and narrator. hearing: audio settings, visual alternatives to sounds, captions, and hearing-device support. interaction: speech, keyboard, mouse, and eye control. focus: notification timing, reduced animation, taskbar simplification, and other distraction-reduction settings. part 2 - open and navigate accessibility settings 2.1 open accessibility settings what you will learn: reach the central windows accessibility hub quickly. before you begin: windows 11 is running. exactly how to do it press windows+u. wait for settings to open. press tab once or more until the accessibility categories/settings are announced or visibly focused. use up/down arrow through available accessibility pages when focus is in the navigation list. press enter on the category you want. press shift+tab or alt+left arrow to return when needed. what should happen: settings > accessibility opens. if that does not happen: if another app receives u instead, make sure the windows key is held down. practice: open accessibility, enter magnifier, return, then enter keyboard. search alternative: press windows, type the name of a feature such as 'live captions' or 'magnifier settings,' then press enter on the matching settings result. part 3 - text size and visual effects 3.1 increase text size without enlarging everything what you will learn: make text easier to read while keeping overall screen layout similar. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it open text size. move to the text size slider. increase the percentage gradually. use the preview area to judge the result. activate apply. wait for windows to update text. what should happen: text becomes larger across supported windows interfaces without applying full-screen magnification. if that does not happen: if controls become crowded, reduce the percentage and reapply. practice: try one moderate increase and restore it if not useful. 3.2 reduce animation and transparency what you will learn: reduce motion and visual distraction. before you begin: open accessibility > visual effects. exactly how to do it find animation effects. turn it off if movement is distracting. find transparency effects. turn it off if translucent backgrounds reduce readability. review notification-dismiss timing on the same page when available. what should happen: windows uses fewer animations and/or more solid backgrounds. if that does not happen: some apps have their own animation settings and may not follow every windows preference. practice: toggle each setting and compare. part 4 - mouse pointer and touch 4.1 make the mouse pointer easier to see what you will learn: increase pointer size or use a more visible pointer style. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it open mouse pointer and touch. move to the pointer-size slider. increase size gradually. move to mouse pointer style. choose white, black, inverted, or another visible style. if offered, choose a custom pointer color. what should happen: the pointer becomes easier to locate. if that does not happen: if the pointer is too large and covers controls, reduce its size. practice: try two sizes and two pointer styles. touch indicator: on touch-capable devices, windows can show a visual touch indicator so finger contact is easier to see. part 5 - text cursor 5.1 make the text cursor easier to find what you will learn: add a visible indicator around the insertion caret. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it open text cursor. turn text cursor indicator on. adjust the indicator size. choose a high-visibility color. adjust text cursor thickness if needed. open notepad and type a sentence to test the caret. what should happen: the insertion point is easier to locate in supported text fields. if that does not happen: if the indicator is distracting, reduce size or turn it off while retaining a thicker cursor. practice: test in notepad and a browser edit field. part 6 - magnifier task command / path turn magnifier on windows+plus turn magnifier off windows+escape zoom in / out windows+plus / windows+minus open magnifier settings windows+ctrl+m pan ctrl+alt+arrow keys invert colors ctrl+alt+i 6.1 start and control magnifier what you will learn: enlarge screen content quickly. before you begin: windows is running. exactly how to do it press windows+plus. press windows+plus again to increase magnification. press windows+minus to reduce magnification. use ctrl+alt+arrow keys to pan if your current magnifier view supports it. press windows+escape to turn magnifier off. what should happen: the screen enlarges and then returns to normal. if that does not happen: if the keyboard has a layout where plus requires shift, hold windows and press the key that produces plus. practice: turn magnifier on, change zoom twice, then turn it off. 6.2 choose a magnifier view what you will learn: select the magnification style that fits the task. before you begin: magnifier is on. exactly how to do it press windows+ctrl+m. move to view. choose full screen, len
